p0.title: Earth's systems
p0.description: How sunlight, water, carbon, nutrients, rock and life work together as one system. Filled in level by level by people and their AI agents.

boundary.start: Energy from the Sun, and heat from the Earth's interior, flows into the Earth system and sets its water, carbon, nutrient, rock and life cycles in motion.
boundary.end: Energy leaves as heat to space, while matter stays and cycles: what living things and rock return to the air, water and soil feeds the next turn of the cycles.

p1.title: Energy flow
p1.description: How sunlight enters the Earth system, is reflected, absorbed and sent back out, and how heat moves around the planet through the air and oceans.

p2.title: Water cycle
p2.description: How water moves between oceans, air, land and ice: evaporation and transpiration, clouds and rain, rivers and groundwater, snow and ice.

p3.title: Carbon cycling
p3.description: How carbon moves between the air, oceans, living things, soil and rock, and how burning fossil fuels adds to the air.

p4.title: Nutrient cycling
p4.description: How nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients are taken up by living things, returned by decay, and gained or lost through air, water and rock.

p5.title: Geological cycling
p5.description: How rock is made, moved and destroyed over millions of years: plate tectonics and volcanism, weathering and erosion, and the rock cycle.

p6.title: Biological processes
p6.description: How living things capture energy, grow, die and interact: photosynthesis and respiration, life in the ocean, biodiversity, and the land ecosystems that include living soil.

p8.title: Living soil system
p8.description: The living soil: weathered minerals, organic matter, water, gases, roots and organisms interacting to build structure, cycle nutrients and carbon, and exchange water, gases, dust and solutes with the atmosphere, ocean and geology.

p9.title: Plate tectonics and volcanism
p9.description: Layer 1 geology: plate motion, subduction, volcanism and outgassing that deliver carbon, sulfur and water to the surface and drive the long-term carbon cycle.

p10.title: Weathering, erosion and sediment transport
p10.description: Layer 1 geology: chemical and physical weathering of rock, erosion, and river and wind transport of sediment, which supply solutes to the ocean and sediment to basins.

p11.title: Rock cycle: burial, lithification, metamorphism and melting
p11.description: The geological leg of the rock cycle: sediment burial and lithification, metamorphism and partial melting when heat and pressure rise enough, and uplift that re-exposes rock at the surface.

p12.title: Mineral weathering and parent material
p12.description: How rock and parent material break down physically and chemically into soil minerals, releasing nutrients and forming secondary clays and oxides. Covers carbonic acid, hydrolysis, oxidation, organic acid attack and the rates that climate and biology set.

p13.title: Cation exchange, pH and soil solution chemistry
p13.description: How charged clay and humus surfaces hold exchangeable cations and set soil pH and solution chemistry. Covers acidification, buffering, base cation loss, aluminium, salinity and the nutrient availability that results.

p14.title: Aggregate formation and pore structure
p14.description: How roots, hyphae, polysaccharides, oxides and fauna bind particles into aggregates that give soil its pore network. Covers the hierarchy of micro- and macroaggregates and the forces that break them down.

p15.title: Water infiltration, retention and movement
p15.description: How rain enters, is held in and moves through soil. Covers infiltration versus runoff, retention by matric potential, drainage, root uptake and evaporation, and the wet, optimal and dry states.

p16.title: Soil gas exchange and redox
p16.description: How oxygen and carbon dioxide move through soil pores and how the supply of oxygen sets redox state. Covers aerobic and anaerobic respiration, denitrification, methane production and oxidation, and reduced metal chemistry.

p17.title: Nutrient availability and leaching
p17.description: How nutrients are held, released, taken up and lost in soil. Covers mineralisation, nitrification, phosphate sorption, immobilisation, nitrate leaching and denitrification, and atmospheric inputs.

p18.title: Biological coupling: organic matter and soil food web
p18.description: How plant litter, roots, fungi, bacteria and fauna together decompose organic matter and build stable soil carbon. Covers the soil food web and the disturbance forks that tip soil toward carbon gain or loss.

p19.title: Primary production
p19.description: Fixation of solar energy and carbon dioxide into plant biomass by photosynthesis, the base of terrestrial food webs, constrained by light, water and nutrients.

p20.title: Energy transfer through food webs
p20.description: Transfer of energy and carbon from plants to herbivores, predators and decomposers through food webs, with large losses as heat at each step.

p21.title: Decomposition
p21.description: Breakdown of dead plant and animal material by fragmentation, leaching and microbial enzymes, releasing CO2 and mineral nutrients and forming soil organic matter.

p22.title: Terrestrial nutrient cycling
p22.description: Uptake of nutrients by plants, return in litter, mineralization by decomposers and loss by leaching or gases in terrestrial ecosystems.

p23.title: Soil formation
p23.description: Layer 2 soil formation from parent material, climate, organisms, relief and time, covering regolith production, organic matter accumulation and horizon differentiation.

p24.title: Water movement
p24.description: How water moves through the terrestrial ecosystem: infiltration into soil, uptake by roots and transpiration, and drainage, runoff and evaporation, which set water supply to plants and streams.

p25.title: Weathering
p25.description: Layer 2 weathering of rock in terrestrial ecosystems by physical, carbonic-acid and biological pathways, releasing mineral nutrients and producing the regolith that becomes soil.

p26.title: Organism-environment interactions
p26.description: How organisms shape and respond to their physical surroundings: ecosystem engineers, plant-soil feedbacks, fire, snow and drought, and how those feed back to climate.

p27.title: Roots and rhizosphere
p27.description: Roots release carbon (exudates, mucilage, sloughed cells) into the soil around them, which feeds and selects microbes, shifts pH, mobilizes phosphorus and iron, and glues particles into the rhizosheath. Depletion zones and nutrient demand feed back on how much carbon the roots release.

p28.title: Mycorrhizal fungi network
p28.description: Mycorrhizal fungi colonize roots and extend hyphae into soil, trading phosphorus, nitrogen and water for plant carbon. The network also binds aggregates, links neighbouring plants and returns fungal necromass to soil carbon.

p29.title: Saprotrophic fungi
p29.description: Saprotrophic fungi colonize litter, secrete cellulases and ligninolytic enzymes, and move nutrients through mycelium. Their respiration, biomass turnover and grazing losses return carbon dioxide, nutrients and chitin-rich necromass to soil.

p30.title: Bacteria and archaea
p30.description: Soil bacteria and archaea consume dissolved substrates and drive nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorus, iron and methane transformations according to oxygen supply. Their biomass, polysaccharides and necromass feed aggregation and soil organic matter.

p31.title: Soil fauna
p31.description: Soil fauna from earthworms and termites to mites, nematodes and protozoa fragment litter, graze microbes, burrow and excrete nutrients. They regulate decomposition, mineralize nitrogen and create pores and aggregates.

p32.title: Soil food web energy transfer
p32.description: Carbon and energy from litter and root exudates move through fungal, bacterial and root channels to grazers and predators, losing most energy to respiration at each step. Excretion and dead matter return nutrients and detritus to the soil.

p33.title: Organic matter decomposition
p33.description: Litter is leached, fragmented and depolymerized by extracellular enzymes, then microbes take up the products and split the carbon between respiration and growth. Litter quality, moisture, temperature and priming set the rate and the nitrogen outcome.

p34.title: Humification and SOM stabilization
p34.description: Decomposition products and microbial necromass are stabilized as particulate organic matter, mineral-associated organic matter, occluded carbon in aggregates or pyrogenic carbon. Destabilization by disturbance, warming and low oxygen can release this persistent carbon.

p36.title: Marine biological pump and ocean life

p41.title: Surface heat release
p41.description: How absorbed sunlight warms Earth's surface and how the surface sheds that heat by latent heat of evaporation, sensible heat to the air and net infrared radiation, loading the atmosphere with heat.

p42.title: Greenhouse trapping and release to space

p44.title: Heat redistribution by air and ocean
p44.description: How the tropical energy surplus is carried to the poles by atmospheric winds and storms and by ocean currents, until polar regions radiate the heat to space.

p45.title: Evaporation and transpiration
p45.description: How liquid water becomes vapour at Earth's surface, by ocean evaporation and by land transpiration and soil or canopy evaporation, absorbing latent heat and mixing vapour into the lower atmosphere.

p47.title: Land water: infiltration, runoff and groundwater
p47.description: What happens to precipitation that reaches land: evapotranspiration back to the air, infiltration into soil and aquifers, slow groundwater flow, and river transport of water, sediment and dissolved nutrients to the sea.

p48.title: Snow, ice and meltwater storage
p48.description: Storage of water as snow and ice in cold regions, its high albedo, centuries-long residence in ice sheets, and the seasonal meltwater that feeds rivers and soils.

p49.title: Enzymatic depolymerization of plant polymers
p49.description: Microbes release extracellular cellulases, proteases, phosphatases and oxidases that cut plant polymers into monomers they can take up. Enzyme production is regulated by supply and demand, and enzymes can sorb to minerals or be lost.

p52.title: Biological uptake, litter return and mineralization
p52.description: How plants take up nutrients, allocate and resorb them, and return the remainder in litter, followed by decomposition that either mineralizes nutrients for reuse or immobilizes them in microbial biomass.

p53.title: Mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) formation
p53.description: Dissolved organic matter and microbial products reach mineral surfaces and bind by ligand exchange, cation bridging or weak adsorption, forming layered organo-mineral complexes. Binding capacity is limited by clay and iron oxide content and can be reversed by desorption or microbial mining.

p54.title: Occlusion in aggregates
p54.description: Clay flocculation, roots, hyphae, polysaccharides and earthworm casts bind particles into aggregates that enclose organic matter and shield it from decomposers. Wetting-drying, raindrops, slaking and tillage break aggregates and expose the carbon.

p55.title: Soil sulfur cycling
p55.description: How sulfur enters soil, cycles among organic, sulfate and sulfide forms and leaves by leaching, uptake or gas emission.

p56.title: Nitrification-driven acidification of ammonium fertilised soil
p56.description: How nitrification of ammonium fertiliser releases hydrogen ions, and how nitrate uptake, leaching and buffering determine whether the soil acidifies.

p57.title: Denitrification chain in anaerobic microsites
p57.description: The stepwise reduction of nitrate to nitrite, nitric oxide, nitrous oxide and dinitrogen in oxygen-poor soil microsites by denitrifying bacteria.

p58.title: Slaking, crust formation and runoff
p58.description: How raindrops slake aggregates and form a surface crust that cuts infiltration and raises runoff and erosion.

p59.title: Silicate weathering rate control and CO2 drawdown
p59.description: How temperature, runoff and mineral supply set the rate at which silicate minerals dissolve and consume atmospheric carbon dioxide as bicarbonate. Includes the long-term climate thermostat that results.

p60.title: Soil CO2 and biotic enhancement of weathering
p60.description: How roots, mycorrhizal fungi and microbes raise soil carbon dioxide and release organic acids that speed mineral dissolution and nutrient release from rock.

p61.title: Pedogenic age sequence: from apatite phosphorus to occluded phosphorus
p61.description: How soil phosphorus changes over thousands to millions of years from primary apatite to organic, sorbed and finally occluded forms, shifting ecosystems from nitrogen to phosphorus limitation.

p62.title: Soil production and erosion balance
p62.description: The balance between soil production from bedrock and soil loss by erosion, which sets soil thickness and the age of the soil surface.

p63.title: Base cation cycling (calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium)
p63.description: How calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium are supplied by weathering and deposition, held on exchange sites, taken up by plants and leached.

p64.title: Clay mineralogy and organic matter set cation exchange capacity
p64.description: How the type of clay mineral and the amount of organic matter set the total cation exchange capacity of a soil.

p65.title: Sequential soil pH buffer systems
p65.description: How soil pH is held in turn by carbonate, silicate and exchange, aluminium and iron oxide buffer systems, each active over its own pH range.

p66.title: Macroaggregate turnover and microaggregate formation
p66.description: How macroaggregates form and break down on a cycle of months to years and release microaggregates that hold organic matter.

p67.title: Iron redox cycling and the enzyme latch in wet soil
p67.description: How iron-reducing bacteria and oxygen cycle iron between Fe3+ and Fe2+ in wet soil, and how this links to phenol accumulation and slow decomposition in peat.

p68.title: Soil nitrogen mineralization and immobilization turnover
p68.description: Cycle of nitrogen between organic matter, microbial biomass and mineral ammonium. Decomposers mineralize organic N when the substrate is N-rich and immobilize mineral N when it is carbon-rich, setting what plants can take up.

p69.title: Root exudate chemistry, fate and priming
p69.description: Roots release sugars, amino acids, organic anions and signalling compounds by passive and active efflux. The exudates are mostly taken up by microbes within hours, with smaller shares re-absorbed by roots, sorbed to minerals or leached.

p70.title: Exudate priming and microbial nitrogen mining
p70.description: A pulse of labile carbon from roots activates microbes, which may mine native organic matter for nitrogen and respire extra soil carbon (positive priming) or switch to the easy substrate (negative priming). Plant nitrogen uptake and microbial nitrogen limitation feed back on the process.

p71.title: Mycorrhizal nutrient trade: phosphorus, nitrogen and carbon market
p71.description: Fungal hyphae take up phosphorus and nitrogen and deliver them to the root at arbuscules, while the plant pays hexoses and fatty acids. The outcome ranges from mutualism to parasitism depending on soil phosphorus and light, and plant phosphorus status regulates the payment.

p72.title: Reciprocal reward and sanctioning
p72.description: Plants and fungi reward partners who deliver more and penalize poor ones: plants give more carbon to roots hosting generous fungi and fungi give more phosphorus to roots paying more carbon. Arbuscules of low-delivery partners degenerate.

p73.title: Soil nitrification, nitrate reduction and nitrogen gas losses
p73.description: Fate of ammonium and nitrate in soil: ammonia oxidizers and nitrite oxidizers make nitrate, which denitrifiers reduce to N2O and N2 in oxygen-poor microsites, and anammox and nitrifier denitrification add further gas losses.

p74.title: Clay mineral transformation sequence
p74.description: The stepwise transformation of clay minerals, for example mica to vermiculite to smectite to kaolinite, as weathering removes potassium and silica.

p75.title: Redox ladder: sequential electron acceptors in waterlogged soil
p75.description: The order in which microbes use electron acceptors when oxygen is gone: nitrate, then manganese and iron, then sulfate, then carbon dioxide.

p76.title: Preferential flow and macropore bypass
p76.description: How continuous macropores let water and solutes bypass the soil matrix during intense rain, carrying nitrate and pesticides rapidly to depth.

p77.title: Freeze-thaw cycling and soil structure
p77.description: How repeated freezing and thawing and ice lens growth break or reorganise soil aggregates and pores.

p78.title: Bioturbation: fauna remodel soil structure
p78.description: How earthworms, ants, termites and burrowing mammals mix soil and create burrows and casts that remodel structure, pores and organic matter distribution.

p79.title: Biochar and charcoal in soil
p79.description: How biochar and charcoal persist in soil, change pH, water and nutrient retention, and affect microbes and carbon storage.

p80.title: Salinity and sodicity
p80.description: How soluble salts and sodium accumulate in soil, raise osmotic stress and disperse clay, and how leaching or amendments reverse it.

p81.title: Carbon priming, microbial efficiency and soil carbon sequestration
p81.description: How labile carbon inputs prime decomposition of older organic matter, and how microbial carbon use efficiency decides whether carbon ends up as CO2 or stable microbial residues and mineral-bound carbon.

p82.title: Pedogenesis and soil horizon development
p82.description: Slow formation of soil horizons from parent material under climate, organisms, relief and time. Inputs, losses, transformations and translocations produce the O, A, E, B and C layers and pathways such as podzolization and lessivage.

p83.title: Predator-prey nitrogen release (microbial loop)
p83.description: Protozoa and bacterivorous nematodes graze N-rich bacteria and excrete the nitrogen they do not need as ammonium near roots (the microbial loop). Grazing also keeps bacteria growing and shapes the bacterial community.

p84.title: Predator-prey oscillation of bacteria and grazers
p84.description: Short-term population cycle in which bacteria grow on a fresh substrate pulse, protozoa follow with a lag of days, grazing cuts bacterial numbers, and protozoa encyst until substrate returns. Damps into a stable ratio of prey to grazer.

p85.title: Enzyme kinetics: Michaelis-Menten rates and temperature response
p85.description: How extracellular enzyme rates follow Michaelis-Menten saturation with substrate and Arrhenius-type rise with temperature. Sets the speed at which polymers are cut into units microbes can absorb.

p86.title: Ecoenzymatic stoichiometry: matching enzymes to nutrient limitation
p86.description: How soil microbes adjust the mix of carbon-, nitrogen- and phosphorus-acquiring enzymes to the nutrient they lack. Global enzyme activity ratios sit near 1:1:1, and deviations signal nitrogen or phosphorus limitation.

p87.title: Microbial necromass pathway to stable organic matter
p87.description: Dead microbial cells release labile cytoplasm while cell wall remnants such as chitin, peptidoglycan and melanin persist. Necromass is recycled, sorbed to minerals, entombed in aggregates, or lost as carbon dioxide and dissolved carbon.

p88.title: Carbon use efficiency controls necromass production
p88.description: Carbon use efficiency sets how much taken-up carbon becomes biomass and necromass rather than carbon dioxide. Substrate quality, nutrient limitation and temperature change it, with warming and acclimation shaping the soil carbon response.

p89.title: Soil disturbance (fire, tillage, drought) and recovery
p89.description: How fire, tillage and drought damage soil structure, organic matter and microbial communities, and the recovery steps that follow. Shows reinforcing degradation loops and the balancing processes that rebuild structure.

p90.title: Soil-plant-water coupling and drought response
p90.description: Coupling between soil water, roots and plant water status during drought. Covers soil drying, falling hydraulic conductivity at the root-soil interface, stomatal closure, hydraulic redistribution and recovery after rain.

p91.title: Biological nitrogen fixation: nitrogenase, oxygen protection and regulation
p91.description: How diazotrophic bacteria and archaea convert atmospheric N2 to ammonia with the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase enzyme, in free-living, associative and nodule-symbiotic forms. It covers the energy cost, oxygen protection, metal cofactor limits and feedback that switch fixation off when mineral nitrogen is plentiful.

p92.title: Methane oxidation by methanotrophs: the upland soil sink
p92.description: How aerobic methane-oxidising bacteria in the upper soil consume atmospheric and locally produced methane using particulate methane monooxygenase. It covers the high-affinity and low-affinity guilds, diffusion and moisture control, ammonium inhibition, land-use legacy and the global soil sink.

p93.title: Actinomycetes: Streptomyces hyphal life cycle, extracellular enzymes and antibiotics
p93.description: The filamentous Gram-positive actinomycetes (mostly Streptomyces) that grow as branching mycelium in soil, degrade chitin and cellulose, make antibiotics and geosmin, and survive drought as spores. It also covers nitrogen-fixing Frankia in actinorhizal nodules.

p94.title: Atmospheric dust deposition and loess as soil parent material
p94.description: Wind-blown mineral dust from deserts and glacial outwash settles on land and ocean, adding fine parent material (loess), base cations and phosphorus to soils and iron to the sea.

p95.title: Wind erosion and dust emission from dry soil
p95.description: Dry, bare soil emits dust when wind exceeds a threshold, removing the finest and most nutrient-rich fraction and sending it to the atmosphere.

p96.title: Soil-atmosphere exchange of methane and nitrous oxide
p96.description: Aerated soils oxidise atmospheric methane while nitrification and denitrification in the same soils emit nitrous oxide, so soil is both a small sink and a large source of greenhouse gases.

p97.title: Soil export to rivers and ocean: sediment, dissolved carbon and nutrients
p97.description: Water leaving soil carries particles, dissolved organic carbon, nitrate and phosphorus to streams, rivers and the coast, linking the soil to the ocean carbon and nutrient cycles.

p98.title: Soil viruses and bacteriophages: lysis, lysogeny and the viral shunt
p98.description: How bacteriophages and other soil viruses infect bacterial and archaeal hosts, either killing them (lytic) or integrating as prophage (lysogenic), and how their lysate returns carbon and nitrogen to the microbial pool. It covers host resistance and coevolution, phage-encoded metabolic genes, and clay adsorption.

p99.title: Pyrite oxidation and acid sulfate weathering
p99.description: Iron sulfide (pyrite) exposed to Oxygen by drainage or excavation oxidises to sulfuric acid, which dissolves clays and mobilises Al, until carbonate or exchangeable bases neutralise it. Describes the Fe3+ and Acidithiobacillus feedback that makes the reaction self-accelerating below pH 4.

p100.title: Volcanic ash weathering to allophane and imogolite (andic soils)
p100.description: Volcanic glass weathers within centuries in humid climates to nanoscale allophane, imogolite or Al-humus complexes, which give andic soils very low bulk density, high phosphate retention and large organic carbon stocks.

p101.title: Pedogenic carbonate accumulation and calcrete formation
p101.description: In dry climates Ca from dust and rain re-precipitates as calcite when soil water is lost by evapotranspiration, forming nodules and then cemented calcic horizons at the mean depth of wetting. The carbonate buffers pH near 8 and stores inorganic carbon.

p102.title: Phosphate sorption on Fe and Al oxides and phosphorus availability
p102.description: Phosphate from solution binds to Fe and Al oxide surfaces by ligand exchange, first fast and then through slow diffusion into the oxide, until little remains available to plants. Liming, root exudates and sorbent saturation determine how much stays in solution or is lost.

p103.title: Aluminium toxicity and liming of acid soils
p103.description: Below about pH 5 Al3+ dominates the exchange complex, buffers pH through hydrolysis and damages root tips at micromolar concentrations. Lime neutralises acid and displaces Al3+, but acid inputs and base removal slowly bring the problem back.

p104.title: Biofilms and quorum signalling in soil microcolonies
p104.description: How soil bacteria attach to particles and roots, embed themselves in an extracellular polymer matrix, and use diffusible signals such as acyl-homoserine lactones to coordinate gene expression when signal accumulates. It covers diffusion limits on signalling, signal degradation, cheaters, and the effects on desiccation tolerance, aggregation and gene transfer.

p105.title: Biological nitrogen fixation: free-living and symbiotic
p105.description: How diazotrophic bacteria and archaea turn atmospheric dinitrogen into ammonia with nitrogenase, what they need (energy, molybdenum, low oxygen), and how fixed nitrogen is returned to soil. Covers the carbon cost to host plants and the nitrate feedback that throttles fixation.

p106.title: Rhizobia-legume signalling and nodule formation
p106.description: The molecular dialogue that makes a nitrogen-fixing nodule: flavonoids from the root, Nod factors from the bacterium, infection threads, bacteroid differentiation, and the plant controls that cap nodule number and sanction poor partners.

p107.title: Methane cycle: methanogenesis and methanotrophy
p107.description: Where soil methane comes from and where it goes. Methanogenic archaea make CH4 in strictly anoxic microsites after other electron acceptors are used up, and methanotrophs oxidize it in oxic zones; the balance sets whether a soil is a methane source or sink.

p108.title: Viral shunt: phage lysis recycles bacterial carbon and nitrogen
p108.description: How bacteriophages kill soil bacteria and release their cell contents as dissolved organic matter that other microbes re-use. Includes the lytic versus lysogenic choice, viral genes that boost host metabolism, and the density-dependent control of dominant strains.

p109.title: Microbial dormancy, the seed bank and reactivation after rewetting
p109.description: Most soil microbial cells are dormant at any moment. This subprocess traces how starvation and drying push cells into dormancy, how a seed bank preserves diversity, and how rewetting or substrate pulses wake cells and produce a respiration flush.

p110.title: Permafrost thaw and release of frozen soil carbon
p110.description: Frozen high-latitude soils hold a very large carbon stock; warming deepens the seasonally thawed layer, letting microbes decompose old organic matter and release carbon dioxide or methane.

p111.title: Peat accumulation and wetland methane
p111.description: Waterlogged organic soils accumulate peat because decomposition is slower than plant production, while anaerobic microbes in the same soils release methane to the atmosphere.

p112.title: Soil inorganic carbon: pedogenic carbonate formation and dissolution
p112.description: In dry soils dissolved calcium and bicarbonate precipitate as calcium carbonate at the depth of wetting, storing carbon for thousands of years until acidification or irrigation dissolves it.

p113.title: Volcanic ash parent material, short-range-order minerals and Andosol carbon
p113.description: Volcanic ash weathers quickly into poorly crystalline minerals such as allophane and ferrihydrite that bind organic matter and phosphate strongly, giving Andosols very high carbon storage and phosphorus fixation.

p114.title: Microbial dormancy, the seed bank and resuscitation
p114.description: How most soil microbial cells sit in a dormant state, entering it by sporulation or reversible metabolic shutdown under starvation or drying, and how wetting, substrate pulses and resuscitation factors wake them in sequence. It covers the active fraction, the seed-bank effect on diversity, relic DNA, and the Birch effect pulse.

p115.title: Soil compaction and loss of macroporosity
p115.description: Wheel or hoof loads above the soil's precompression stress, worst when wet, collapse the largest pores, raise bulk density and strength, and cut air and water flow. Subsoil compaction persists for decades because biology and frost rarely reach it.

p116.title: Shrink-swell cracking and self-mulching in smectitic soils
p116.description: In soils with 30 percent or more smectite-rich clay, drying shrinks the matrix into deep cracks, surface crumbs fall in, and wetting swells the soil shut again. This churns the profile (self-mulching, slickensides) and controls infiltration and gas exchange.

p117.title: Soil evaporation stages and capillary rise from shallow groundwater
p117.description: Bare soil loses water first at the atmosphere's demand rate (stage I) and then far more slowly as a dry surface layer limits vapour diffusion (stage II). Shallow groundwater can resupply the surface by capillary rise, but also carries salts upward.

p118.title: Plant-available water from field capacity to wilting point
p118.description: Water held in pores between about -10 kPa (field capacity) and -1.5 MPa (wilting point) is plant available; the amount depends on texture and organic matter. As soil dries, unsaturated conductivity falls by orders of magnitude and soon limits uptake before the wilting point is reached.

p119.title: Soil respiration: temperature and moisture control and climate feedback
p119.description: Soil CO2 efflux is about 98 Pg C per year and responds to temperature (Q10 about 1.5 to 3) and to water-filled pore space (optimum near 60 percent). Warming increases CO2 release and creates a positive climate feedback, partly limited by substrate depletion.

p120.title: Aerenchyma, radial oxygen loss and the oxidised rhizosphere of wetland plants
p120.description: In waterlogged soil, where oxygen diffuses about ten thousand times slower than in air, wetland plants such as rice carry oxygen through air-filled aerenchyma to the roots, and some leaks into the soil. This creates a thin oxic zone that precipitates iron plaque, detoxifies reduced compounds and couples nitrification to denitrification.

p121.title: Nitrate leaching from the root zone to groundwater and coastal waters
p121.description: Nitrate, a mobile anion not held by negatively charged soil, is flushed out of the root zone by autumn and winter drainage, reaching drains, groundwater and rivers. Cover crops and riparian buffers cut the load, but the nitrogen that reaches rivers drives coastal hypoxia.

p122.title: Micronutrient availability: pH, redox and plant mobilisation of Fe and Zn
p122.description: Iron, zinc, manganese and copper become far less soluble as pH rises (iron about 1000-fold per pH unit) but more soluble under waterlogging. Plants counter low availability with rhizosphere acidification, reduction and chelators, and about half of the world's cereal soils are low in zinc.

p123.title: Nematode feeding groups, the c-p scale and nitrogen release
p123.description: Soil nematodes live in water films and sort into trophic groups (bacterial feeders, fungal feeders, omnivore-predators, plant parasites, insect parasites) that differ in life history and disturbance tolerance. The process covers pore access, nitrogen release from grazing, trapping fungi, drying survival, and the nematode maturity index used to diagnose the food web.

p124.title: Nematode feeding guilds and control of root feeders
p124.description: Soil nematodes split into bacterial feeders, fungal feeders, plant parasites, omnivores and predators. This subprocess shows how each guild affects nitrogen release or root damage, how natural enemies hold plant parasites in check, and how nematode community indices read disturbance.

p125.title: Springtail and mite grazing of fungi: stimulation, defence and dispersal
p125.description: Collembola and oribatid mites graze fungal hyphae. Moderate grazing stimulates fungal regrowth and nitrogen release, heavy grazing cuts hyphal biomass, fungi defend with secondary metabolites, and grazers spread spores and bacteria.

p126.title: Earthworm gut passage, casts and the drilosphere
p126.description: What happens as earthworms ingest soil: gut mucus primes microbes, the anoxic gut hosts denitrifiers that emit nitrous oxide, fresh casts are nutrient-rich, aged casts protect carbon, and burrow walls form a biologically active zone that raises plant production.

p127.title: Disease-suppressive soils and the rhizosphere cry for help
p127.description: How a root microbiome protects plants from soil-borne pathogens: infected plants recruit antagonists through exudates, Pseudomonas that make DAPG and siderophores suppress pathogens, resident microbes compete generally, and rhizobacteria prime plant defences.

p128.title: Rhizosphere phosphorus mobilization: phosphatases, organic acids and fast re-sorption
p128.description: How roots and microbes free phosphorus that is bound in organic molecules and sorbed to iron and aluminium oxides. Low phosphate triggers phosphatases and organic acid release; released phosphate is re-sorbed within hours unless taken up, and rising supply switches the response off.

p129.title: Microarthropods: springtails and oribatid mites as fungal grazers and litter processors
p129.description: Springtails (Collembola) and mites (Oribatida, Mesostigmata) live in the air-filled pores and litter of the upper soil, graze fungi, break down litter and make faecal pellets. The process covers feeding guilds, grazing effects on fungal activity and mycorrhizal networks, slow versus fast life histories, predator control and nitrogen release.

p130.title: Matric potential and the soil water retention curve
p130.description: How capillary and adsorptive forces hold water at negative pressure in pores of different size, producing a retention curve that links water content to suction and sets field capacity, wilting point and plant-available water.

p131.title: Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity and Richards flow
p131.description: How the flux of liquid water in soil follows the Buckingham-Darcy law, with hydraulic conductivity falling by orders of magnitude as pores drain, controlling infiltration, redistribution and the supply of water to roots.

p132.title: Soil evaporation stages and vapour transport
p132.description: Evaporation from bare or lightly covered soil runs through an energy-limited wet stage, a liquid-supply-limited falling-rate stage and a vapour-diffusion stage, with latent cooling and thermal vapour flow coupling water and heat.

p133.title: Capillary rise from shallow groundwater and salt accumulation
p133.description: Water tables within a metre or two of the surface can resupply the root zone by capillary rise, but evaporation concentrates dissolved salts near the surface unless leaching removes them.

p134.title: Earthworm drilosphere: gut passage, casts, middens and greenhouse gas effects
p134.description: What earthworms do to soil biology after ingesting soil and litter: gut mucus wakes dormant microbes, casts and burrow linings form a microbially active zone (the drilosphere), and casts either stabilise carbon, are re-eaten or release nitrogen gases. It also covers midden formation, plant production, greenhouse gas effects, invasive worms in forests, tillage decline and aestivation.

p135.title: Gas diffusion and air-filled porosity control of soil aeration
p135.description: Gas moves through soil mainly by diffusion in connected air-filled pores, so air-filled porosity and pore connectivity set how fast oxygen is resupplied and how fast carbon dioxide and trace gases escape.

p136.title: Soil thermal regime and heat flow
p136.description: How net radiation becomes heat that conducts through soil, with water content, snow and depth controlling temperature, and how soil temperature in turn sets microbial rates and the stability of frozen carbon.

p137.title: Shrink-swell cycles and crack dynamics in clay soils
p137.description: In soils rich in smectite, repeated wetting and drying swells and shrinks the soil, opening and closing cracks that route water, shear the profile into slickensides and mix material between layers.

p138.title: Soil compaction: stress, density, root limitation and recovery
p138.description: Wheel and hoof loads press soil into a denser state, closing macropores, raising strength and cutting infiltration and aeration, with effects that persist for years in the subsoil and are only slowly reversed by freeze-thaw, roots and fauna.

p139.title: Soil protists: flagellates, amoebae and ciliates as selective bacterial grazers
p139.description: Single-celled protists in soil water films graze bacteria and each other. Flagellates, naked amoebae and ciliates differ in where and what they eat, they graze selectively, bacteria evolve defences, and grazing shifts community composition, releases nitrogen and can change root growth. Cysts carry them through drying.

p140.title: White-rot and brown-rot fungi: two routes to lignin and cellulose decay
p140.description: How wood and litter fungi attack lignified plant material. White-rot fungi use peroxidases and laccases to oxidize lignin; brown-rot fungi use Fenton chemistry to depolymerize cellulose and leave modified lignin. Mineral nitrogen from decomposition feeds back by repressing ligninolytic enzymes.

p141.title: Cord-forming mycelial networks: foraging, translocation and rerouting
p141.description: How wood-decay fungi that form cords and rhizomorphs search for new litter, thicken links to food, move carbon and nutrients between patches, prune unused links, and reroute flow when the network is grazed or cut.

p142.title: Ectomycorrhizal organic nitrogen mining and the Gadgil effect
p142.description: How ectomycorrhizal fungi pull nitrogen out of soil organic matter with peroxidases and proteases, how that can starve free-living decomposers and slow carbon turnover (the Gadgil effect, a contested idea), and how this shapes soil carbon storage in ectomycorrhizal forests.

p143.title: Common mycorrhizal networks: what the evidence supports and what it does not
p143.description: Whether fungal networks connecting trees move meaningful carbon and nutrients between plants. Lists the isotope and seedling-survival experiments that support transfer and the recent re-examinations that find the strongest claims weakly supported.

p144.title: Biological soil crusts: cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses on dryland surfaces
p144.description: Living surface skins of cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses in drylands. They bind particles, fix nitrogen and carbon, trap dust, change infiltration, and are slow to recover when trampled or burned.

p145.title: Predatory bacteria: Bdellovibrio and Myxococcus hunting soil prey
p145.description: Two predatory bacterial lifestyles in soil: Bdellovibrio-like organisms that invade the periplasm of Gram-negative prey and consume them from within, and myxobacteria such as Myxococcus xanthus that hunt in groups, lyse prey outside the cell and form spore-filled fruiting bodies when starved. The process covers attack, prey escape, spores and nutrient release.

p146.title: Wind erosion: saltation, dust emission and deposition
p146.description: Wind detaches and moves soil particles when friction velocity exceeds a threshold set by particle size, moisture, aggregates and cover, removing fine nutrient-rich material and delivering dust to distant ecosystems.

p147.title: Mineral surface area, reactive metals and the saturation of mineral-associated carbon
p147.description: What limits how much organic carbon minerals can hold: specific surface area, reactive iron, aluminium and calcium, a layered binding structure and a finite capacity, plus the processes that release bound carbon.

p148.title: Light-use efficiency control of gross primary production
p148.description: How much carbon a canopy fixes per unit of absorbed light, and how sky conditions (direct versus diffuse light) change that efficiency.

p149.title: Respiratory losses and carbon-use efficiency
p149.description: How much of gross primary production is respired by leaves, wood and roots, which sets carbon-use efficiency (NPP divided by GPP) and the carbon left for growth.

p150.title: Nutrient limitation of net primary production
p150.description: How nitrogen and phosphorus supply caps plant growth, and how nitrogen fixation and nutrient losses shape which element limits production over time.

p151.title: Litter quality and soil fertility reinforcing loop
p151.description: Plants on poor soils shed slow-decaying, low-nitrogen litter that keeps the soil poor, while plants on fertile soils shed fast-decaying litter that keeps it fertile; a reinforcing plant-soil feedback on nutrient supply.

p152.title: Progressive nitrogen limitation under rising CO2
p152.description: Rising atmospheric CO2 boosts plant growth, which locks more nitrogen in biomass and organic matter and gradually lowers the nitrogen left for growth; plants and fungi can partly compensate by foraging for more soil nitrogen.

p153.title: Nitrogen fixation supply-demand feedback
p153.description: Nitrogen-fixing plants and microbes gain an advantage where soil nitrogen is scarce, add nitrogen to the ecosystem and then lose that advantage as nitrogen accumulates; a balancing loop that tracks nitrogen demand.

p154.title: Nutrient recycling versus new inputs across ecosystem age
p154.description: Young ecosystems live on nutrients supplied by weathering and deposition, whereas old, weathered ecosystems run mostly on tight recycling of nutrients through plants, litter and microbes, with phosphorus gradually occluded.

p155.title: Belowground carbon allocation to roots and mycorrhizal fungi
p155.description: Part of net primary production goes to roots and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi as a carbon payment for nutrient uptake, and this cost shrinks when nutrients are abundant.

p156.title: Trophic transfer efficiency between levels
p156.description: The fraction of energy that passes from one trophic level to the next, which varies with ecosystem type, temperature, consumer physiology and trophic position.

p157.title: Energy channels in the soil food web
p157.description: How plant carbon enters soil food webs through roots, fungi and bacteria, is passed to fauna such as nematodes and earthworms, and returns as mineral nutrients or stored microbial necromass.

p158.title: Predator control of herbivory (trophic cascade)
p158.description: How predators change plant biomass indirectly by reducing herbivore numbers or altering herbivore feeding behavior.

p159.title: Plant-soil feedback and species coexistence
p159.description: Each plant species conditions the soil community beneath it, and that community then helps or harms the next seedlings of the same or other species; negative feedbacks favour coexistence and positive ones favour dominance.

p160.title: Ecosystem engineering feedbacks
p160.description: Organisms that physically change their habitat, such as earthworms, ants, beavers or shrubs, alter resources for themselves and for other species; the effect can reinforce or limit the engineer.

p161.title: Vegetation-water feedback and dryland patchiness
p161.description: In dry lands vegetation raises infiltration of the water that falls, which feeds more vegetation; loss of cover breaks the loop and bare crusted soil sheds water, so ecosystems can flip between vegetated and bare states.

p162.title: Fire-vegetation feedback and savanna-forest states
p162.description: Grass fuel carries fire that keeps trees from closing the canopy, while a closed forest canopy shades out grass and stops fire; the two self-reinforcing states make savanna and forest alternative stable biomes across a wide rainfall range.

p163.title: Vegetation, snow, albedo and carbon feedbacks across scales
p163.description: Plants and soil microbes link small-scale processes to regional and global climate: shrub expansion, snow trapping, darker surfaces, soil warming and carbon release can amplify warming, while vegetation-rain coupling can amplify or damp drought.

p164.title: Controls on net primary production
p164.description: How light, CO2 and nutrients set gross primary production, how much of it plants respire, and how the remainder is allocated above and below ground.

p165.title: Nutrient-driven carbon allocation belowground
p165.description: Plants facing nutrient scarcity send a larger share of new carbon to roots and exudates, which raises nutrient uptake and so photosynthesis.

p166.title: Trophic efficiency and top-down control
p166.description: How much energy each trophic step passes on (around ten percent), how predators change plant biomass, and the parallel detrital channel that eats dead material.

p167.title: Detrital energy channel
p167.description: Most terrestrial plant production is not eaten alive but enters the detrital food web of microbes and soil fauna, where grazing on microbes speeds nutrient turnover.

p168.title: Litter quality, climate and fauna control decay
p168.description: What sets how fast litter is decomposed (chemistry, temperature, moisture, sunlight, fauna) and what fraction of litter carbon is respired versus stabilised in soil.

p169.title: Temperature and moisture regulation of decay
p169.description: Warmth speeds enzyme-driven decay, dryness slows it, and sunlight can break down litter directly in dry ecosystems; the CO2 released feeds back on warming.

p170.title: Nitrogen and phosphorus supply and limitation
p170.description: How soil organic nitrogen is released, how microbes and plants compete for it, and how phosphorus availability declines with soil age and is rescued by plant and microbial strategies.

p171.title: Phosphorus decline and rescue across soil ages
p171.description: As soils age primary-mineral phosphorus is depleted and occluded, shifting ecosystems from nitrogen to phosphorus limitation unless plants and microbes mobilise organic and bound phosphorus.

p172.title: Mycorrhizal carbon-for-nutrient exchange loop
p172.description: Plants pay mycorrhizal fungi with sugars and receive nitrogen and phosphorus in return; extra photosynthate under high CO2 can expand the fungal network and the nutrient supply, up to the point where the fungus itself holds nutrients back.

p173.title: Infiltration and surface partitioning of rain (rain intensity vs 1-1000 mm/h soil capacity)
p173.description: How rain that reaches the ground is split between entering the soil matrix, bypassing it through macropores, and leaving as overland flow. Rain intensity relative to the soil's saturated hydraulic conductivity (about 1 mm/h in clays to several hundred mm/h in sands) decides the split.

p174.title: Evapotranspiration partitioning (about 61 percent transpiration, range 35-90)
p174.description: How the water that returns to the air from land splits into plant transpiration, soil evaporation, canopy interception evaporation and open-water or snow loss. Each kilogram evaporated absorbs about 2.45 MJ of latent heat.

p175.title: Drainage, groundwater recharge and runoff (about 65 percent of rain returns to air, 35 percent runs off)
p175.description: Where land precipitation that is not evapotranspired goes: surface runoff, interflow, and deep drainage that recharges aquifers and later returns as baseflow. Also covers capillary rise and solute export.

p176.title: Hydraulic redistribution by roots (0.04-1.3 mm per day)
p176.description: Roots act as passive conduits that move water along water-potential gradients, usually from wet deep soil to dry shallow soil at night (hydraulic lift) and sometimes downward after rain, buffering drought for plants and soil microbes.

p177.title: Physical weathering: frost cracking, thermal stress and root wedging
p177.description: Mechanical breakdown of rock without chemical change: water freezing in cracks, repeated heating and cooling, and growing roots. It multiplies reactive surface area (a 1 cm cube split into 1 mm cubes gains 10 times the area).

p178.title: Chemical weathering: CO2-driven dissolution and CO2 consumption
p178.description: Dissolution and alteration of minerals by water and acids: carbonic acid attacks carbonates and silicates, releasing cations, silica and bicarbonate to rivers. Silicate weathering is the slow geologic sink that regulates atmospheric CO2.

p179.title: Biological weathering by roots, mycorrhizal fungi and microbes (plants speed weathering about 2-10 fold)
p179.description: Plants, fungi and bacteria speed up rock breakdown by exuding organic acids, raising soil CO2, tunneling minerals with hyphae and shifting rhizosphere pH. They pay for it with photosynthate, tying weathering to the carbon cycle.

p180.title: Weathering regime: supply-limited versus kinetically limited
p180.description: What sets how fast rock weathers: how fast fresh mineral is supplied by erosion and uplift, and how fast reactions run at a given temperature and runoff. Granitic soils span about 0.02 to 0.7 chemical depletion.

p181.title: Litter quality (lignin:N) sets the decay trajectory
p181.description: How litter chemistry sets the speed and phases of decay: an early phase on soluble sugars and cellulose, then a late phase limited by lignin and by nitrogen supply, with litter N concentration rising as carbon is lost.

p182.title: Fauna fragment, graze and condition litter
p182.description: Detritivores such as isopods, millipedes, springtails and earthworms shred litter, graze microbes and spread inoculum; their effect on decay depends on climate and litter quality.

p183.title: Photodegradation of litter in drylands
p183.description: In dry, open ecosystems where microbes are water-limited, solar radiation breaks down litter directly and can make it easier for microbes to decay.

p184.title: Soil state factors and the erosion-formation balance
p184.description: How climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time shape soil properties such as where organic carbon sits in the profile, and whether erosion or soil production dominates a landscape.

p185.title: Erosion versus soil production balance
p185.description: Tillage and bare ground raise erosion above the rate at which weathering produces soil; thinner soil holds less water and supports less plant cover, which accelerates further erosion.

p186.title: Land water partitioning and plant water flux
p186.description: How precipitation on land is divided between evapotranspiration and runoff, how large the plant share of that evaporative flux is, and how roots redistribute water through soil.

p187.title: Plant-mediated water flux
p187.description: Transpiration is the dominant part of evapotranspiration; roots also move water between wet and dry soil layers, extending the time plants can stay active.

p188.title: Biotic enhancement and climate control of weathering
p188.description: How roots and fungi accelerate mineral dissolution, how erosion and climate set long-term chemical weathering rates, and how spreading crushed silicate rock on cropland could draw down CO2.

p189.title: Enhanced rock weathering on cropland
p189.description: Spreading crushed basalt on cropland speeds silicate dissolution, which converts CO2 to dissolved bicarbonate carried to rivers and the ocean; rising pH slows the dissolution as it proceeds.

p190.title: Ecosystem engineering and plant-soil feedback
p190.description: How organisms modify their physical environment, how plant traits drive litter quality and fertility, and how these changes feed back to favour similar species.

p191.title: Plant-soil feedback via litter quality
p191.description: Acquisitive fast-growing plants produce nutrient-rich litter that decomposes quickly and raises soil fertility, which favours more acquisitive plants; conservative species do the reverse.

p192.title: Temperature and moisture control microbial decay rate
p192.description: Warming speeds enzyme reactions, while water content sets an optimum: too dry limits substrate diffusion, too wet limits oxygen. Together they set seasonal and geographic decay rates and the warming-decomposition feedback.

p193.title: Chronosequence: limiting nutrient and nutrient source shift as soil ages
p193.description: As a soil ages over thousands to millions of years, rock-derived phosphorus is weathered out and occluded while nitrogen accumulates, so plant growth moves from nitrogen limitation to phosphorus limitation and the nutrient supply shifts from rock to atmospheric dust.

p194.title: Soil production versus erosion (soil thickness balance)
p194.description: New soil forms where bedrock weathers at a rate that declines as soil thickens, while erosion removes soil from the surface. Natural soils sit near a balance, but ploughing can erode far faster than soil forms.

p195.title: Roots, fungi and burrowers engineer soil formation
p195.description: Living organisms speed soil formation: roots and mycorrhizal fungi acidify and dissolve minerals, deep roots pump cations upward to the surface, and burrowing animals mix layers.

p196.title: Mineral surfaces accumulate and protect organic carbon as soil ages
p196.description: Weathering creates reactive iron, aluminium and short-range-order minerals that bind organic carbon and slow its turnover, so soil carbon storage depends on mineralogy and climate together.

evidence.claim: Meta-analysis: plants respond more where P is low and N is not limiting; shares are estimates

s714.label: Mutualism: P supplied exceeds carbon cost, growth rises

evidence.source: Hoeksema et al. 2010, A meta-analysis of context-dependency in plant response to inoculation with mycorrhizal fungi, Ecology Letters 13:394-407
evidence.claim: Positive growth response in P-limited soils

s715.label: Neutral: carbon cost and phosphorus benefit roughly cancel

evidence.source: Johnson, Graham & Smith 1997, Functioning of mycorrhizal associations along the mutualism-parasitism continuum, New Phytologist 135:575-585
evidence.claim: Neutral outcomes occur at intermediate fertility

s716.label: Parasitism: plant has abundant P and carbon cost becomes a net loss

evidence.source: Johnson, Graham & Smith 1997, Functioning of mycorrhizal associations along the mutualism-parasitism continuum, New Phytologist 135:575-585
evidence.claim: Mycorrhizal parasitism with high P and low light

s717.label: Plant phosphorus status falls or rises and systemically regulates colonization

evidence.source: Breuillin et al. 2010, Phosphate systemically inhibits development of arbuscular mycorrhiza in Petunia hybrida, New Phytologist 185:1016-1030
evidence.claim: High plant P systemically represses arbuscular mycorrhiza development and function genes

s718.label: Hyphal growth and turnover are fuelled by plant carbon

evidence.source: Smith & Read 2008, Mycorrhizal Symbiosis, 3rd ed., Academic Press
evidence.claim: External hyphae are carbon sinks that expand when carbon is supplied

evidence.source: Kiers et al. 2011, Reciprocal rewards stabilize cooperation in the mycorrhizal symbiosis, Science 333:880-882
evidence.claim: Plants and fungi both reward better trading partners (reciprocal rewards)

s720.label: Start: Plant and fungus compare returns

evidence.source: Kiers et al. 2011, Reciprocal rewards stabilize cooperation in the mycorrhizal symbiosis, Science 333:880-882

evidence.source: Kiers et al. 2011, Reciprocal rewards stabilize cooperation in the mycorrhizal symbiosis, Science 333:880-882

s722.label: Plant allocates more carbon to roots hosting fungi that deliver more phosphorus

evidence.source: Kiers et al. 2011, Reciprocal rewards stabilize cooperation in the mycorrhizal symbiosis, Science 333:880-882
evidence.claim: Host plant rewards the better fungal partner with more carbohydrate

s723.label: Fungus allocates more phosphorus to roots that supply more carbon

evidence.source: Kiers et al. 2011, Reciprocal rewards stabilize cooperation in the mycorrhizal symbiosis, Science 333:880-882
evidence.claim: Fungus delivers more P to hosts offering more carbon, observed with 33P tracing in root organ cultures

s724.label: Low-delivery arbuscules degenerate when plant phosphate transport fails

evidence.source: Javot et al. 2007, A Medicago truncatula phosphate transporter indispensable for the arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis, PNAS 104:1720-1725
evidence.claim: MtPT4 mutants show premature arbuscule collapse

s725.label: Cheater fungi that take carbon without phosphorus lose colonization

evidence.source: Kiers et al. 2011, Reciprocal rewards stabilize cooperation in the mycorrhizal symbiosis, Science 333:880-882
evidence.claim: Sanctions penalize fungal partners that provide little P

s726.label: Soil nitrification, nitrate reduction and nitrogen gas losses

s729.label: Which ammonia oxidizer dominates this soil?

evidence.source: Prosser & Nicol 2012, Trends in Microbiology 20:523, Archaeal and bacterial ammonia-oxidisers in soil
evidence.claim: AOA tend to dominate low-ammonium, acidic soils and AOB high-ammonium fertilized soils; comammox share is poorly quantified, so these shares are rough estimates.

s730.label: Archaea oxidize ammonia at low supply and in acid soils

evidence.source: Leininger et al. 2006, Nature 442:806, Archaea predominate among ammonia-oxidizing prokaryotes in soils
evidence.claim: Archaeal amoA genes outnumber bacterial amoA in many soils and archaea grow at low NH3 supply.

s731.label: Bacteria oxidize ammonia where ammonium is plentiful

evidence.source: Prosser & Nicol 2012, Trends in Microbiology 20:523, Archaeal and bacterial ammonia-oxidisers in soil
evidence.claim: AOB respond to high ammonium (fertilizer, manure urine patches) and are more active at neutral pH.

s732.label: Comammox Nitrospira oxidize ammonia all the way to nitrate

evidence.source: Daims et al. 2015, Nature 528:504, Complete nitrification by Nitrospira bacteria
evidence.claim: Single Nitrospira cells can complete both oxidation steps, the comammox pathway.

s733.label: Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria convert nitrite to nitrate

evidence.source: Kuypers, Marchant & Kartal 2018, Nature Reviews Microbiology 16:263, The microbial nitrogen-cycling network
evidence.claim: Nitrobacter and Nitrospira oxidize nitrite to nitrate so that nitrite rarely accumulates.

s734.label: Nitrate pool in soil solution (mobile anion)

evidence.source: Brady & Weil 2016, The Nature and Properties of Soils, 15th ed., Pearson
evidence.claim: Nitrate is negatively charged, is weakly retained by most soils and moves with drainage water.

s735.label: Nitrification releases protons and acidifies soil

evidence.source: Brady & Weil 2016, The Nature and Properties of Soils, 15th ed., Pearson
evidence.claim: Oxidation of one NH4+ yields two H+, a major acidifying process in fertilized soils.

evidence.source: Subbarao et al. 2006, Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences 25:303, Scope and strategies for regulation of nitrification in agricultural systems
evidence.claim: Some grasses such as Brachiaria release compounds that suppress nitrifiers, slowing nitrate formation.

s737.label: Oxygen and moisture window: nitrification peaks at moderate water-filled pore space

evidence.source: Stark & Firestone 1995, Applied and Environmental Microbiology 61:218, Mechanisms for soil moisture effects on activity of nitrifying bacteria
evidence.claim: Nitrifier activity is limited by substrate diffusion when dry and by oxygen when wet, peaking at intermediate moisture.

s738.label: Nitrate reaches anoxic microsites inside aggregates

evidence.source: Firestone & Davidson 1989, Microbiological basis of NO and N2O production and consumption in soil, in Exchange of Trace Gases between Terrestrial Ecosystems and the Atmosphere
evidence.claim: Anoxic microsites form where respiration outpaces oxygen diffusion, often in wet aggregates with high carbon supply.

s739.label: Where does nitrate go in an anoxic microsite?

evidence.source: Rutting et al. 2011, Ecological Applications 21:3, Assessment of the importance of dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium for the terrestrial nitrogen cycle
evidence.claim: Denitrification usually dominates, DNRA is favoured at high carbon to nitrate ratios and strongly reducing conditions, anammox is minor in most soils; shares are broad estimates.

s740.label: Denitrifiers reduce nitrate stepwise via nitrite and nitric oxide to nitrous oxide and dinitrogen

evidence.source: Zumft 1997, Microbiology and Molecular Biology Reviews 61:533, Cell biology and molecular basis of denitrification
evidence.claim: Denitrification is a four-step reduction with separate enzymes (nar, nir, nor, nos).

s741.label: What is the nitrous oxide to dinitrogen ratio?

evidence.source: Bakken et al. 2012, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 367:1226, Regulation of denitrification at the cellular level
evidence.claim: Acidic pH impairs assembly of functional N2O reductase, raising the N2O share; shares are illustrative of acid versus near-neutral soils.

s742.label: Acid or nitrate-rich, carbon-poor soil: N2O reductase fails and N2O is released

evidence.source: Bakken et al. 2012, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 367:1226, Regulation of denitrification at the cellular level
evidence.claim: Low pH and high nitrate relative to carbon raise the N2O product ratio.

s743.label: Near-neutral, carbon-rich soil: reduction completes to dinitrogen

evidence.source: Jones et al. 2014, Nature Climate Change 4:801, Recently identified microbial guild mediates soil N2O sink capacity
evidence.claim: Clade II nosZ organisms are a soil sink for N2O and reduce it to N2.

s744.label: DNRA bacteria reduce nitrate back to ammonium and conserve nitrogen

evidence.source: Rutting et al. 2011, Ecological Applications 21:3, Assessment of the importance of dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium for the terrestrial nitrogen cycle
evidence.claim: Dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium retains N in the system, favoured where carbon is abundant relative to nitrate.

s745.label: Anammox bacteria combine ammonium and nitrite into dinitrogen

evidence.source: Kuypers, Marchant & Kartal 2018, Nature Reviews Microbiology 16:263, The microbial nitrogen-cycling network
evidence.claim: Anaerobic ammonium oxidation produces N2 and is detected in soils, usually of minor importance.

s746.label: Nitrifier denitrification and chemodenitrification make nitrous oxide at the oxic-anoxic boundary

evidence.source: Wrage et al. 2001, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 33:1723, Role of nitrifier denitrification in the production of nitrous oxide
evidence.claim: Nitrifiers reduce nitrite to N2O under low O2 and abiotic reactions of nitrite with Fe and organic matter add N2O.

s747.label: Nitrate leaches below the root zone with drainage water

evidence.source: Di & Cameron 2002, Nutrient Cycling in Agroecosystems 64:237, Nitrate leaching in temperate agroecosystems
evidence.claim: Leaching of nitrate is the main loss pathway in humid agricultural soils and reaches groundwater and streams.

s748.label: Ammonia volatilizes from high-pH soil surfaces

evidence.source: Sommer, Schjoerring & Denmead 2004, Advances in Agronomy 82:557, Ammonia emission from mineral fertilizers and fertilized crops
evidence.claim: Loss of NH3 rises with pH (NH4+/NH3 pKa about 9.25), temperature and wind.

s749.label: Nitrous oxide and dinitrogen escape to the atmosphere

evidence.source: Butterbach-Bahl et al. 2013, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 368:20130122, Nitrous oxide emissions from soils: how well do we understand the processes and their controls?
evidence.claim: Soils emit about 60% of global N2O, mostly from nitrification and denitrification.

s750.label: Clay minerals fix ammonium in interlayers

evidence.source: Nieder, Benbi & Scherer 2011, Biology and Fertility of Soils 47:1, Fixation and defixation of ammonium in soils: a review
evidence.claim: Vermiculite and illite fix NH4+ in interlayer sites, making it temporarily unavailable.

evidence.source: Jackson & Sherman 1953, Advances in Agronomy 5:219-318
evidence.claim: Defines the weathering sequence of clay minerals from micas to vermiculite, smectite, kaolinite and finally gibbsite and Fe oxides as leaching intensifies.

s754.label: Mica and feldspar lose interlayer K and alter to illite

evidence.source: Fanning & Keramidas 1977, Micas, in Minerals in Soil Environments (SSSA)
evidence.claim: Biotite and muscovite lose interlayer K+ to solution, leaving hydrous mica (illite) and expandable layers.

s755.label: Interlayer K loss opens layers; high-charge vermiculite forms

evidence.source: Brady & Weil 2008, The Nature and Properties of Soils 14th ed., ch. 8 (silicate clays)
evidence.claim: Vermiculite is a weathered mica with high charge (CEC about 100-150 cmol/kg) and partly fixed interlayer K.

s756.label: Leaching intensity and silica activity decide the clay type

evidence.source: Borchardt 1989, Smectites, in Minerals in Soil Environments 2nd ed. (SSSA)
evidence.claim: Smectite favours Si- and Mg-rich solutions in poorly drained settings; strong leaching removes Si and favours kaolinite. Shares of outcomes are estimates (range 30-50%).

s757.label: Smectite forms: 2:1 clay, high CEC and strong shrink-swell

evidence.source: Brady & Weil 2008, ch. 8
evidence.claim: Smectites have CEC of roughly 80-150 cmol/kg and swell strongly on wetting.

s758.label: Kaolinite forms with desilication: 1:1 clay, low CEC, little swelling

evidence.source: Brady & Weil 2008, ch. 8
evidence.claim: Kaolinite has CEC of about 3-15 cmol/kg and is non-expanding; dominant in strongly weathered humid soils.

s759.label: Gibbsite, goethite and hematite accumulate in extreme weathering

evidence.source: Sanchez 1976, Properties and Management of Soils in the Tropics (Wiley), ch. 3
evidence.claim: Oxisols are dominated by kaolinite plus Fe and Al oxides with variable charge and anion sorption.

s760.label: Fixed K is re-fixed or slowly released from collapsed interlayers

evidence.source: Sparks & Huang 1985, Role of K in soils: potassium fixation, in Potassium in Agriculture (ASA)
evidence.claim: High K or drying collapses vermiculite layers (K fixation); depletion of solution K slowly releases it.

s761.label: Clay mineralogy sets CEC, swelling and aggregate behaviour

evidence.source: Brady & Weil 2008, ch. 8
evidence.claim: Clay type controls CEC, shrink-swell and nutrient retention of the soil.

s762.label: Redox ladder: sequential electron acceptors in waterlogged soil

evidence.source: Ponnamperuma 1972, Advances in Agronomy 24:29-96 (The chemistry of submerged soils)
evidence.claim: After oxygen is gone, flooded soil reduces nitrate, Mn(IV), Fe(III), sulfate and CO2 in thermodynamic order, with pH drifting toward neutral.

s765.label: Respiration outpaces oxygen diffusion through water-filled pores; Oxygen disappears

evidence.source: Glinski & Stepniewski 1985, Soil Aeration and Its Role for Plants (CRC Press)
evidence.claim: Oxygen diffuses about 10,000 times more slowly in water than in air, so saturated soil runs out of oxygen within hours to days.

s766.label: Nitrate is reduced first (about +250 mV at pH 7)

evidence.source: Patrick & Jugsujinda 1992, Soil Science Society of America Journal 56:1071
evidence.claim: In flooded soil, nitrate disappears before Mn and Fe are reduced, at roughly +200 to +300 mV.

s767.label: Manganese(IV) oxides are reduced to soluble Mn2+

evidence.source: Patrick & Jugsujinda 1992, SSSAJ 56:1071
evidence.claim: Mn2+ appears at about +200 mV after nitrate is exhausted.

s768.label: Iron(III) oxides are reduced to Fe2+; pH converges toward 6.5-7.5

evidence.source: Ponnamperuma 1972, Advances in Agronomy 24:29
evidence.claim: Fe reduction consumes protons so acid soils rise and alkaline soils fall in pH toward near neutral within weeks of flooding.

evidence.source: Reddy & DeLaune 2008, Biogeochemistry of Wetlands (CRC Press), ch. 4
evidence.claim: Duration of saturation determines how far down the redox ladder soil goes. Shares are estimates (40-60%).

s770.label: Sulfate is reduced to sulfide; FeS gives black colour

evidence.source: Reddy & DeLaune 2008, ch. 8
evidence.claim: Sulfate reduction proceeds below about -100 to -150 mV and precipitates iron sulfides.

s771.label: CO2 is reduced to Methane below about -200 mV

evidence.source: Conrad 1996, Microbiological Reviews 60:609
evidence.claim: Methanogenesis starts only after nitrate, Fe(III) and sulfate are depleted; methane production needs strongly reducing conditions.

s772.label: Drainage reoxidises Fe2+ and Mn2+: mottles, rust coats and nodules

evidence.source: Vepraskas 2004, Redoximorphic Features for Identifying Aquic Conditions, NC State Tech. Bulletin 301
evidence.claim: Fe oxides precipitate along root channels and pore walls where oxygen re-enters, forming diagnostic redox features.

evidence.source: Beven & Germann 1982, Water Resources Research 18:1311-1325 (Macropores and water flow in soils)
evidence.claim: Macropores carry water through soil faster than Darcy matrix flow predicts, bypassing most of the soil volume.

s774.label: Start: Preferential flow and macropore bypass

evidence.source: Beven & Germann 1982, Water Resources Research 18:1311-1325 (Macropores and water flow in soils)

evidence.source: Beven & Germann 2013, Water Resources Research 49:3071 (Macropores and water flow in soils revisited)
evidence.claim: Review of how structured pore networks conduct water and solutes rapidly.

s777.label: Rain intensity versus matrix infiltration capacity and soil wetness

evidence.source: Jarvis 2007, European Journal of Soil Science 58:523
evidence.claim: Macropore flow is triggered when rain intensity or ponding exceeds matrix infiltration capacity; shares are estimates (+-10 points).

s778.label: Bypass flow delivers water and solutes to depth with little contact with the matrix

evidence.source: Flury et al. 1994, Water Resources Research 30:1945
evidence.claim: Dye tracing in field soils showed preferential flow in most of them regardless of texture.

s779.label: Fingered flow in water-repellent or layered sand

evidence.source: Ritsema & Dekker 1994, Water Resources Research 30:2519
evidence.claim: Water-repellent sand shows unstable fingers that conduct most water through a small fraction of the volume.

s780.label: Macropore-matrix exchange: imbibition slows the front and stores water in aggregates

evidence.source: Gerke & van Genuchten 1993, Water Resources Research 29:305
evidence.claim: Dual-porosity model shows water exchange between macropore and matrix domains controls how far bypass water travels.

s781.label: Swelling clay closes cracks as soil wets, sealing macropores

evidence.source: Bronswijk 1988, Journal of Hydrology 97:199
evidence.claim: In cracking clay soils, crack volume shrinks as soil swells, so bypass flow ends when the soil is wet.

s782.label: Fast transport of Nitrate, pesticides and pathogens to drains and groundwater

evidence.source: Kladivko et al. 1991, Journal of Environmental Quality 20:264
evidence.claim: Pesticides reached tile drains within days of rainfall through macropores in silt loam.

evidence.source: Edwards 2013, European Journal of Soil Science 64:300-315 (The impact of freezing and thawing on soil structure)
evidence.claim: Freeze-thaw can fragment large aggregates and shifts stability depending on water content and cycle number.

s784.label: Start: Freeze-thaw cycling and soil structure

evidence.source: Edwards 2013, European Journal of Soil Science 64:300-315 (The impact of freezing and thawing on soil structure)
evidence.claim: Freeze-thaw can fragment large aggregates and shifts stability depending on water content and cycle number.

s785.label: End: Freeze-thaw cycling and soil structure

s786.label: Pore water freezes and expands about 9%

evidence.source: Taber 1930, Journal of Geology 38:303 (The mechanics of frost heaving)
evidence.claim: Water expands about 9% on freezing, but heave is mainly caused by ice lens growth.

s787.label: Unfrozen water migrates to the freezing front and grows ice lenses

evidence.source: Konrad & Morgenstern 1980, Canadian Geotechnical Journal 17:473
evidence.claim: Water is drawn to the freezing front by suction, building segregated ice lenses.

s788.label: Ice lenses compress and fracture aggregates along planes of weakness

evidence.source: Oztas & Fayetorbay 2003, Catena 52:1
evidence.claim: Aggregate stability of wet soils fell with the number of freeze-thaw cycles.

evidence.source: Edwards 2013, EJSS 64:300
evidence.claim: Effect size depends strongly on moisture at freezing; shares are estimates (+-10 points).

s790.label: Thaw flush: lysed microbes and broken aggregates release carbon and N

evidence.source: Wagner-Riddle et al. 2017, Nature Geoscience 10:279
evidence.claim: Freeze-thaw periods accounted for roughly 17-28% of annual cropland N2O emissions in the dataset.

s791.label: Frost loosens dense surface soil and creates fine seedbed tilth

evidence.source: Kvaerno & Oygarden 2006, Catena 67:175
evidence.claim: Freeze-thaw changed aggregate size distribution in Norwegian soils, loosening some while weakening others.

s792.label: Frozen wet subsoil is near impermeable; spring melt runs off and erodes

evidence.source: Granger, Gray & Dyck 1984, Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences 21:669
evidence.claim: Snowmelt infiltration into frozen prairie soils depends on ice content at freeze-up; wet soils freeze nearly impermeable.

evidence.source: Wilkinson, Richards & Humphreys 2009, Earth-Science Reviews 97:254-269 (Breaking ground)

s794.label: Start: Bioturbation: fauna remodel soil structure

s796.label: Earthworms ingest soil and litter and mix organic with mineral material

evidence.source: Lee 1985, Earthworms: Their Ecology and Relationships with Soils and Land Use (Academic Press)
evidence.claim: Annual cast production is reported over a wide range, about 2 to 250 tonnes per hectare.

s797.label: Gut passage and mucus bind particles into water-stable casts

evidence.source: Six, Bossuyt, Degryze & Denef 2004, Soil and Tillage Research 79:7
evidence.claim: Reviews that casts are stable aggregates with organic matter protected inside.

s798.label: Burrows form biopores that raise infiltration and root access

evidence.source: Blouin et al. 2013, European Journal of Soil Science 64:161
evidence.claim: Earthworm presence increases infiltration and aeration via burrow networks.

s799.label: Ants and termites build galleries and mounds, moving subsoil upward

evidence.source: Jouquet et al. 2011, European Journal of Soil Biology 47:215
evidence.claim: Termites alter soil texture and porosity and concentrate clay and nutrients in mounds and galleries.

s800.label: Burrowing mammals and tree-throw create pit-and-mound mixing

evidence.source: Gabet, Reichman & Seabloom 2003, Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences 31:249
evidence.claim: Bioturbation by burrowers and tree throw drives soil turnover and sediment transport.

s801.label: Net effect on structure depends on species, soil and management

evidence.source: Bohlen et al. 2004, Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment 2:427
evidence.claim: Invasive earthworms in North American forests removed the litter layer, showing that effects can be negative. Shares are estimates (+-15 points).

s802.label: Structure improved: stable casts, interconnected pores, mixed organic matter

s806.label: Pyrolysis or wildfire turns biomass into aromatic carbon charcoal

evidence.claim: Charcoal is condensed aromatic carbon formed at 350-700 C without oxygen.

evidence.source: Wang, Xiong & Kuzyakov 2016, GCB Bioenergy 8:512
evidence.claim: Meta-analysis estimated mean residence time of about 556 years for the stable biochar pool and about 108 days for the labile pool.

s808.label: Surface oxidises, gaining carboxyl groups and CEC; pores adsorb water and nutrients

evidence.source: Liang et al. 2006, Soil Science Society of America Journal 70:1719
evidence.claim: Aged black carbon in Amazonian dark earths had higher CEC per unit carbon than neighbouring soil.

s809.label: Soil and char type decide the response

evidence.source: Jeffery et al. 2011, Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment 144:175
evidence.claim: Meta-analysis showed an average 10% productivity increase, largest in acidic and coarse-textured soils. Shares are estimates (+-10 points).

s810.label: Ash carbonates raise pH and reduce Aluminum toxicity

evidence.source: Van Zwieten et al. 2010, Plant and Soil 327:235
evidence.claim: Papermill biochar raised soil pH and cut exchangeable Al, improving wheat and radish growth in an acid soil.

s811.label: Lower bulk density and higher water holding in sandy soil

evidence.source: Omondi et al. 2016, Geoderma 274:28
evidence.claim: Meta-analysis found biochar lowered bulk density and raised porosity and water holding capacity; effects larger in coarse soils.

s812.label: Pores shelter microbes and N2O emission falls

s817.label: Salts accumulate where evapotranspiration exceeds leaching

evidence.source: Rengasamy 2006, Journal of Experimental Botany 57:1017
evidence.claim: Salinity develops in arid zones and under irrigation or rising saline water tables where leaching is limited.

s818.label: Shallow water table rises by capillary action; salt is left at the surface

evidence.source: Ghassemi, Jakeman & Nix 1995, Salinisation of Land and Water Resources (CAB International)
evidence.claim: Capillary rise and evaporation concentrate salts in the root zone and surface.

s819.label: Classify salt-affected soil by EC_e and ESP

evidence.source: Richards 1954, USDA Handbook 60
evidence.claim: Saline: EC_e above 4 dS/m and ESP below 15; sodic: ESP above 15; saline-sodic: both.

s820.label: Saline soil: osmotic stress reduces water uptake

evidence.source: Maas & Hoffman 1977, Journal of the Irrigation and Drainage Division ASCE 103:115
evidence.claim: Yield thresholds differ: wheat about 6.0 dS/m and maize about 1.7 dS/m, with yield loss per dS/m above the threshold.

s821.label: Sodic soil: Na on exchange sites disperses clay when electrolyte is low

s915.label: Microbes take up substrate and split carbon between respiration and biomass synthesis (anabolism)

evidence.source: Liang, Schimel & Jastrow 2017, The importance of anabolism in microbial control over soil carbon storage, Nature Microbiology 2:17105
evidence.claim: Anabolism increases the microbial contribution to stable soil carbon

s916.label: High CUE (about 0.5-0.6) shunts more carbon into biomass and necromass

evidence.source: Sinsabaugh et al. 2013, Carbon use efficiency of microbial communities: stoichiometry, methodology and modelling, Ecology Letters 16:930-939
evidence.claim: Community CUE ranges roughly 0.3-0.6; high-quality, N-rich substrate raises it

s917.label: Low CUE (about 0.2-0.3) from poor-quality substrate, nutrient limitation or heat sends more carbon to CO2

evidence.source: Sinsabaugh et al. 2013, Carbon use efficiency of microbial communities: stoichiometry, methodology and modelling, Ecology Letters 16:930-939
