evidence.claim: Low CUE under nutrient imbalance

s918.label: Warming lowers CUE in models by about 0.016 per degree Celsius

evidence.source: Allison, Wallenstein & Bradford 2010, Soil-carbon response to warming dependent on microbial physiology, Nature Geoscience 3:336-340
evidence.claim: Model assumed CUE declining with temperature, value used about 0.016 per degree, estimate not measured everywhere

s919.label: Lower necromass inputs and more respiration reduce soil carbon

evidence.source: Allison, Wallenstein & Bradford 2010, Soil-carbon response to warming dependent on microbial physiology, Nature Geoscience 3:336-340
evidence.claim: Lower CUE leads to lower microbial biomass and soil carbon

s920.label: More CO2 to the atmosphere adds to warming

evidence.source: Davidson & Janssens 2006, Temperature sensitivity of soil carbon decomposition and feedbacks to climate change, Nature 440:165-173
evidence.claim: Soil carbon decomposition feedback to climate

s921.label: Soil disturbance (fire, tillage, drought) and recovery

evidence.source: Griffiths & Philippot 2013, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 37:112, Insights into the resistance and resilience of the soil microbial community
evidence.claim: Soil microbial communities and their functions respond to disturbance through resistance and resilience, which differ among disturbance types.

s922.label: Start: Soil disturbance (fire, tillage, drought) and recovery

evidence.source: Griffiths & Philippot 2013, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 37:112, Insights into the resistance and resilience of the soil microbial community
evidence.claim: Soil microbial communities and their functions respond to disturbance through resistance and resilience, which differ among disturbance types.

s923.label: End: Soil disturbance (fire, tillage, drought) and recovery

evidence.source: Griffiths & Philippot 2013, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 37:112, Insights into the resistance and resilience of the soil microbial community
evidence.claim: Soil microbial communities and their functions respond to disturbance through resistance and resilience, which differ among disturbance types.

evidence.source: Griffiths & Philippot 2013, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 37:112, Insights into the resistance and resilience of the soil microbial community
evidence.claim: Pulse (fire, tillage) and press (drought) disturbances produce different resistance and resilience patterns; shares are an illustrative mix for managed and wildland soils.

s925.label: Fire heats the soil surface and burns the litter layer

evidence.source: Neary, Klopatek, DeBano & Ffolliott 1999, Forest Ecology and Management 122:51, Fire effects on belowground sustainability
evidence.claim: Soil heating above about 200-300 C volatilizes organic matter and N, with loss of litter and humus.

s926.label: Heating makes hydrophobic coatings that distil downward and form a water-repellent layer

evidence.source: DeBano 2000, Journal of Hydrology 231:195, The role of fire and soil heating on water repellency in wildland environments
evidence.claim: Vaporized hydrophobic compounds condense on cooler soil below, forming a water-repellent layer.

s927.label: Infiltration falls, runoff and erosion rise after fire

evidence.source: Shakesby & Doerr 2006, Earth-Science Reviews 74:269, Wildfire as a hydrological and geomorphological agent
evidence.claim: Water repellency and loss of cover increase post-fire runoff and sediment yield by orders of magnitude on steep burned slopes.

s928.label: Fire adds ash nutrients and pyrogenic carbon and mineralizes nitrogen

evidence.source: Certini 2005, Oecologia 143:1, Effects of fire on properties of forest soils: a review
evidence.claim: Burning makes a nutrient pulse as ammonium, base cations and pH rise and charcoal is added.

s929.label: Tillage inverts soil and breaks aggregates

evidence.source: Six, Elliott & Paustian 2000, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 32:2099, Soil macroaggregate turnover and microaggregate formation under no-tillage
evidence.claim: Tillage breaks macroaggregates, exposing protected organic matter.

s930.label: Exposed organic matter is oxidized and carbon dioxide is lost

evidence.source: West & Post 2002, Soil Science Society of America Journal 66:1930, Soil organic carbon sequestration rates by tillage and crop rotation
evidence.claim: Conventional tillage lowers soil organic carbon relative to no-till in many soils, though the gain from no-till is often limited to upper layers.

s931.label: Drying soil stresses microbes and cuts diffusion of substrates

evidence.source: Schimel 2018, Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics 49:409, Life in dry soils
evidence.claim: Drought reduces activity by cutting water films that carry substrates and by direct physiological stress.

s932.label: Microbes accumulate osmolytes, go dormant or die

evidence.source: Schimel, Balser & Wallenstein 2007, Ecology 88:1386, Microbial stress-response physiology and its implications for ecosystem function
evidence.claim: Microbes allocate carbon and N to osmolytes at the expense of growth during drying.

s933.label: Rewetting causes a pulse of carbon dioxide and nitrogen release (Birch effect)

evidence.source: Birch 1958, Plant and Soil 10:9, The effect of soil drying on humus decomposition and nitrogen availability
evidence.claim: Rewetting dry soil releases a flush of CO2 and mineral N.

s934.label: Osmolyte release and dead cells supply the rewetting flush

evidence.source: Fierer & Schimel 2003, Soil Science Society of America Journal 67:798, A proposed mechanism for the pulse in carbon dioxide production following rewetting of dry soil
evidence.claim: Osmolytes released and microbial cell lysis supply substrate for the flush after rapid rewetting.

s935.label: Community composition shifts toward tolerant taxa

evidence.source: Allison & Martiny 2008, PNAS 105:11512, Resistance, resilience, and redundancy in microbial communities
evidence.claim: Disturbance selects for tolerant taxa and alters function where redundancy is low.

s936.label: Vegetation regrows or crops are replanted and supply new carbon

evidence.source: Pellegrini et al. 2018, Nature 553:194, Fire frequency drives decadal changes in soil carbon and nitrogen and ecosystem productivity
evidence.claim: Plant regrowth rebuilds litter and root inputs that drive soil recovery.

s937.label: Aggregates and structure rebuild through roots, fungi and organic binding

evidence.source: Six, Elliott & Paustian 2000, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 32:2099, Soil macroaggregate turnover and microaggregate formation under no-tillage
evidence.claim: Aggregate turnover and rebuilding follow undisturbed residue and root input.

s938.label: Repeated or frequent disturbance depletes carbon and nitrogen pools

evidence.source: Pellegrini et al. 2018, Nature 553:194, Fire frequency drives decadal changes in soil carbon and nitrogen and ecosystem productivity
evidence.claim: In a long-term experiment, frequent fire reduced soil C and N in savanna soils over decades.

s939.label: Microbial function recovers toward pre-disturbance rates

evidence.source: Allison & Martiny 2008, PNAS 105:11512, Resistance, resilience, and redundancy in microbial communities
evidence.claim: Resilience is the rate and extent of return to undisturbed function; it varies widely among functions.

s940.label: Soil is left degraded, eroded or in an alternative state

evidence.source: Neary, Klopatek, DeBano & Ffolliott 1999, Forest Ecology and Management 122:51, Fire effects on belowground sustainability
evidence.claim: Severe burns and repeated cultivation can degrade soils for decades.

evidence.source: Sperry, Adler, Campbell & Comstock 1998, Plant, Cell & Environment 21:347, Limitation of plant water use by rhizosphere and xylem conductance
evidence.claim: Plant water use is limited by the combined hydraulic conductance of the rhizosphere and xylem along the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum.

s942.label: Start: Soil-plant-water coupling and drought response

evidence.source: Sperry, Adler, Campbell & Comstock 1998, Plant, Cell & Environment 21:347, Limitation of plant water use by rhizosphere and xylem conductance
evidence.claim: Plant water use is limited by the combined hydraulic conductance of the rhizosphere and xylem along the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum.

s943.label: End: Soil-plant-water coupling and drought response

evidence.source: Sperry, Adler, Campbell & Comstock 1998, Plant, Cell & Environment 21:347, Limitation of plant water use by rhizosphere and xylem conductance
evidence.claim: Plant water use is limited by the combined hydraulic conductance of the rhizosphere and xylem along the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum.

s944.label: Atmospheric demand pulls water through leaves, creating negative pressure in xylem

evidence.source: Passioura 1988, Annual Review of Plant Physiology and Plant Molecular Biology 39:245, Water transport in and to roots
evidence.claim: Transpiration creates a water potential gradient from soil to leaf along the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum.

s945.label: Roots take water up through the root cortex and endodermis

evidence.source: Passioura 1988, Annual Review of Plant Physiology and Plant Molecular Biology 39:245, Water transport in and to roots
evidence.claim: Radial water flow in roots can be a major resistance and is regulated by aquaporins.

s946.label: Soil water moves to the root along a potential gradient

evidence.source: Gardner 1960, Soil Science 89:63, Dynamic aspects of water availability to plants
evidence.claim: Water supply to roots depends on soil hydraulic conductivity, which falls steeply as soil dries.

s947.label: Soil dries near roots as conductivity falls and a gap forms at the root-soil interface

evidence.source: Carminati & Javaux 2020, Trends in Plant Science 25:868, Soil rather than xylem vulnerability controls stomatal response to drought
evidence.claim: In drying soil, the drop in soil hydraulic conductivity near roots limits uptake before xylem fails.

s948.label: Roots exude mucilage that holds water and eases uptake from dry soil

evidence.source: Ahmed, Kroener, Holz, Zarebanadkouki & Carminati 2014, Functional Plant Biology 41:1129, Mucilage exudation facilitates root water uptake in dry soils
evidence.claim: Mucilage keeps the rhizosphere wetter than bulk soil and facilitates uptake in dry soil.

s949.label: Roots sense drying and send abscisic acid signals to the shoot

evidence.source: Davies & Zhang 1991, Annual Review of Plant Physiology and Plant Molecular Biology 42:55, Root signals and the regulation of growth and development of plants in drying soil
evidence.claim: Roots in drying soil produce ABA that signals soil water status to the leaves independent of leaf water potential.

s950.label: Stomata partly close, reducing transpiration and carbon uptake

evidence.source: Tardieu & Davies 1993, Plant, Cell & Environment 16:341, Integration of hydraulic and chemical signalling in the control of stomatal conductance
evidence.claim: Chemical and hydraulic signals jointly set stomatal conductance.

s951.label: Is the plant drawing water faster than xylem and soil can supply it?

evidence.source: Tyree & Sperry 1989, Annual Review of Plant Physiology 40:19, Vulnerability of xylem to cavitation and embolism
evidence.claim: If xylem pressure falls below the cavitation threshold, air embolism blocks conduits; share depends on species safety margin; values here are illustrative.

s952.label: Stomatal control keeps xylem tension within safe limits

evidence.source: Sperry, Adler, Campbell & Comstock 1998, Plant, Cell & Environment 21:347, Limitation of plant water use by rhizosphere and xylem conductance
evidence.claim: Stomatal closure limits water loss so that xylem remains conductive.

s953.label: Xylem cavitation blocks conduits and cuts conductance

evidence.source: Tyree & Sperry 1989, Annual Review of Plant Physiology 40:19, Vulnerability of xylem to cavitation and embolism
evidence.claim: Embolism is produced by air entering xylem conduits under high tension and lowers hydraulic conductance.

s954.label: Hydraulic failure leads to leaf shedding and tree mortality

evidence.source: Anderegg et al. 2016, PNAS 113:5024, Meta-analysis reveals that hydraulic traits explain cross-species patterns of drought-induced tree mortality
evidence.claim: Hydraulic safety margins explain cross-species patterns of drought-induced mortality.

s955.label: Deep roots reach moist subsoil and groundwater

evidence.source: Canadell et al. 1996, Oecologia 108:583, Maximum rooting depth of vegetation types at the global scale
evidence.claim: Maximum rooting depths exceed 10 m in some tropical and desert species.

s956.label: Roots move water between wet and dry layers (hydraulic redistribution)

evidence.source: Richards & Caldwell 1987, Oecologia 73:486, Hydraulic lift: substantial nocturnal water transport between soil layers by Artemisia tridentata roots
evidence.claim: Roots move water from wet deep soil to dry shallow soil at night (hydraulic lift) along water potential gradients.

s957.label: Redistributed water supports shallow roots, mycorrhizae and nutrient uptake

evidence.source: Caldwell, Dawson & Richards 1998, Oecologia 113:151, Hydraulic lift: consequences of water efflux from the roots of plants
evidence.claim: Hydraulic lift keeps shallow roots and microbes active and may extend nutrient uptake in dry topsoil.

s958.label: Rooting depth tracks the water table and rainfall regime

evidence.source: Fan, Miguez-Macho, Jobbagy, Jackson & Otero-Casal 2017, PNAS 114:10572, Hydrologic regulation of plant rooting depth
evidence.claim: Global patterns of rooting depth reflect water-table depth and rainfall across landscapes.

s959.label: Transpired water returns to the air as vapour and cools leaves

evidence.source: Rodriguez-Iturbe & Porporato 2004, Ecohydrology of Water-Controlled Ecosystems, Cambridge University Press
evidence.claim: Transpiration is a major fraction of terrestrial evapotranspiration and cools the canopy.

s960.label: Biological nitrogen fixation: nitrogenase, oxygen protection and regulation

evidence.source: Hoffman et al. 2014, Chemical Reviews 114:4041-4062 (Mechanism of nitrogen fixation by nitrogenase)
evidence.claim: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to NH3 with obligatory H2 evolution; the ATP and electron demand makes fixation a costly pathway.

s961.label: Start: Diazotroph in N-poor, carbon-rich microsite

evidence.source: Hoffman et al. 2014, Chemical Reviews 114:4041-4062 (Mechanism of nitrogen fixation by nitrogenase)
evidence.claim: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to NH3 with obligatory H2 evolution; the ATP and electron demand makes fixation a costly pathway.

s962.label: End: Fixed nitrogen released as ammonium to the soil pool

evidence.source: Hoffman et al. 2014, Chemical Reviews 114:4041-4062 (Mechanism of nitrogen fixation by nitrogenase)
evidence.claim: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to NH3 with obligatory H2 evolution; the ATP and electron demand makes fixation a costly pathway.

s963.label: Diazotroph senses low mineral nitrogen and expresses nif genes (NifA activates nifHDK)

evidence.source: Dixon & Kahn 2004, Nature Reviews Microbiology 2:621-631 (Genetic regulation of biological nitrogen fixation)
evidence.claim: nif gene expression is repressed by fixed nitrogen and by oxygen through NifL/NifA-type control, so fixation is induced only under N limitation.

s964.label: Nitrogenase (Mo-Fe protein) reduces N2 using 16 ATP and 8 electrons per N2, with 1 H2 co-produced

evidence.source: Hoffman et al. 2014, Chemical Reviews 114:4041-4062
evidence.claim: Minimum reaction N2 + 8 H+ + 8 e- + 16 MgATP -> 2 NH3 + H2 + 16 MgADP + 16 Pi.

s965.label: Oxygen exposure irreversibly damages nitrogenase, so the cell must exclude or burn oxygen

evidence.source: Gallon 1981, Trends in Biochemical Sciences 6:19-23 (The oxygen sensitivity of nitrogenase)
evidence.claim: Both nitrogenase components are irreversibly inactivated by O2, forcing every diazotroph to evolve a protection strategy. Shares below are an estimate (roughly 40-55% of fixation in nodules in managed legume soils), not a measured census.

s966.label: Nodule: leghemoglobin buffers free oxygen near 10-50 nM while supplying respiring bacteroids

evidence.source: Appleby 1984, Annual Review of Plant Physiology 35:443-478 (Leghemoglobin and Rhizobium respiration)
evidence.claim: Leghemoglobin keeps free O2 in nodules in the nanomolar range while delivering O2 to bacteroid oxidases at high flux.

s967.label: Free-living protection: Azotobacter respiratory protection, anaerobic microsites, or conformational shielding

evidence.source: Robson & Postgate 1980, Annual Review of Microbiology 34:183-207 (Oxygen and hydrogen in biological nitrogen fixation)
evidence.claim: Azotobacter has among the highest respiration rates measured in bacteria, burning oxygen at the cell surface to protect nitrogenase; obligate anaerobes fix inside anoxic pores.

s968.label: Cyanobacteria in biological soil crusts fix N2 in heterocysts or at night

evidence.source: Belnap 2002, Biology and Fertility of Soils 35:128-135 (Nitrogen fixation in biological soil crusts from southeast Utah)
evidence.claim: Crust cyanobacteria and cyanolichens fix on the order of 1-9 kg N per ha per year in Colorado Plateau crusts, and rates rise with crust development.

s969.label: Fixation is limited by molybdenum, phosphorus and iron supply, and alternative V or Fe nitrogenases are less efficient

evidence.source: Barron et al. 2009, Nature Geoscience 2:42-45 (Molybdenum limitation of asymbiotic nitrogen fixation in tropical forest soils)
evidence.claim: Adding Mo raised asymbiotic fixation in Panamanian lowland forest litter and soils, showing the metal cofactor can be limiting.

s970.label: Fixed N is exported as ammonium or amino acids to the host, or released by free-living cells on death or grazing

evidence.source: Udvardi & Poole 2013, Annual Review of Plant Biology 64:781-805 (Transport and metabolism in legume-rhizobia symbioses)
evidence.claim: Bacteroids export ammonium (and amino acids) to the plant, which returns dicarboxylates as carbon source.

s971.label: Nodule number is limited by autoregulation of nodulation signalled from shoot to root

evidence.source: Ferguson et al. 2010, Journal of Integrative Plant Biology 52:61-76 (Molecular analysis of legume nodule development and autoregulation)
evidence.claim: Systemic shoot-derived signals (CLE peptides sensed by receptor kinases such as HAR1/SUNN) cap nodule number.

s972.label: Combined mineral nitrogen suppresses nodulation and nitrogenase activity (nitrate inhibition)

evidence.source: Streeter & Wong 1988, Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences 7:1-23 (Inhibition of legume nodule formation and N2 fixation by nitrate)
evidence.claim: Nitrate inhibits nodule initiation, growth and nitrogenase, with strong inhibition at millimolar supply.

s973.label: Fixed nitrogen enters the soil by nodule senescence, root and litter turnover, and diazotroph death

evidence.source: Herridge, Peoples & Boddey 2008, Plant and Soil 311:1-18 (Global inputs of biological nitrogen fixation in agricultural systems)
evidence.claim: Crop legumes derive about 50-70% of their N from fixation, and below-ground N is a significant share of the legume N budget.

s974.label: Natural terrestrial biological fixation totals roughly 50-60 Tg N per year, with a wide model range

evidence.source: Vitousek et al. 2013, Biogeochemistry 114:1-14 (Biological nitrogen fixation: rates, patterns and ecological controls in terrestrial ecosystems)
evidence.claim: Natural terrestrial biological N fixation estimated around 58 Tg N per year in pre-industrial terrestrial ecosystems, with substantial uncertainty.

s975.label: Methane oxidation by methanotrophs: the upland soil sink

evidence.source: Hanson & Hanson 1996, Microbiological Reviews 60:439-471 (Methanotrophic bacteria)
evidence.claim: Methanotrophs oxidise CH4 via methane monooxygenase to methanol, formaldehyde and CO2, assimilating part into biomass.

evidence.source: Hanson & Hanson 1996, Microbiological Reviews 60:439-471 (Methanotrophic bacteria)
evidence.claim: Methanotrophs oxidise CH4 via methane monooxygenase to methanol, formaldehyde and CO2, assimilating part into biomass.

s977.label: End: Methane converted to CO2 and biomass

evidence.source: Hanson & Hanson 1996, Microbiological Reviews 60:439-471 (Methanotrophic bacteria)
evidence.claim: Methanotrophs oxidise CH4 via methane monooxygenase to methanol, formaldehyde and CO2, assimilating part into biomass.

s978.label: Methane diffuses from the air or deeper soil into gas-filled pores toward oxidising cells

evidence.source: Smith et al. 2003, European Journal of Soil Science 54:779-791 (Exchange of greenhouse gases between soil and atmosphere: interactions of soil physical factors and biological processes)
evidence.claim: Gas diffusivity through air-filled pore space controls CH4 uptake rate in well-drained soils.

s979.label: Methane concentration regime selects the methanotroph guild at the microsite

evidence.source: Conrad 1996, Microbiological Reviews 60:609-640 (Soil microorganisms as controllers of atmospheric trace gases)
evidence.claim: Ambient-air soils oxidise CH4 at about 1.8-1.9 ppmv with kinetics distinct from soils exposed to high CH4. Shares are an estimate: most aerated upland area is at atmospheric concentration.

s980.label: High-affinity oxidisers (upland soil clusters, USC-alpha and USC-gamma, and a Methylocystis pMMO2) consume atmospheric methane

evidence.source: Baani & Liesack 2008, PNAS 105:10203-10208 (Two isozymes of particulate methane monooxygenase with different methane oxidation kinetics in Methylocystis sp. strain SC2)
evidence.claim: A second pMMO isozyme with a much lower Km allowed oxidation of CH4 at atmospheric mixing ratios.

s981.label: Low-affinity Type I and Type II methanotrophs oxidise elevated methane near wet soil, rice paddies and landfill covers

evidence.source: Bender & Conrad 1992, FEMS Microbiology Ecology 101:261-270 (Kinetics of CH4 oxidation in oxic soils exposed to ambient air or high CH4 mixing ratios)
evidence.claim: Soils exposed to high CH4 develop a low-affinity oxidation with a Km and Vmax orders of magnitude higher than ambient-air soils.

s982.label: Particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO) oxidises CH4 to methanol using O2 and a reductant, then methanol dehydrogenase yields formaldehyde

evidence.source: Hanson & Hanson 1996, Microbiological Reviews 60:439-471
evidence.claim: pMMO is a copper-containing membrane enzyme; CH4 + O2 + 2 e- + 2 H+ -> CH3OH + H2O.

s983.label: Soil moisture sets an optimum: dry soil limits cell activity, wet soil blocks diffusion

evidence.source: Del Grosso et al. 2000, Global Biogeochemical Cycles 14:999-1019 (General CH4 oxidation model and comparisons of CH4 oxidation in natural and managed systems)
evidence.claim: Modelled CH4 oxidation depends on water-filled pore space through gas diffusivity and on soil water stress, peaking at intermediate moisture.

s984.label: Ammonium inhibits methane oxidation because the two substrates compete at the same enzyme family and nitrifiers co-oxidise

evidence.source: Bedard & Knowles 1989, Microbiological Reviews 53:68-84 (Physiology, biochemistry, and specific inhibitors of CH4, NH4+, and CO oxidation by methanotrophs and nitrifiers)
evidence.claim: Methane monooxygenase oxidises NH4+ and ammonia monooxygenase oxidises CH4, giving mutual competitive inhibition.

s985.label: Land-use conversion from forest to arable cuts uptake, and recovery takes many decades

evidence.source: Priemé et al. 1997, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 29:1269-1273 (Slow increase in rate of methane oxidation in soils with time following land use change from arable agriculture to woodland)
evidence.claim: Methane oxidation rose only slowly after arable fields were afforested, taking on the order of a century to approach old-forest rates.

s986.label: Wetland and paddy roots and oxic surface layers oxidise a large part (often cited 20-90%) of methane produced below

evidence.source: Segers 1998, Biogeochemistry 41:23-51 (Methane production and methane consumption: a review of processes underlying wetland methane fluxes)
evidence.claim: Oxidation in the oxic surface and rhizosphere removes a variable but often large fraction of produced CH4 before it escapes.

s987.label: Oxidised carbon ends as CO2 (about 40-70% of the carbon) and as methanotroph biomass and EPS

evidence.source: Hanson & Hanson 1996, Microbiological Reviews 60:439-471
evidence.claim: Carbon conversion efficiency into biomass differs between RuMP (Type I) and serine-cycle (Type II) methanotrophs, the remainder being respired as CO2.

s988.label: Upland soils remove about 30-40 Tg CH4 per year, roughly 5% of the global methane sink

evidence.source: Saunois et al. 2020, Earth System Science Data 12:1561-1623 (The global methane budget 2000-2017)
evidence.claim: Soil uptake is estimated around 30-35 Tg CH4 per year with a wide range, a small term next to OH oxidation in the atmosphere.

s989.label: At methane hotspots, oxidation supports cell growth and more oxidising biomass until oxygen or methane runs short

evidence.source: Conrad 1996, Microbiological Reviews 60:609-640
evidence.claim: Low-affinity methanotroph populations grow when exposed to high CH4, raising the oxidation capacity of the soil.

s990.label: Actinomycetes: Streptomyces hyphal life cycle, extracellular enzymes and antibiotics

evidence.source: Flardh & Buttner 2009, Nature Reviews Microbiology 7:36-49 (Streptomyces morphogenetic differentiation)
evidence.claim: Streptomyces grows as vegetative mycelium by tip extension, then forms aerial hyphae and spores when conditions deteriorate.

s991.label: Start: Streptomyces spore meets moisture and nutrients

evidence.source: Flardh & Buttner 2009, Nature Reviews Microbiology 7:36-49 (Streptomyces morphogenetic differentiation)
evidence.claim: Streptomyces grows as vegetative mycelium by tip extension, then forms aerial hyphae and spores when conditions deteriorate.

s992.label: End: Spores dispersed, nutrients and secondary metabolites released

evidence.source: Flardh & Buttner 2009, Nature Reviews Microbiology 7:36-49 (Streptomyces morphogenetic differentiation)
evidence.claim: Streptomyces grows as vegetative mycelium by tip extension, then forms aerial hyphae and spores when conditions deteriorate.

s993.label: Dormant spore germinates in a wet, nutrient-rich pulse and sends out a germ tube

evidence.source: Flardh & Buttner 2009, Nature Reviews Microbiology 7:36-49
evidence.claim: Spores germinate and grow out as hyphae when water and nutrients are available.

s994.label: Vegetative mycelium grows by tip extension and branching, penetrating particles and secreting hydrolases (chitinase, cellulase, xylanase)

evidence.source: Chater et al. 2010, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 34:171-198 (The complex extracellular biology of Streptomyces)
evidence.claim: Streptomyces secretes a large set of hydrolytic enzymes, with up to about 800 predicted secreted proteins in S. coelicolor.

s995.label: Resource depletion sensed: substrate mycelium partly lyses and the colony switches to aerial hyphae

evidence.source: Chater 2006, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 361:761-768 (Streptomyces inside-out: a new perspective on the bacteria that provide us with antibiotics)
evidence.claim: Programmed cell death of the vegetative mycelium releases nutrients that fuel aerial hyphae and sporulation. Shares are an estimate for a typical soil microsite and are not measured.

s996.label: Secondary metabolism switches on: antibiotics, siderophores and geosmin made as growth slows

evidence.source: van der Meij et al. 2017, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 41:392-416 (Chemical ecology of antibiotic production by actinomycetes)
evidence.claim: Antibiotic production is tied to nutrient limitation, competition cues and development.

s997.label: A single genome carries about 20-30 biosynthetic gene clusters (S. coelicolor: 8.67 Mb, 7,825 genes, over 20 clusters)

evidence.source: Bentley et al. 2002, Nature 417:141-147 (Complete genome sequence of the model actinomycete Streptomyces coelicolor A3(2))
evidence.claim: 8.67 Mb linear chromosome with 7,825 predicted genes and at least 20 clusters for secondary metabolites.

s998.label: Antibiotics suppress competing bacteria and fungi and at low dose act as signals that alter neighbour gene expression

evidence.source: Raaijmakers & Mazzola 2012, Annual Review of Phytopathology 50:403-424 (Diversity and natural functions of antibiotics produced by beneficial and pathogenic soil bacteria)
evidence.claim: Soil antibiotics inhibit competitors and, at sub-inhibitory levels, regulate community members.

s999.label: Neighbours evolve resistance, so antibiotic production and resistance co-escalate

evidence.source: D'Costa et al. 2006, Science 311:374-377 (Sampling the antibiotic resistome)
evidence.claim: Soil Streptomyces isolates from a collection were multidrug resistant, with resistance to many antibiotics of both natural and synthetic origin.

s1000.label: Gram-positive thick walls and spores allow activity at low water potential, so actinobacteria are enriched in drying soil

evidence.source: Naylor & Coleman-Derr 2018, Frontiers in Microbiology 9:2223 (Drought stress and root-associated bacterial communities)
evidence.claim: Actinobacteria (monoderm) are consistently enriched in the roots and soils of drought-stressed plants.

s1001.label: Aerial hyphae produce spore chains; geosmin released attracts springtails that eat and disperse spores

evidence.source: Becher et al. 2020, Nature Microbiology 5:821-829 (Developmentally regulated volatiles geosmin and 2-methylisoborneol attract a soil arthropod to Streptomyces bacteria promoting spore dispersal)
evidence.claim: Geosmin acts as an olfactory cue for Folsomia candida, and springtails carry viable spores in guts and on cuticles.

s1002.label: Frankia fixes N2 in actinorhizal nodules (alder, Casuarina), using vesicles with a hopanoid lipid envelope as oxygen barrier

evidence.source: Berry et al. 1993, PNAS 90:6091-6094 (Hopanoid lipids compose the Frankia vesicle envelope, presumptive barrier of oxygen diffusion to nitrogenase)
evidence.claim: Frankia vesicle envelopes are made of hopanoid lipids that restrict O2 diffusion to nitrogenase.

s1003.label: Death and lysis of colonies return amino sugars and cell wall carbon to the soil organic pool

evidence.source: Chater et al. 2010, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 34:171-198
evidence.claim: Programmed lysis recycles colony material, and hyphal necromass is rich in peptidoglycan amino sugars.

s1004.label: Atmospheric dust deposition and loess as soil parent material

evidence.source: Pye (1995) Quaternary Science Reviews 14:653-667, The nature, origin and accumulation of loess
evidence.claim: Loess and loess-like silt mantle roughly 10% of the land surface and reach tens to hundreds of metres in thickness.

s1005.label: Start: Atmospheric dust deposition and loess as soil parent material

evidence.source: Pye (1995) Quaternary Science Reviews 14:653-667, The nature, origin and accumulation of loess
evidence.claim: Loess and loess-like silt mantle roughly 10% of the land surface and reach tens to hundreds of metres in thickness.

s1006.label: End: Atmospheric dust deposition and loess as soil parent material

evidence.source: Pye (1995) Quaternary Science Reviews 14:653-667, The nature, origin and accumulation of loess
evidence.claim: Loess and loess-like silt mantle roughly 10% of the land surface and reach tens to hundreds of metres in thickness.

s1007.label: Wind lifts silt and clay from arid, glacial-outwash and dry-lake surfaces

evidence.source: Kok et al. (2021) Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 21:8169-8193
evidence.claim: North Africa and Asia supply most global dust emission, roughly 1,000-3,000 Tg per year.

s1008.label: Dust travels days to weeks and settles by gravity and rain washout

evidence.source: Jickells et al. (2005) Science 308:67-71, Global iron connections between desert dust, ocean biogeochemistry and climate
evidence.claim: Atmospheric transport carries dust over ocean basins before dry and wet deposition.

evidence.source: Jickells et al. (2005) Science 308:67-71
evidence.claim: Model estimates place deposition to the ocean at roughly a quarter to a third of total dust deposition and the rest on land; shares are model dependent (estimate 70/30).

s1010.label: Dust adds phosphorus, calcium and fine particles to downwind soils (Saharan dust supplies the Amazon with about 22,000 t P per year)

evidence.source: Yu et al. (2015) Geophysical Research Letters 42:1984-1991, The fertilizing role of African dust in the Amazon rainforest
evidence.claim: About 28 Tg of Saharan dust per year reaches the Amazon basin, carrying roughly 22 Gg of phosphorus, comparable to the P lost by leaching and runoff.

s1011.label: Dust iron reaches high-nutrient low-chlorophyll ocean regions and relieves iron limitation of phytoplankton

evidence.source: Martin (1990) Paleoceanography 5:1-13, Glacial-interglacial CO2 change: the iron hypothesis; Jickells et al. 2005
evidence.claim: Iron supply from dust controls productivity in the Southern Ocean, equatorial and subarctic Pacific.

s1012.label: Persistent deposition builds silt-rich, carbonate-rich loess that weathers into fertile soil

evidence.source: Pye (1995) Quaternary Science Reviews 14:653-667
evidence.claim: Loess is a silt-dominated, often calcareous sediment; Chinese Loess Plateau deposits reach 200-300 m.

s1013.label: Wind erosion and dust emission from dry soil

evidence.source: Shao (2008) Physics and Modelling of Wind Erosion, 2nd ed., Springer
evidence.claim: Dust emission is governed by threshold friction velocity, soil moisture, surface roughness and particle size.

s1014.label: Start: Wind erosion and dust emission from dry soil

evidence.source: Shao (2008) Physics and Modelling of Wind Erosion, 2nd ed., Springer
evidence.claim: Dust emission is governed by threshold friction velocity, soil moisture, surface roughness and particle size.

s1015.label: End: Wind erosion and dust emission from dry soil

evidence.source: Shao (2008) Physics and Modelling of Wind Erosion, 2nd ed., Springer
evidence.claim: Dust emission is governed by threshold friction velocity, soil moisture, surface roughness and particle size.

s1016.label: Drought, grazing or tillage lowers vegetation cover and dries the surface soil

evidence.source: Webb & Strong (2011) Aeolian Research 3:165-179, Soil erodibility dynamics and its representation for wind erosion and dust emission models
evidence.claim: Cover, crusting and surface moisture control erodibility; small moisture increases raise the threshold sharply.

s1017.label: Wind friction speed exceeds a threshold (about 0.2-0.5 m/s for loose bare soil) and sand grains begin to hop

evidence.source: Marticorena & Bergametti (1995) Journal of Geophysical Research 100:16415-16430, Modeling the atmospheric dust cycle: design of a soil-derived dust emission scheme
evidence.claim: Threshold friction velocity for dust emission varies with roughness and particle size, typically a few tens of cm/s.

s1018.label: Sandblasting by saltating grains breaks aggregates and releases silt and clay; flux scales with roughly the cube of friction velocity above threshold

evidence.source: Gillette & Passi (1988) Journal of Geophysical Research 93:14233-14242; Shao (2008)
evidence.claim: Vertical dust flux is proportional to horizontal saltation flux, which scales as friction velocity cubed.

s1019.label: Global dust emission is about 1,700 Tg per year, mostly from North Africa and Asian deserts

evidence.source: Kok et al. (2021) ACP 21:8169-8193; Huneeus et al. (2011) ACP 11:7781-7816 (AeroCom median 1,840 Tg)
evidence.claim: Independent syntheses place global emission of dust below 20 micrometres near 1,700-1,800 Tg per year with a factor-of-two uncertainty.

s1020.label: Topsoil loses its finest, most organic and nutrient-rich fraction; remaining soil coarsens and holds less water

evidence.source: Larney et al. (1998) Journal of Soil and Water Conservation 53:133-140, Wind erosion effects on nutrient redistribution and soil productivity
evidence.claim: Eroded material is enriched in organic carbon and nutrients relative to the parent soil.

s1021.label: Soil-atmosphere exchange of methane and nitrous oxide

evidence.source: Saunois et al. (2020) Earth System Science Data 12:1561-1623, The Global Methane Budget 2000-2017; Tian et al. (2020) Nature 586:248-256
evidence.claim: Soils are a net methane sink of about 30 Tg CH4 per year and the largest nitrous oxide source.

s1022.label: Start: Soil-atmosphere exchange of methane and nitrous oxide

evidence.source: Saunois et al. (2020) Earth System Science Data 12:1561-1623, The Global Methane Budget 2000-2017; Tian et al. (2020) Nature 586:248-256
evidence.claim: Soils are a net methane sink of about 30 Tg CH4 per year and the largest nitrous oxide source.

s1023.label: End: Soil-atmosphere exchange of methane and nitrous oxide

evidence.source: Saunois et al. (2020) Earth System Science Data 12:1561-1623, The Global Methane Budget 2000-2017; Tian et al. (2020) Nature 586:248-256
evidence.claim: Soils are a net methane sink of about 30 Tg CH4 per year and the largest nitrous oxide source.

s1024.label: Aerated upland soil oxidises atmospheric Methane with high-affinity methanotrophs

evidence.source: Knief (2015) Frontiers in Microbiology 6:1346
evidence.claim: Uncultivated upland-soil methanotrophs (USC-alpha, USC-gamma) consume methane at near-atmospheric mixing ratios.

s1025.label: Methane uptake is limited by diffusion: wet or compacted soil slows uptake, ammonium fertiliser inhibits it

evidence.source: Smith et al. (2000) Global Change Biology 6:791-803; Aronson & Helliker (2010) Ecology 91:3242-3251
evidence.claim: Uptake rises as soil dries and falls with nitrogen addition (meta-analysis).

s1026.label: Nitrous oxide emission peaks at about 60-70% water-filled pore space where nitrification and denitrification both run

evidence.source: Bateman & Baggs (2005) Biology and Fertility of Soils 41:379-388
evidence.claim: Nitrification dominates N2O at 35-60% WFPS, denitrification at about 70% and above.

s1027.label: Above about 80% water-filled pore space denitrification runs on to N2 and the N2O share falls

evidence.source: Davidson & Verchot (2000) Global Biogeochemical Cycles 14:1035-1043
evidence.claim: N2O:N2 product ratio decreases as soils become wetter and more reduced.

s1028.label: Soils emit about 6 Tg N per year of N2O naturally; fertiliser and manure add about 4 Tg N

evidence.source: Tian et al. (2020) Nature 586:248-256
evidence.claim: Global N2O emission 17 Tg N per year (2007-2016); natural soils around 6-7 Tg N, agriculture 3.8 Tg N.

s1029.label: Nitrous oxide persists about 109 years with 100-year warming potency of about 273 times CO2; methane sink offsets only a little

evidence.source: IPCC AR6 WGI (2021) Chapter 7, Table 7.15
evidence.claim: N2O lifetime 109 years and GWP-100 of 273; CH4 GWP-100 about 27-30.

s1030.label: Soil export to rivers and ocean: sediment, dissolved carbon and nutrients

evidence.source: Cole et al. (2007) Ecosystems 10:172-185, Plumbing the global carbon cycle; Syvitski et al. (2005) Science 308:376-380
evidence.claim: Inland waters receive about 1.9 Pg C per year from land and rivers deliver roughly 12-13 Gt of sediment per year to the ocean.

s1031.label: Start: Soil export to rivers and ocean: sediment, dissolved carbon and nutrients

evidence.source: Cole et al. (2007) Ecosystems 10:172-185, Plumbing the global carbon cycle; Syvitski et al. (2005) Science 308:376-380
evidence.claim: Inland waters receive about 1.9 Pg C per year from land and rivers deliver roughly 12-13 Gt of sediment per year to the ocean.

s1032.label: End: Soil export to rivers and ocean: sediment, dissolved carbon and nutrients

evidence.source: Cole et al. (2007) Ecosystems 10:172-185, Plumbing the global carbon cycle; Syvitski et al. (2005) Science 308:376-380
evidence.claim: Inland waters receive about 1.9 Pg C per year from land and rivers deliver roughly 12-13 Gt of sediment per year to the ocean.

s1033.label: Rain beyond infiltration capacity or on saturated soil produces runoff and subsurface drainage

evidence.source: Hillel (1998) Environmental Soil Physics, Academic Press
evidence.claim: Runoff occurs when rain intensity exceeds infiltration or the profile is saturated.

s1034.label: Runoff and erosion carry particles; rivers deliver about 12-13 Gt of sediment per year to the ocean

evidence.source: Syvitski et al. (2005) Science 308:376-380
evidence.claim: Humans raised soil-erosion sediment flux but reservoirs trap more; net delivery near 12.6 Gt per year.

s1035.label: Drainage leaches dissolved organic carbon from organic horizons; rivers carry about 0.2-0.4 Gt C per year to the ocean

evidence.source: Ludwig et al. (1996) Global Biogeochemical Cycles 10:23-41; Dai et al. (2012) Global Biogeochemical Cycles 26:GB3026
evidence.claim: Riverine DOC export to the ocean is of order 0.2-0.4 Pg C per year.

s1036.label: Nitrate and particulate phosphorus reach the coast and drive eutrophication and hypoxia

evidence.source: Diaz & Rosenberg (2008) Science 321:926-929, Spreading dead zones
evidence.claim: More than 400 coastal dead zones, most linked to land nutrient loading.

s1037.label: Part of the eroded soil carbon is buried in floodplains, reservoirs and coastal sediment instead of respired (about 0.12 Gt C per year sink)

evidence.source: Van Oost et al. (2007) Science 318:626-629
evidence.claim: Erosion-deposition on agricultural land creates a sink of about 0.12 Pg C per year, with large uncertainty.

s1038.label: Soil viruses and bacteriophages: lysis, lysogeny and the viral shunt

evidence.source: Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 127:305-317 (Viruses in soil: nano-scale undead drivers of microbial life, biogeochemical turnover and ecosystem functions)
evidence.claim: Soil viruses are abundant and their lysis of hosts releases cell carbon and nitrogen, while the rates are poorly quantified in soil.

s1039.label: Start: Phage particle meets a host cell in a water film

evidence.source: Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 127:305-317 (Viruses in soil: nano-scale undead drivers of microbial life, biogeochemical turnover and ecosystem functions)
evidence.claim: Soil viruses are abundant and their lysis of hosts releases cell carbon and nitrogen, while the rates are poorly quantified in soil.

s1040.label: End: Host killed or converted; lysate carbon and nitrogen returned

evidence.source: Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 127:305-317 (Viruses in soil: nano-scale undead drivers of microbial life, biogeochemical turnover and ecosystem functions)
evidence.claim: Soil viruses are abundant and their lysis of hosts releases cell carbon and nitrogen, while the rates are poorly quantified in soil.

s1041.label: Virus-like particles number about 10^8-10^9 per gram dry soil, usually exceeding or matching bacterial counts

evidence.source: Williamson, Radosevich & Wommack 2005, Applied and Environmental Microbiology 71:3119-3125 (Abundance and diversity of viruses in six Delaware soils)
evidence.claim: Direct counts of 1.5x10^8 to 1.1x10^9 virus-like particles per gram of dry soil across six soils, with virus-to-bacterium ratios near 1-8 in most.

s1042.label: Contact is limited to connected water films; clay and organic matter adsorb phage and can protect or inactivate them

evidence.source: Kimura, Jia, Nakayama & Asakawa 2008, Soil Science and Plant Nutrition 54:1-32 (Ecology of viruses in soils: past, present and future perspectives)
evidence.claim: Soil viruses adsorb to clay and organic colloids, which limits their transport to hosts and affects persistence of infectivity.

s1043.label: Infection outcome: lytic cycle, lysogeny, or failed infection by host defence

evidence.source: Williamson et al. 2007, Environmental Microbiology 9:2563-2574 (Incidence of lysogeny within temperate and extreme soil environments)
evidence.claim: Inducible prophage were detected in a large share of soil bacteria in many temperate and extreme soils, so both strategies occur. Shares below are estimates (about 35-65% lytic) and not measured in situ.

s1044.label: Lytic cycle: phage takes over the host, replicates and bursts the cell, with a burst of tens to hundreds of particles

evidence.source: Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 127:305-317
evidence.claim: Lytic phage destroy host cells and release new virions together with the cell contents.

s1045.label: Phage-encoded auxiliary metabolic genes (glycoside hydrolases and others) rewire host carbon metabolism during infection

evidence.source: Emerson et al. 2018, Nature Microbiology 3:870-880 (Host-linked soil viral ecology along a permafrost thaw gradient)
evidence.claim: Of 1,907 viral populations recovered from Stordalen Mire, genes for carbon degradation such as glycoside hydrolases were found on soil viruses.

s1046.label: Viral shunt: lysate (labile carbon, amino acids, nucleotides, ammonium) goes back to the dissolved pool instead of up the grazer food web

evidence.source: Suttle 2007, Nature Reviews Microbiology 5:801-812 (Marine viruses, major leaders in the global ecosystem)
evidence.claim: The viral shunt concept: lysis converts particulate cell carbon and nutrients into dissolved pools, increasing respiration and nutrient recycling. Defined for the ocean, applied to soil by Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018.

s1047.label: Phages in microcosms raised soil nitrate and ammonium availability and reshaped the bacterial community

evidence.source: Braga et al. 2020, Microbiome 8:52 (Impact of phages on soil bacterial communities and nitrogen availability under different assembly scenarios)
evidence.claim: Adding a phage mix to soil microcosms changed bacterial community composition and increased available nitrogen in some assembly scenarios.

s1048.label: Lysogeny: prophage integrates in the host genome, giving immunity to related phage and passing to daughter cells

evidence.source: Williamson et al. 2007, Environmental Microbiology 9:2563-2574
evidence.claim: Inducible prophage detected in bacterial isolates from soil, indicating a stable lysogenic state.

s1049.label: Stress (DNA damage, starvation, drying and rewetting) can induce prophage and switch cells to the lytic cycle

evidence.source: Williamson et al. 2007, Environmental Microbiology 9:2563-2574
evidence.claim: Mitomycin C and other induction agents triggered lytic release of prophage in soil bacterial assemblages.

s1050.label: Resistant hosts (receptor mutation, CRISPR-Cas, restriction) survive, and phage evolve counter-infectivity in an arms race

evidence.source: Gomez & Buckling 2011, Science 332:106-109 (Bacteria-phage antagonistic coevolution in soil)
evidence.claim: In soil, Pseudomonas fluorescens and phage showed antagonistic coevolution, with phages driving rapid bacterial resistance evolution and soil-specific limits on the dynamics.

s1051.label: Dominant hosts are infected most often, which caps their abundance (kill-the-winner) and preserves diversity

evidence.source: Thingstad 2000, Limnology and Oceanography 45:1320-1328 (Elements of a theory for the mechanisms controlling abundance, diversity, and biogeochemical role of lytic bacterial viruses in aquatic systems)
evidence.claim: Lytic viral attack scaled to host abundance suppresses the best competitors; mostly shown in aquatic systems and not proven for soil.

s1052.label: Excess mineral nitrogen represses ligninolytic enzyme synthesis in late-stage litter

evidence.source: Carreiro, Sinsabaugh, Repert & Parkhurst (2000) Ecology 81:2359-2365, Microbial enzyme shifts explain litter decay responses to simulated nitrogen deposition
evidence.claim: Added N raised hydrolase activity but suppressed phenol oxidase and peroxidase activity in high-lignin litter, slowing late-stage decay

evidence.source: Fog (1988) Biological Reviews 63:433-462, The effect of added nitrogen on the rate of decomposition of organic matter
evidence.claim: N addition stimulates early decay of low-lignin litter but inhibits decay of lignified litter

s1053.label: Comammox Nitrospira oxidize ammonium directly to nitrate in one organism

evidence.source: Daims et al. (2015) Nature 528:504-509, Complete nitrification by Nitrospira bacteria
evidence.claim: Nitrospira inopinata oxidises ammonia through nitrite to nitrate by itself

evidence.source: van Kessel et al. (2015) Nature 528:555-559, Complete nitrification by a single microorganism
evidence.claim: Candidatus Nitrospira nitrosa enriched from an aquaculture biofilter carries all genes for complete ammonia oxidation

s1054.label: Microbial thermal acclimation and substrate depletion partly restore CUE under sustained warming

evidence.source: Frey, Lee, Melillo & Six (2013) Nature Climate Change 3:395-398, The temperature response of soil microbial efficiency and its feedback to climate
evidence.claim: After long-term warming the CUE response to temperature was small or absent, contrary to a constant decline

evidence.source: Tucker, Bell, Pendall & Ogle (2013) Global Change Biology 19:252-263
evidence.claim: Declining CUE explains only part of thermal acclimation of soil respiration

s1055.label: Pyrite oxidation and acid sulfate weathering

evidence.source: Nordstrom (1982), Aqueous pyrite oxidation and the consequent formation of secondary iron minerals, in Acid Sulfate Weathering, SSSA Special Publication 10, pp. 37-56
evidence.claim: Overall reaction FeS2 + 15/4 O2 + 7/2 H2O gives Fe(OH)3 + 2 SO4(2-) + 4 H+, so each mole of pyrite makes up to 4 mol H+.

s1056.label: Start: Pyrite oxidation and acid sulfate weathering

evidence.source: Nordstrom (1982), Aqueous pyrite oxidation and the consequent formation of secondary iron minerals, in Acid Sulfate Weathering, SSSA Special Publication 10, pp. 37-56
evidence.claim: Overall reaction FeS2 + 15/4 O2 + 7/2 H2O gives Fe(OH)3 + 2 SO4(2-) + 4 H+, so each mole of pyrite makes up to 4 mol H+.

s1057.label: End: Pyrite oxidation and acid sulfate weathering

evidence.source: Nordstrom (1982), Aqueous pyrite oxidation and the consequent formation of secondary iron minerals, in Acid Sulfate Weathering, SSSA Special Publication 10, pp. 37-56
evidence.claim: Overall reaction FeS2 + 15/4 O2 + 7/2 H2O gives Fe(OH)3 + 2 SO4(2-) + 4 H+, so each mole of pyrite makes up to 4 mol H+.

s1058.label: Pyrite is exposed to Oxygen when drainage lowers the water table or sulfidic sediment is excavated

evidence.source: Dent & Pons (1995), A world perspective on acid sulphate soils, Geoderma 67:263-276
evidence.claim: Acid sulfate soils form when sulfidic (pyritic) material is drained and aerated; pyrite is stable only while saturated.

s1059.label: Oxygen oxidises pyrite: Fe2+ and sulfate are released, giving about 2 mol H+ per mol FeS2 before Fe2+ is oxidised

evidence.source: Nordstrom (1982), SSSA Special Publication 10, pp. 37-56
evidence.claim: FeS2 + 7/2 O2 + H2O gives Fe2+ + 2 SO4(2-) + 2 H+; the Fe2+ then oxidises and hydrolyses to give 2 more H+.

s1060.label: Fork: does solution pH fall below about 4 (no carbonate to buffer)

evidence.source: Dent & Pons (1995), Geoderma 67:263-276
evidence.claim: Acid sulfate soils are defined by pH below about 4 after oxidation; soils with carbonate stay near pH 6-8. Probabilities are an estimate (40 to 60 percent range) for drained coastal sulfidic sediments.

s1061.label: Fe2+ oxidation is rate-limiting; Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans speeds it by orders of magnitude (about 10^5 to 10^6) below pH 3.5

evidence.source: Singer & Stumm (1970), Acidic mine drainage: the rate-determining step, Science 167:1121-1123
evidence.claim: Abiotic oxidation of Fe2+ is very slow at low pH; iron-oxidising bacteria accelerate it by several orders of magnitude.

s1062.label: Fe3+ attacks pyrite directly, 10 to 100 times faster than Oxygen, making more Fe2+ and acid

evidence.source: Moses, Nordstrom, Herman & Mills (1987), Aqueous pyrite oxidation by dissolved oxygen and by ferric iron, Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta 51:1561-1571
evidence.claim: Ferric iron is a far faster pyrite oxidant than dissolved oxygen at low pH, and the cycle Fe2+ to Fe3+ to Fe2+ is self-propagating.

s1063.label: Sulfuric acid dissolves clays and releases Al3+; jarosite forms as yellow mottles below about pH 3.7

evidence.source: Van Breemen & Buurman (2002), Soil Formation, 2nd ed., Springer, chapter on acid sulphate soils
evidence.claim: Jarosite KFe3(SO4)2(OH)6 is stable below pH of about 3.7 and marks acid sulfate soil horizons; clay dissolution releases Al.

s1064.label: Calcite and exchangeable bases neutralise acid (CaCO3 consumes 2 mol H+ per mol) and raise pH

evidence.source: Stumm & Morgan (1996), Aquatic Chemistry, 3rd ed., Wiley, carbonate buffer chapter
evidence.claim: CaCO3 + 2H+ gives Ca2+ + CO2 + H2O, so carbonate neutralises acid stoichiometrically until exhausted.

s1065.label: Acid, Al and sulfate drain to ditches and estuaries and cause fish kills and metal release

evidence.source: Sammut, Melville, Callinan & Fraser (1996), Estuarine acidification and fish kills in the Richmond River, Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science 43
evidence.claim: Drainage of sulfidic floodplain soils exported acid and aluminium pulses that caused fish kills in Australian coastal rivers.

s1066.label: Volcanic ash weathering to allophane and imogolite (andic soils)

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993), Volcanic Ash Soils: Genesis, Properties and Utilization, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Volcanic ash glass weathers rapidly to short-range-order Al-Si minerals and Al-humus complexes, and these dominate the colloid fraction of Andosols.

s1067.label: Start: Volcanic ash weathering to allophane and imogolite (andic soils)

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993), Volcanic Ash Soils: Genesis, Properties and Utilization, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Volcanic ash glass weathers rapidly to short-range-order Al-Si minerals and Al-humus complexes, and these dominate the colloid fraction of Andosols.

s1068.label: End: Volcanic ash weathering to allophane and imogolite (andic soils)

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993), Volcanic Ash Soils: Genesis, Properties and Utilization, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Volcanic ash glass weathers rapidly to short-range-order Al-Si minerals and Al-humus complexes, and these dominate the colloid fraction of Andosols.

s1069.label: Volcanic ash (Si-Al-rich glass) is deposited as young parent material

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993), Volcanic Ash Soils, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Tephra glass has a large surface area and weathers faster than crystalline silicates.

s1070.label: Glass hydrolyses within centuries in humid, well-drained conditions, releasing Al3+ and Si(OH)4

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993), Volcanic Ash Soils, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Weathering of basaltic to andesitic ash in humid climates forms allophane within decades to centuries.

s1071.label: Fork: strongly acidic humus-rich soil versus weakly acidic to neutral soil

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993), Volcanic Ash Soils, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Below about pH 5 with abundant humus, Al is complexed by organic matter (non-allophanic Andosols); above about pH 5 Al and Si co-precipitate as allophane. Shares are an estimate (range 35 to 60 percent).

s1072.label: Al-humus complexes form and hold Al so it is not available to precipitate with Si

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993), Volcanic Ash Soils, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Organic ligands complex Al, preventing allophane formation and producing Al-humus Andosols.

s1073.label: Al and Si co-precipitate as allophane spherules (about 3.5 to 5 nm) and imogolite tubes (about 2 nm outer diameter)

evidence.source: Parfitt (2009), Allophane and imogolite: role in soil biogeochemical processes, Clay Minerals 44:135-155
evidence.claim: Allophane is a hollow nanosphere of 3.5-5 nm diameter; imogolite is a tube about 2 nm outer diameter.

s1074.label: Large variable-charge surface (several hundred m2 per g) retains over 85 percent of added phosphate and binds organic carbon

evidence.source: Soil Survey Staff (2014), Keys to Soil Taxonomy, 12th ed., USDA-NRCS, andic soil properties
evidence.claim: Andic soil materials require phosphate retention of 85 percent or more and high oxalate-extractable Al + 0.5 Fe.

s1075.label: Open allophane aggregates give bulk density below 0.9 g per cm3 and very high water retention

evidence.source: Soil Survey Staff (2014), Keys to Soil Taxonomy, 12th ed., USDA-NRCS
evidence.claim: Andic soil properties include bulk density of 0.90 g per cm3 or less at 33 kPa.

s1076.label: With drying and Si accumulation allophane converts slowly to halloysite over thousands of years

evidence.source: Parfitt (2009), Clay Minerals 44:135-155
evidence.claim: Allophane is metastable and in drier or Si-rich settings alters to halloysite over millennia.

s1077.label: Pedogenic carbonate accumulation and calcrete formation

evidence.source: Gile, Peterson & Grossman (1966), Morphological and genetic sequences of carbonate accumulation in desert soils, Soil Science 101:347-360
evidence.claim: Carbonate accumulates in sequential morphological stages from filaments to plugged and laminar horizons in desert soils.

s1078.label: Start: Pedogenic carbonate accumulation and calcrete formation

evidence.source: Gile, Peterson & Grossman (1966), Morphological and genetic sequences of carbonate accumulation in desert soils, Soil Science 101:347-360
evidence.claim: Carbonate accumulates in sequential morphological stages from filaments to plugged and laminar horizons in desert soils.

s1079.label: End: Pedogenic carbonate accumulation and calcrete formation

evidence.source: Gile, Peterson & Grossman (1966), Morphological and genetic sequences of carbonate accumulation in desert soils, Soil Science 101:347-360
evidence.claim: Carbonate accumulates in sequential morphological stages from filaments to plugged and laminar horizons in desert soils.

s1080.label: Dust and rain deliver Ca2+ and carbonate to the surface of arid and semi-arid soils

evidence.source: Machette (1985), Calcic soils of the southwestern United States, GSA Special Paper 203:1-21
evidence.claim: Eolian dust and rain are the main Ca sources for calcic horizons where parent material has little carbonate.

s1081.label: Infiltrating water dissolves carbonate in the wetter upper profile as soil CO2 raises carbonic acid

evidence.source: Breecker, Sharp & McFadden (2009), Seasonal bias in the formation and stable isotopic composition of pedogenic carbonate in modern soils, GSA Bulletin 121:630-640
evidence.claim: Soil CO2 from root and microbial respiration drives dissolution and sets carbonate precipitation conditions.

s1082.label: Evapotranspiration removes water and CO2 degasses, so Ca2+ + 2HCO3- precipitates as CaCO3

evidence.source: Breecker, Sharp & McFadden (2009), GSA Bulletin 121:630-640
evidence.claim: Pedogenic carbonate forms mainly in dry seasons when the soil dries and pCO2 is low.

s1083.label: Nodules and coatings concentrate at the mean wetting depth, which rises with mean annual precipitation

evidence.source: Retallack (2005), Pedogenic carbonate proxies for amount and seasonality of precipitation in paleosols, Geology 33:333-336
evidence.claim: Depth to the Bk carbonate horizon correlates with mean annual precipitation in modern soils.

s1084.label: Pores fill and cement into a plugged horizon (Gile stage III to IV) that limits infiltration and root penetration

evidence.source: Gile, Peterson & Grossman (1966), Soil Science 101:347-360
evidence.claim: Carbonate plugs all pores in stage III and forms laminar caps in stage IV, restricting water and roots.

s1085.label: Calcite equilibrium buffers pH at 7.5 to 8.5; phosphate precipitates as Ca phosphates and Fe, Zn and Mn availability falls

evidence.source: Lindsay (1979), Chemical Equilibria in Soils, Wiley
evidence.claim: Calcareous soils sit at pH 7.5 to 8.4, where micronutrient cation solubility is very low and phosphate precipitates with Ca.

s1086.label: Soil inorganic carbon stores on the order of 700 to 950 Pg C in the top metre globally

evidence.source: Lal (2004), Soil carbon sequestration impacts on global climate change and food security, Science 304:1623-1627
evidence.claim: Soil inorganic carbon pool estimated at roughly 695-940 Pg C in the top metre.

s1087.label: Phosphate sorption on Fe and Al oxides and phosphorus availability

evidence.source: Parfitt (1978), Anion adsorption by soils and soil materials, Advances in Agronomy 30:1-50
evidence.claim: Phosphate is adsorbed by ligand exchange with surface OH groups on Fe and Al oxides and short-range-order minerals.

s1088.label: Start: Phosphate sorption on Fe and Al oxides and phosphorus availability

evidence.source: Parfitt (1978), Anion adsorption by soils and soil materials, Advances in Agronomy 30:1-50
evidence.claim: Phosphate is adsorbed by ligand exchange with surface OH groups on Fe and Al oxides and short-range-order minerals.

s1089.label: End: Phosphate sorption on Fe and Al oxides and phosphorus availability

evidence.source: Parfitt (1978), Anion adsorption by soils and soil materials, Advances in Agronomy 30:1-50
evidence.claim: Phosphate is adsorbed by ligand exchange with surface OH groups on Fe and Al oxides and short-range-order minerals.

s1090.label: Soil solution holds only about 1 to 10 micromolar phosphate, far less than the amount in the solid phase

evidence.source: Schachtman, Reid & Ayling (1998), Phosphorus uptake by plants: from soil to cell, Plant Physiology 116:447-453
evidence.claim: Soil solution phosphate is typically about 1 micromolar or at most 10 micromolar, so P diffusion limits uptake.

s1091.label: Phosphate displaces OH and OH2 on goethite, gibbsite and allophane surfaces, forming inner-sphere complexes

evidence.source: Parfitt (1978), Advances in Agronomy 30:1-50
evidence.claim: Ligand exchange forms bidentate inner-sphere phosphate complexes; adsorption falls as pH rises.

s1092.label: Sorption capacity scales with oxalate-extractable Al + Fe, and saturation degree is phosphate divided by 0.5 times (Al + Fe)

evidence.source: Beauchemin & Simard (1999), Soil phosphorus saturation degree: review of some indices and their suitability for P management in Quebec, Canadian Journal of Soil Science 79:615-625
evidence.claim: The P saturation index uses oxalate P divided by alpha times (Al + Fe), with alpha about 0.5.

s1093.label: Slow solid-state diffusion into oxide micropores over days to years converts labile to occluded phosphate

evidence.source: Barrow (1983), A mechanistic model for describing the sorption and desorption of phosphate by soil, Journal of Soil Science 34:733-750
evidence.claim: Phosphate reacts in a fast adsorption stage (hours) followed by slow penetration into the solid (days to years).

s1094.label: Liming to pH 6 to 7 reduces positive surface charge on oxides and modestly raises phosphate availability

evidence.source: Haynes (1982), Effects of liming on phosphate availability in acid soils, Plant and Soil 68:289-308
evidence.claim: Liming increases phosphate availability through pH-dependent desorption, with effects that vary among soils.

s1095.label: Roots exude citrate, oxalate and acid phosphatase and form cluster roots, mobilising sorbed and organic phosphate

evidence.source: Lambers, Shane, Cramer, Pearse & Veneklaas (2006), Root structure and functioning for efficient acquisition of phosphorus, Annals of Botany 98:693-713
evidence.claim: Carboxylate release and cluster roots of Proteaceae and Lupinus mobilise phosphate from sorbed pools.

s1096.label: Low solution phosphate triggers more exudation and root proliferation, which lifts supply

evidence.source: Lambers et al. (2006), Annals of Botany 98:693-713
evidence.claim: P deficiency up-regulates carboxylate exudation and root hair density in many species.

s1097.label: Once sorbent saturation passes roughly 25 percent phosphate losses by leaching and runoff rise steeply

evidence.source: Sims, Edwards, Schoumans & Simard (2000), Integrating soil phosphorus testing into environmentally based agricultural management practices, Journal of Environmental Quality 29:60-71
evidence.claim: Change points in P loss versus soil P and degree of saturation indicate loss rises above a threshold.

s1098.label: Aluminium toxicity and liming of acid soils

evidence.source: Kamprath (1970), Exchangeable aluminum as a criterion for liming leached mineral soils, Soil Science Society of America Proceedings 34:252-254
evidence.claim: Lime requirement of leached mineral soils is based on neutralising exchangeable Al.

s1099.label: Start: Aluminium toxicity and liming of acid soils

evidence.source: Kamprath (1970), Exchangeable aluminum as a criterion for liming leached mineral soils, Soil Science Society of America Proceedings 34:252-254
evidence.claim: Lime requirement of leached mineral soils is based on neutralising exchangeable Al.

s1100.label: End: Aluminium toxicity and liming of acid soils

evidence.source: Kamprath (1970), Exchangeable aluminum as a criterion for liming leached mineral soils, Soil Science Society of America Proceedings 34:252-254
evidence.claim: Lime requirement of leached mineral soils is based on neutralising exchangeable Al.

s1101.label: Below pH 5.0 to 5.5 exchangeable Al3+ dominates the exchange complex

evidence.source: Kamprath (1970), Soil Science Society of America Proceedings 34:252-254
evidence.claim: Exchangeable Al appears in quantity below pH 5.5 in mineral soils and is the main acidity.

s1102.label: Al3+ hydrolyses (Al3+ + H2O gives AlOH2+ + H+), so Al buffers pH between about 3 and 4.5

evidence.source: Bloom, McBride & Weaver (1979), Aluminum organic matter in acid soils: buffering and solution aluminum activity, Soil Science Society of America Journal 43:488-493
evidence.claim: Al hydroxy species and Al-organic matter complexes buffer soil pH over this range.

s1103.label: Micromolar Al3+ inhibits root elongation within hours by damaging the root apex cell wall and membranes

evidence.source: Kochian (1995), Cellular mechanisms of aluminum toxicity and resistance in plants, Annual Review of Plant Physiology and Plant Molecular Biology 46:237-260
evidence.claim: Root growth inhibition by Al occurs at micromolar activities in the root apex.

s1104.label: Stunted roots take up less water, Ca, Mg and phosphate, lowering yield

evidence.source: Kochian, Hoekenga & Pineros (2004), How do crop plants tolerate acid soils? Annual Review of Plant Biology 55:459-493
evidence.claim: Al-damaged roots have reduced nutrient and water acquisition, a major yield limit on acid soils.

s1105.label: Lime dissolves (CaCO3 uses 2 mol H+ per mol), Ca2+ displaces Al3+ and Al precipitates as Al(OH)3

evidence.source: Kamprath (1970), Soil Science Society of America Proceedings 34:252-254
evidence.claim: Liming to neutralise exchangeable Al raises pH to about 5.5 and removes Al toxicity.

s1106.label: Surface-applied lime moves down slowly because of its low solubility, so subsoil acidity can persist

evidence.source: Brady & Weil, The Nature and Properties of Soils, 15th ed. (2016), ch. 9 on soil acidity
evidence.claim: Lime is sparingly soluble and moves little below the zone of incorporation without incorporation.

s1107.label: Nitrification, product removal and acid deposition re-acidify the soil over years

evidence.source: Helyar & Porter (1989), Soil acidification, its measurement and the processes involved, in Soil Acidity and Plant Growth, Academic Press
evidence.claim: Agricultural soils acidify by nitrification, removal of alkaline product and leaching; acidification rates are of order several kmol H+ per ha per year.

s1108.label: Biofilms and quorum signalling in soil microcolonies

evidence.source: Flemming & Wingender 2010, Nature Reviews Microbiology 8:623-633 (The biofilm matrix)
evidence.claim: The matrix of extracellular polymeric substances (polysaccharides, proteins, eDNA) makes up much of the biofilm organic carbon and holds cells to surfaces and each other.

s1109.label: Start: Cells land on a particle or root surface in a water film

evidence.source: Flemming & Wingender 2010, Nature Reviews Microbiology 8:623-633 (The biofilm matrix)
evidence.claim: The matrix of extracellular polymeric substances (polysaccharides, proteins, eDNA) makes up much of the biofilm organic carbon and holds cells to surfaces and each other.

s1110.label: End: Collective behaviour expressed or cells dispersed

evidence.source: Flemming & Wingender 2010, Nature Reviews Microbiology 8:623-633 (The biofilm matrix)
evidence.claim: The matrix of extracellular polymeric substances (polysaccharides, proteins, eDNA) makes up much of the biofilm organic carbon and holds cells to surfaces and each other.

s1111.label: Bacterial cells cover under 1% of mineral surface area, so most cells are isolated and microcolonies are patchy

evidence.source: Young, Crawford, Nunan, Otten & Spiers 2008, Advances in Agronomy 100:81-121 (Microbial distribution in soils: physics and scaling)
evidence.claim: Microbial cells occupy a very small fraction of the available soil surface and are clustered in microcolonies around organic substrates.

s1112.label: Cells attach to a surface using pili, flagella and adhesins, then secrete extracellular polymeric substances (EPS)

evidence.source: Flemming & Wingender 2010, Nature Reviews Microbiology 8:623-633
evidence.claim: Attachment and EPS production are early steps in biofilm formation; EPS can be 50-90% of the biofilm organic carbon.

s1113.label: Microcolony grows, matrix thickens, cell density in the pore rises

evidence.source: Flemming & Wingender 2010, Nature Reviews Microbiology 8:623-633
evidence.claim: Biofilms grow as dense multicellular aggregates in a self-produced matrix.

s1114.label: Signal fate in the pore: accumulates above threshold, is diluted away, or is destroyed

evidence.source: Redfield 2002, Trends in Microbiology 10:365-370 (Is quorum sensing a side effect of diffusion sensing?)
evidence.claim: Whether a diffusible signal accumulates depends on diffusion and mass transfer as well as cell density, so quorum may be a measure of confinement. Shares are an estimate for a typical soil colony and are not measured.

s1115.label: Gram-negative cells make acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL) with LuxI-type synthases

evidence.source: Fuqua, Winans & Greenberg 1994, Journal of Bacteriology 176:269-275 (Quorum sensing in bacteria: the LuxR-LuxI family of cell density-responsive transcriptional regulators)
evidence.claim: LuxI-type enzymes synthesise AHL signals that accumulate with cell density.

s1116.label: AHL binds a LuxR-type receptor above a threshold and the complex switches on target genes, including luxI itself (autoinduction)

evidence.source: Fuqua, Winans & Greenberg 1994, Journal of Bacteriology 176:269-275
evidence.claim: LuxR-AHL activates transcription including the signal synthase gene, creating positive feedback.

s1117.label: Quorum-controlled outputs: antibiotics (phenazines), exoenzymes, siderophores, more EPS

evidence.source: Pierson, Wood & Pierson 1998, Annual Review of Phytopathology 36:207-225 (Homoserine lactone-mediated gene regulation in plant-associated bacteria)
evidence.claim: Phenazine antibiotic production by Pseudomonas aureofaciens on wheat roots is regulated by AHL signalling.

s1118.label: Alkaline pH and warmth hydrolyse the AHL lactone ring, so signals persist longer in acid, cool soil

evidence.source: Yates et al. 2002, Infection and Immunity 70:5635-5646 (N-acylhomoserine lactones undergo lactonolysis in a pH-, temperature-, and acyl chain length-dependent manner)
evidence.claim: AHL half-life drops sharply as pH rises above neutral and with higher temperature and shorter acyl chains.

s1119.label: Quorum quenching: AHL lactonases (AiiA) and plant signal mimics degrade or confuse the signal

evidence.source: Dong et al. 2000, PNAS 97:3526-3531 (AiiA, an enzyme that inactivates the acylhomoserine lactone quorum-sensing signal)
evidence.claim: The AiiA lactonase from Bacillus inactivates AHL signals by hydrolysis.

s1120.label: Signal-blind cheaters use public goods without paying the cost, and may spread

evidence.source: Diggle, Griffin, Campbell & West 2007, Nature 450:411-414 (Cooperation and conflict in quorum-sensing bacterial populations)
evidence.claim: Quorum-sensing mutants can exploit cooperative production of public goods and reduce productivity, unless cooperation is stabilised.

s1121.label: EPS retains water and buffers drying, so matrix-rich cells survive desiccation better

evidence.source: Roberson & Firestone 1992, Applied and Environmental Microbiology 58:1284-1291 (Relationship between desiccation and exopolysaccharide production in a soil Pseudomonas sp.)
evidence.claim: EPS-rich Pseudomonas cells held more water and survived desiccation better than low-EPS cells.

s1122.label: EPS and cells glue mineral particles into aggregates and raise aggregate stability

evidence.source: Costa, Raaijmakers & Kuramae 2018, Frontiers in Microbiology 9:1636 (Microbial extracellular polymeric substances: ecological function and impact on soil aggregation)
evidence.claim: EPS bind particles and contribute to soil aggregation and water retention.

s1123.label: Close packing and the matrix raise gene transfer: conjugative plasmids can induce biofilm formation

evidence.source: Ghigo 2001, Nature 412:442-445 (Natural conjugative plasmids induce bacterial biofilm development)
evidence.claim: Conjugative plasmids encode factors that promote biofilm formation, favouring their own transfer.

s1124.label: Nutrient decline signals cells to leave (lower cyclic-di-GMP) and disperse to new surfaces

evidence.source: McDougald et al. 2012, Nature Reviews Microbiology 10:39-50 (Should we stay or should we go: mechanisms and ecological consequences for biofilm dispersal)
evidence.claim: Starvation and other cues trigger biofilm dispersal through signalling that lowers cyclic-di-GMP.

s1125.label: Signal diluted below threshold: cells remain solitary or in loose microcolonies

evidence.source: Redfield 2002, Trends in Microbiology 10:365-370
evidence.claim: In open, well-mixed water films signal does not build up, so the response is not triggered.

s1126.label: Biological nitrogen fixation: free-living and symbiotic

evidence.source: Hoffman, Lukoyanov, Yang, Dean & Seefeldt 2014, Chemical Reviews 114:4041, Mechanism of nitrogen fixation by nitrogenase
evidence.claim: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to NH3 using 16 ATP per N2 with obligatory H2 release.

s1127.label: Start: Biological nitrogen fixation: free-living and symbiotic

evidence.source: Hoffman, Lukoyanov, Yang, Dean & Seefeldt 2014, Chemical Reviews 114:4041, Mechanism of nitrogen fixation by nitrogenase
evidence.claim: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to NH3 using 16 ATP per N2 with obligatory H2 release.

s1128.label: End: Biological nitrogen fixation: free-living and symbiotic

evidence.source: Hoffman, Lukoyanov, Yang, Dean & Seefeldt 2014, Chemical Reviews 114:4041, Mechanism of nitrogen fixation by nitrogenase
evidence.claim: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to NH3 using 16 ATP per N2 with obligatory H2 release.

s1129.label: Nitrogenase reduces Dinitrogen to Ammonia at about 16 ATP per N2 (N2 + 8 H+ + 8 e- + 16 ATP gives 2 NH3 + H2)

evidence.source: Hoffman, Lukoyanov, Yang, Dean & Seefeldt 2014, Chemical Reviews 114:4041
evidence.claim: Canonical stoichiometry of the Mo nitrogenase is 16 MgATP and 8 electrons per N2 reduced, with one H2 evolved.

s1130.label: Nitrogenase needs molybdenum, iron and phosphorus; Mo limits free-living fixation in some tropical forest litter

evidence.source: Barron, Purves, Hedin 2009, Nature Geoscience 2:42, Molybdenum limitation of asymbiotic nitrogen fixation in tropical forest soils
evidence.claim: Adding Mo, but not P, raised asymbiotic fixation in lowland Panamanian forest litter and soil.

s1131.label: Oxygen irreversibly damages nitrogenase, so fixers shield it (leghemoglobin holds free O2 near 10 nM in nodules; heterocysts; respiratory protection)

evidence.source: Appleby 1984, Annual Review of Plant Physiology 35:443, Leghemoglobin and Rhizobium respiration
evidence.claim: Leghemoglobin buffers free O2 in infected nodule cells at nanomolar levels while carrying the O2 flux for bacteroid respiration.

s1132.label: Free-living heterotrophic fixers add only about 1-5 kg N per ha per year in most ecosystems

evidence.source: Reed, Cleveland & Townsend 2011, Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics 42:489, Functional ecology of free-living nitrogen fixation
evidence.claim: Free-living fixation rates are typically a few kg N/ha/yr, far below legume symbioses; range across biomes roughly 1-20.

s1133.label: Bacteroids assimilate ammonia by GS-GOGAT and the plant exports it as amides or ureides (asparagine; allantoin and allantoic acid in soybean)

evidence.source: Udvardi & Poole 2013, Annual Review of Plant Biology 64:781, Transport and metabolism in legume-rhizobia symbioses
evidence.claim: Fixed NH3 is assimilated via glutamine synthetase and exported as amides or ureides depending on legume species.

s1134.label: Carbon cost: the legume pays roughly 4-7 g carbon per g nitrogen fixed (estimate; midpoint 5)

evidence.source: Minchin & Witty 2005, in Werner & Newton (eds), Nitrogen Fixation in Agriculture, Forestry, Ecology and the Environment, Springer, respiratory and carbon costs of symbiotic N2 fixation in legumes
evidence.claim: Reported carbon cost of nodulated N2 fixation is a few grams of C per gram of N, estimates vary with method.

s1135.label: Legume symbioses supply tens to over 100 kg N per ha per year; agricultural fixation totals about 50-70 Tg N per year

evidence.source: Herridge, Peoples & Boddey 2008, Plant and Soil 311:1, Global inputs of biological nitrogen fixation in agricultural systems
evidence.claim: Crop and forage legumes plus other agricultural fixers are estimated to fix about 50-70 Tg N per year globally.

s1136.label: Nodule senescence, root turnover and rhizodeposition return fixed nitrogen to soil (below-ground N is about 4-70% of legume plant N across studies)

evidence.source: Fustec, Mariotti, Grandgirard & Amarger 2010, Agronomy for Sustainable Development 30:57, Nitrogen rhizodeposition of legumes. A review
evidence.claim: Below-ground N of legumes spans a very wide range (roughly 4-70% of plant N), depending on species and method.

s1137.label: Soil mineral nitrogen inhibits nodulation and nodule activity, so fixation falls as nitrate rises

evidence.source: Streeter 1988, Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences 7:1, Inhibition of legume nodule formation and N2 fixation by nitrate
evidence.claim: Nitrate suppresses nodule initiation, growth and nitrogenase activity, with inhibition increasing with nitrate supply.

evidence.source: Oldroyd, Murray, Poole & Downie 2011, Annual Review of Genetics 45:119, The rules of engagement in the legume-rhizobial symbiosis
evidence.claim: Flavonoid and Nod-factor exchange, infection threads and organogenesis are the sequential steps of nodule formation.

s1139.label: Start: Rhizobia-legume signalling and nodule formation
