evidence.source: Oldroyd, Murray, Poole & Downie 2011, Annual Review of Genetics 45:119, The rules of engagement in the legume-rhizobial symbiosis
evidence.claim: Flavonoid and Nod-factor exchange, infection threads and organogenesis are the sequential steps of nodule formation.

s1140.label: End: Rhizobia-legume signalling and nodule formation

evidence.source: Oldroyd, Murray, Poole & Downie 2011, Annual Review of Genetics 45:119, The rules of engagement in the legume-rhizobial symbiosis
evidence.claim: Flavonoid and Nod-factor exchange, infection threads and organogenesis are the sequential steps of nodule formation.

s1141.label: Legume roots exude flavonoids (luteolin, genistein, daidzein) that activate rhizobial NodD

evidence.source: Oldroyd, Murray, Poole & Downie 2011, Annual Review of Genetics 45:119
evidence.claim: Host flavonoids bind NodD and switch on nod gene expression in the compatible rhizobial species.

s1142.label: Rhizobia secrete Nod factors (lipochitooligosaccharides) that act at nanomolar to picomolar concentration

evidence.source: Denarie, Debelle & Prome 1996, Annual Review of Biochemistry 65:503, Rhizobium lipo-chitooligosaccharide nodulation factors
evidence.claim: Nod factors are host-specific signals active on root hairs at about 10^-9 to 10^-12 M.

s1143.label: Root-hair LysM receptor kinases (NFR1 and NFR5 in Lotus) perceive Nod factors and trigger calcium spiking

evidence.source: Radutoiu et al. 2003, Nature 425:585, Plant recognition of symbiotic bacteria requires two LysM receptor-like kinases
evidence.claim: Mutants in NFR1 or NFR5 fail to respond to Nod factors and do not nodulate.

s1144.label: An infection thread grows through the root hair into the cortex while cortical cells divide to form the nodule primordium

evidence.source: Oldroyd, Murray, Poole & Downie 2011, Annual Review of Genetics 45:119
evidence.claim: Infection thread progression is coordinated with cortical cell division under cytokinin signalling.

s1145.label: Autoregulation of nodulation: shoot-acting CLE peptides and the SUNN/HAR1 receptor kinase cap nodule number

evidence.source: Ferguson et al. 2010, Journal of Integrative Plant Biology 52:61, Molecular analysis of legume nodule development and autoregulation
evidence.claim: Mutants of HAR1/SUNN hypernodulate, showing a root-shoot loop limits nodule number.

s1146.label: Rhizobia are released into plant cells and differentiate into nitrogen-fixing bacteroids (in Medicago via NCR peptides, with genome endoreduplication)

evidence.source: Van de Velde et al. 2010, Science 327:1122, Plant peptides govern terminal differentiation of bacteria in symbiosis
evidence.claim: Nodule-specific cysteine-rich peptides drive terminal bacteroid differentiation in Medicago.

s1147.label: The nodule fixes Dinitrogen and delivers ammonium-derived amino acids to the plant

evidence.source: Udvardi & Poole 2013, Annual Review of Plant Biology 64:781
evidence.claim: Bacteroids import dicarboxylates and export fixed nitrogen across the symbiosome membrane.

s1148.label: Host sanctions: nodules that fix less nitrogen get less oxygen and their rhizobia reproduce about 50% less

evidence.source: Kiers, Rousseau, West & Denison 2003, Nature 425:78, Host sanctions and the legume-rhizobium mutualism
evidence.claim: Soybean nodules with N2 fixation prevented (Ar:O2) had about 50% lower rhizobial reproduction.

evidence.source: Conrad 2009, Environmental Microbiology Reports 1:285, The global methane cycle: recent advances in understanding the microbial processes involved
evidence.claim: Methane flux is the balance of anaerobic production and aerobic oxidation by distinct microbial groups.

s1150.label: Start: Methane cycle: methanogenesis and methanotrophy

evidence.source: Conrad 2009, Environmental Microbiology Reports 1:285, The global methane cycle: recent advances in understanding the microbial processes involved
evidence.claim: Methane flux is the balance of anaerobic production and aerobic oxidation by distinct microbial groups.

s1151.label: End: Methane cycle: methanogenesis and methanotrophy

evidence.source: Conrad 2009, Environmental Microbiology Reports 1:285, The global methane cycle: recent advances in understanding the microbial processes involved
evidence.claim: Methane flux is the balance of anaerobic production and aerobic oxidation by distinct microbial groups.

s1152.label: Methanogenesis starts only after Nitrate, Mn(IV), Fe(III) and Sulfate are depleted, at Eh below about -150 to -200 mV

evidence.source: Peters & Conrad 1996, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 28:371, Sequential reduction processes and initiation of CH4 production upon flooding of oxic upland soils
evidence.claim: After flooding, nitrate, Mn(IV), Fe(III) and sulfate reduction precede CH4 production, which begins at low redox potential.

s1153.label: Which substrate feeds methanogenesis (roughly two thirds acetate, one third H2 plus CO2 in moderate-temperature paddy and sediment; bogs shift toward H2/CO2)

evidence.source: Conrad 1999, FEMS Microbiology Ecology 28:193, Contribution of hydrogen to methane production and control of hydrogen concentrations in methanogenic soils and sediments
evidence.claim: In anoxic soils at moderate temperature about two thirds of CH4 derives from acetate and one third from H2/CO2; estimate varies with temperature and pH.

s1154.label: Acetoclastic methanogens (Methanosarcina, Methanosaeta) split Acetate into Methane and Carbon dioxide

evidence.source: Conrad 1999, FEMS Microbiology Ecology 28:193
evidence.claim: Acetoclastic methanogenesis is the main route in most flooded soils.

s1155.label: Hydrogenotrophic methanogens reduce Carbon dioxide with Hydrogen supplied by syntrophic fermenters (H2 must stay at a few Pa)

evidence.source: Stams & Plugge 2009, Nature Reviews Microbiology 7:568, Electron transfer in syntrophic communities of anaerobic bacteria and archaea
evidence.claim: Fermenters can only oxidize their substrates when methanogens keep H2 partial pressure very low.

s1156.label: Methanogenesis is more temperature sensitive than methane oxidation (Q10 about 2-4 versus 1.5-2), so warming favours emission

evidence.source: Segers 1998, Biogeochemistry 41:23, Methane production and methane consumption: a review of processes underlying wetland methane fluxes
evidence.claim: Reported Q10 values for CH4 production are mostly higher than for CH4 consumption.

s1157.label: Methane reaches the surface by diffusion, bubbling or plant aerenchyma (in rice, over 90% of emitted CH4 passes through the plants)

evidence.source: Butterbach-Bahl, Papen & Rennenberg 1997, Plant, Cell and Environment 20:1175, Impact of gas transport through rice cultivars on methane emission from rice paddy fields
evidence.claim: Plant-mediated transport accounted for the large majority of CH4 emission from rice paddies.

s1158.label: Methanotrophs oxidize Methane with methane monooxygenase in oxic layers and the rhizosphere, consuming roughly 20-80% of the methane produced (midpoint about 50% in paddies)

evidence.source: Conrad 2009, Environmental Microbiology Reports 1:285
evidence.claim: A large part, often tens of percent up to the majority, of the CH4 produced is oxidized before reaching the atmosphere.

s1159.label: Aerated upland soils with high-affinity methanotrophs take up atmospheric Methane: global soil sink about 30 Tg CH4 per year (range 11-49)

evidence.source: Saunois et al. 2020, Earth System Science Data 12:1561, The Global Methane Budget 2000-2017
evidence.claim: Soil uptake in the 2008-2017 budget is about 30 (11-49) Tg CH4 per year.

s1160.label: Viral shunt: phage lysis recycles bacterial carbon and nitrogen

evidence.source: Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 127:305, Viruses in soil: nano-scale undead drivers of microbial life, biogeochemical turnover and ecosystem functions
evidence.claim: Viral lysis is a major cause of bacterial mortality and a source of labile dissolved organic matter in soil.

s1161.label: Start: Viral shunt: phage lysis recycles bacterial carbon and nitrogen

evidence.source: Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 127:305, Viruses in soil: nano-scale undead drivers of microbial life, biogeochemical turnover and ecosystem functions
evidence.claim: Viral lysis is a major cause of bacterial mortality and a source of labile dissolved organic matter in soil.

s1162.label: End: Viral shunt: phage lysis recycles bacterial carbon and nitrogen

evidence.source: Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 127:305, Viruses in soil: nano-scale undead drivers of microbial life, biogeochemical turnover and ecosystem functions
evidence.claim: Viral lysis is a major cause of bacterial mortality and a source of labile dissolved organic matter in soil.

s1163.label: Soil holds roughly 10^7-10^10 virus-like particles per gram, often one to ten per bacterial cell

evidence.source: Williamson, Radosevich & Wommack 2017, Annual Review of Virology 4:201, Viruses in soil ecosystems: an unknown quantity within an unexplored territory
evidence.claim: Soil viral abundance ranges about 10^7-10^10 per g dry soil with virus-to-bacteria ratios of order 1-10.

s1164.label: Phage infection mode (estimate: more lysogeny than lysis in dry, nutrient-poor soil; range 30-70% lytic)

evidence.source: Williamson, Radosevich & Wommack 2017, Annual Review of Virology 4:201
evidence.claim: Lysogeny is common in soil bacteria and appears favoured when hosts are slow-growing; the lytic share is poorly constrained (estimate 30-70%, midpoint 50 shifted to 40 for dry soil).

s1165.label: Lytic phage adsorbs, replicates and bursts the host (burst size about 10-100 virions)

evidence.source: Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 127:305
evidence.claim: Active host cells lyse, releasing tens of progeny virions per cell and the cell contents.

s1166.label: Lysogenic phage integrates as prophage; drought, nutrient pulses or other stress can induce lysis

evidence.source: Williamson, Radosevich & Wommack 2017, Annual Review of Virology 4:201
evidence.claim: Prophage induction by environmental stress converts lysogens to lytic infections.

s1167.label: Lysis releases cytoplasm, rich in labile carbon and nitrogen (cell C:N about 4-6), as Dissolved organic carbon

evidence.source: Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 127:305
evidence.claim: Lysates are small, labile and N-rich compared with plant litter.

s1168.label: Viral auxiliary metabolic genes (for example glycoside hydrolases) may boost host carbon degradation

evidence.source: Emerson et al. 2018, Nature Microbiology 3:870, Host-linked soil viral ecology along a permafrost thaw gradient
evidence.claim: Soil viral genomes along a thaw gradient encoded glycoside hydrolases and other carbon-processing genes.

s1169.label: Surviving microbes take up the lysate and mineralize part of it; the rest sorbs to minerals or becomes necromass (the viral shunt)

evidence.source: Wilhelm & Suttle 1999, BioScience 49:781, Viruses and nutrient cycles in the sea
evidence.claim: Defines the viral shunt: lysis diverts biomass from higher trophic levels back into the dissolved pool for microbial re-use (marine concept applied to soil by Kuzyakov & Mason-Jones 2018).

s1170.label: Host density of the dominant strain rises on recycled nutrients and invites more infection (kill the winner)

evidence.source: Thingstad 2000, Limnology and Oceanography 45:1320, Elements of a theory for the mechanisms controlling abundance, diversity and biogeochemical role of lytic bacterial viruses in aquatic systems
evidence.claim: Density-dependent infection caps the abundance of the best competitor and sustains diversity; soil evidence is limited.

s1171.label: Microbial dormancy, the seed bank and reactivation after rewetting

evidence.source: Lennon & Jones 2011, Nature Reviews Microbiology 9:119, Microbial seed banks: the ecological and evolutionary implications of dormancy
evidence.claim: Dormant microbes form a seed bank that is reactivated by environmental cues.

s1172.label: Start: Microbial dormancy, the seed bank and reactivation after rewetting

evidence.source: Lennon & Jones 2011, Nature Reviews Microbiology 9:119, Microbial seed banks: the ecological and evolutionary implications of dormancy
evidence.claim: Dormant microbes form a seed bank that is reactivated by environmental cues.

s1173.label: End: Microbial dormancy, the seed bank and reactivation after rewetting

evidence.source: Lennon & Jones 2011, Nature Reviews Microbiology 9:119, Microbial seed banks: the ecological and evolutionary implications of dormancy
evidence.claim: Dormant microbes form a seed bank that is reactivated by environmental cues.

s1174.label: Only about 0.1-2% of soil microbial cells are active at one time in bulk soil; the share is higher near roots and fresh litter

evidence.source: Blagodatskaya & Kuzyakov 2013, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 67:192, Active microorganisms in soil: critical review of estimation criteria and approaches
evidence.claim: Active microorganisms are roughly 0.1-2% of total cells in bulk soil, with larger shares in hotspots.

s1175.label: Starvation and drying drive cells into dormancy: spores, fewer ribosomes, smaller cells and osmolyte accumulation

evidence.source: Lennon & Jones 2011, Nature Reviews Microbiology 9:119
evidence.claim: Sporulation and other dormancy states are triggered by starvation and desiccation cues.

s1176.label: Dormant cells cut maintenance metabolism to orders of magnitude below growth rates

evidence.source: Price & Sowers 2004, PNAS 101:4631, Temperature dependence of metabolic rates for microbial growth, maintenance, and survival
evidence.claim: Basal survival metabolic rates are many orders of magnitude lower than growth rates.

s1177.label: The dormant seed bank preserves rare taxa for years and lets the community rebound after disturbance

evidence.source: Lennon & Jones 2011, Nature Reviews Microbiology 9:119
evidence.claim: Seed banks buffer populations against environmental change and maintain diversity.

s1178.label: Rewetting dry soil wakes cells within minutes to hours: Carbon dioxide pulse and Dissolved organic carbon flush (Birch effect)

evidence.source: Birch 1958, Plant and Soil 10:9, The effect of soil drying on humus decomposition and nitrogen availability
evidence.claim: Drying then rewetting causes a flush of mineralization and CO2 well above steady rates.

s1179.label: Resuscitation-promoting factors and substrate pulses wake neighbouring cells; waking is uneven, so community composition shifts after each pulse

evidence.source: Mukamolova, Kaprelyants, Young & Kell 1998, PNAS 95:8916, A bacterial cytokine
evidence.claim: A secreted protein from Micrococcus luteus resuscitates dormant cells at picomolar concentrations.

s1180.label: Reactivated cells grow on lysed-cell and exudate carbon until substrate is used up, which re-triggers dormancy

evidence.source: Blagodatskaya & Kuzyakov 2013, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 67:192
evidence.claim: Substrate addition raises the active fraction from under 5% to tens of percent for hours to days, then it declines.

s1181.label: Permafrost thaw and release of frozen soil carbon

evidence.source: Hugelius et al. (2014) Biogeosciences 11:6573-6593, Estimated stocks of circumpolar permafrost carbon
evidence.claim: Northern permafrost-region soils hold roughly 1,300 Pg C (about 1,000 Pg in the top 3 m), nearly twice the carbon in the atmosphere.

s1182.label: Start: Permafrost thaw and release of frozen soil carbon

evidence.source: Hugelius et al. (2014) Biogeosciences 11:6573-6593, Estimated stocks of circumpolar permafrost carbon
evidence.claim: Northern permafrost-region soils hold roughly 1,300 Pg C (about 1,000 Pg in the top 3 m), nearly twice the carbon in the atmosphere.

s1183.label: End: Permafrost thaw and release of frozen soil carbon

evidence.source: Hugelius et al. (2014) Biogeosciences 11:6573-6593, Estimated stocks of circumpolar permafrost carbon
evidence.claim: Northern permafrost-region soils hold roughly 1,300 Pg C (about 1,000 Pg in the top 3 m), nearly twice the carbon in the atmosphere.

s1184.label: Cold, waterlogged soils preserve about 1,300 Gt of organic carbon because decomposition is frozen out

evidence.source: Hugelius et al. (2014) Biogeosciences 11:6573-6593
evidence.claim: Permafrost region covers about 15% of land area but holds about half of global belowground organic carbon.

s1185.label: Warming deepens the seasonally thawed active layer and thaws previously frozen organic matter (permafrost temperatures rose about 0.3 C in 2007-2016)

evidence.source: Biskaborn et al. (2019) Nature Communications 10:264, Permafrost is warming at a global scale
evidence.claim: Mean permafrost temperature increased by 0.29 +/- 0.12 C from 2007 to 2016.

s1186.label: Microbes decompose the thawed carbon; well-drained thaw releases mostly Carbon dioxide, saturated thaw ponds release Methane

evidence.source: Schuur et al. (2015) Nature 520:171-179, Climate change and the permafrost carbon feedback
evidence.claim: Aerobic thaw releases CO2; anaerobic thaw releases CH4, a small share of carbon but a large share of warming effect.

s1187.label: Under high emissions about 5-15% of permafrost carbon is released as greenhouse gas by 2100, with decades-to-centuries continuing

evidence.source: Schuur et al. (2015) Nature 520:171-179
evidence.claim: Expert assessment: 5-15% of permafrost carbon released by 2100 under RCP8.5, mostly as CO2.

s1188.label: Thaw settling, ponding and abrupt thermokarst collapse expose still more carbon in wet, ice-rich ground

evidence.source: Turetsky et al. (2020) Nature 579:32-34, Carbon release through abrupt permafrost thaw; Nature Geoscience 13:138-143
evidence.claim: Abrupt thaw affects a small land area but could roughly double the warming impact of gradual thaw carbon release.

evidence.source: Yu et al. (2010) Geophysical Research Letters 37:L13402, Global peatland dynamics since the Last Glacial Maximum
evidence.claim: Northern peatlands hold about 547 Pg C; peatlands cover about 3% of land.

s1190.label: Start: Peat accumulation and wetland methane

evidence.source: Yu et al. (2010) Geophysical Research Letters 37:L13402, Global peatland dynamics since the Last Glacial Maximum
evidence.claim: Northern peatlands hold about 547 Pg C; peatlands cover about 3% of land.

s1191.label: End: Peat accumulation and wetland methane

evidence.source: Yu et al. (2010) Geophysical Research Letters 37:L13402, Global peatland dynamics since the Last Glacial Maximum
evidence.claim: Northern peatlands hold about 547 Pg C; peatlands cover about 3% of land.

s1192.label: A high water table excludes oxygen and the enzyme latch (phenol oxidase starved of oxygen) slows decomposition

evidence.source: Freeman, Ostle & Kang (2001) Nature 409:149, An enzymic latch on a global carbon store
evidence.claim: Oxygen limitation suppresses phenol oxidase, letting phenolics inhibit hydrolases and preserve peat carbon.

s1193.label: Plant production exceeds decay and peat accumulates at about 20 g C per m2 per year (about 1 mm per year)

evidence.source: Loisel et al. (2014) The Holocene 24:1028-1042, A database and synthesis of northern peatland soil properties and Holocene carbon and nitrogen accumulation
evidence.claim: Long-term apparent carbon accumulation in northern peatlands averages about 20 g C per m2 per year.

s1194.label: Methanogens in saturated peat convert acetate and H2 plus CO2 to Methane; production rises steeply with temperature (activation energy about 0.96 eV)

evidence.source: Yvon-Durocher et al. (2014) Nature 507:488-491, Methane fluxes show consistent temperature dependence across microbial to ecosystem scales
evidence.claim: Apparent activation energy of methanogenesis is about 0.96 eV versus 0.65 eV for respiration.

s1195.label: Methanotrophs in the oxic surface layer oxidise commonly half or more (20-90%) of the Methane before it escapes

evidence.source: Le Mer & Roger (2001) European Journal of Soil Biology 37:25-50, Production, oxidation, emission and consumption of methane by soils
evidence.claim: Methane oxidation consumes a large and variable share of produced methane in wetland soils.

s1196.label: Plant aerenchyma and bubbles carry Methane past the oxic layer; wetlands emit about 150-180 Tg CH4 per year, the largest natural source

evidence.source: Saunois et al. (2020) Earth System Science Data 12:1561-1623
evidence.claim: Natural wetlands emit roughly 150-180 Tg CH4 per year of a total of about 570-740 Tg.

s1197.label: Drainage or drought lowers the water table, oxygen enters and peat respires CO2 (drained peatland about 0.3% of land, about 5% of human CO2-equivalent emissions)

evidence.source: Leifeld & Menichetti (2018) Nature Communications 9:1071, The underappreciated potential of peatlands in global climate change mitigation strategies
evidence.claim: Drained peatlands cover about 0.3% of land and emit about 1.9 Gt CO2-equivalent per year (about 5.6% of anthropogenic emissions).

s1198.label: Soil inorganic carbon: pedogenic carbonate formation and dissolution

evidence.source: Batjes (1996) European Journal of Soil Science 47:151-163, Total carbon and nitrogen in the soils of the world; Monger et al. (2015) Geology 43:375-378
evidence.claim: Soil inorganic carbon stocks are of order 700-950 Pg C in the top 1-2 m, comparable to the soil organic carbon pool in drylands.

s1199.label: Start: Soil inorganic carbon: pedogenic carbonate formation and dissolution

evidence.source: Batjes (1996) European Journal of Soil Science 47:151-163, Total carbon and nitrogen in the soils of the world; Monger et al. (2015) Geology 43:375-378
evidence.claim: Soil inorganic carbon stocks are of order 700-950 Pg C in the top 1-2 m, comparable to the soil organic carbon pool in drylands.

s1200.label: End: Soil inorganic carbon: pedogenic carbonate formation and dissolution

evidence.source: Batjes (1996) European Journal of Soil Science 47:151-163, Total carbon and nitrogen in the soils of the world; Monger et al. (2015) Geology 43:375-378
evidence.claim: Soil inorganic carbon stocks are of order 700-950 Pg C in the top 1-2 m, comparable to the soil organic carbon pool in drylands.

s1201.label: Root and microbial respiration raise soil pore CO2 well above the atmosphere, driving carbonic acid and bicarbonate formation

evidence.source: Brady & Weil, The Nature and Properties of Soils, 15th ed., ch. on soil aeration and respiration
evidence.claim: Soil air CO2 is commonly 10 to 100 times atmospheric because root and microbial respiration outpaces diffusion, and dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid.

s1202.label: Calcium arrives from silicate weathering, dust, irrigation water or dissolving old carbonate

evidence.source: Monger et al. (2015) Geology 43:375-378, Sequestration of inorganic carbon in soil and groundwater
evidence.claim: Pedogenic carbonate Ca comes from silicate weathering, dust, rain and groundwater; Ca from limestone makes no net CO2 sink.

s1203.label: Evaporation and root water uptake concentrate the solution, and calcite precipitates (Ca2+ + 2HCO3- gives CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O) at the depth of wetting

evidence.source: Zamanian et al. (2016) Earth-Science Reviews 157:1-17, Soil carbonates: the unaccounted, irrecoverable carbon source
evidence.claim: Carbonate precipitation releases one mole CO2 per mole CaCO3 formed from bicarbonate; net sink only when Ca is silicate-derived.

s1204.label: Carbonate accumulates as nodules, coatings and a calcic (Bk) horizon over thousands to hundreds of thousands of years

evidence.source: Gile, Peterson & Grossman (1966) Soil Science 101:347-360, Morphological and genetic sequences of carbonate accumulation in desert soils
evidence.claim: Carbonate morphology progresses in stages (filaments, nodules, plugged horizons) over millennia.

s1205.label: Acidification from Nitrogen fertiliser, nitrification or acid rain dissolves carbonate and releases CO2

evidence.source: Zamanian et al. (2016) Earth-Science Reviews 157:1-17; West & McBride (2005) Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 108:145-154
evidence.claim: Acid inputs (fertiliser nitrification, acid deposition) dissolve soil carbonate, releasing CO2 or exporting bicarbonate.

s1206.label: Volcanic ash parent material, short-range-order minerals and Andosol carbon

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993) Volcanic Ash Soils: Genesis, Properties and Utilization, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Volcanic ash soils (Andosols) cover about 1% of land and are defined by short-range-order Al and Fe minerals and humus complexes.

s1207.label: Start: Volcanic ash parent material, short-range-order minerals and Andosol carbon

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993) Volcanic Ash Soils: Genesis, Properties and Utilization, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Volcanic ash soils (Andosols) cover about 1% of land and are defined by short-range-order Al and Fe minerals and humus complexes.

s1208.label: End: Volcanic ash parent material, short-range-order minerals and Andosol carbon

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993) Volcanic Ash Soils: Genesis, Properties and Utilization, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Volcanic ash soils (Andosols) cover about 1% of land and are defined by short-range-order Al and Fe minerals and humus complexes.

s1209.label: Fresh ash and tephra (volcanic glass) falls and weathers within decades in humid climates

evidence.source: Shoji, Nanzyo & Dahlgren (1993) Volcanic Ash Soils, Elsevier
evidence.claim: Volcanic glass is far more weatherable than crystalline silicates.

s1210.label: Released Al and Si precipitate as allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite instead of crystalline clay

evidence.source: Wada (1989) in Dixon & Weed (eds) Minerals in Soil Environments, 2nd ed., SSSA, ch. 21, Allophane and imogolite
evidence.claim: Allophane (Si:Al about 0.5-1) forms where Si activity is moderate and pH is above about 5; Al-humus complexes form at lower pH.

s1211.label: Allophane and Al-humus complexes bind organic matter so strongly that Andosols hold large Soil organic matter stocks with slow turnover

evidence.source: Torn et al. (1997) Nature 389:170-173, Mineral control of soil organic carbon storage and turnover
evidence.claim: Across a Hawaiian volcanic-ash chronosequence, soil carbon and its 14C turnover time track the amount of noncrystalline minerals, not climate.

s1212.label: Strong phosphate retention (andic criteria: oxalate Al + half Fe at least 2%, bulk density 0.9 g/cm3 or less, P retention at least 85%) fixes phosphorus

evidence.source: Soil Survey Staff (2014) Keys to Soil Taxonomy, 12th ed., andic soil properties
evidence.claim: Andic properties require oxalate-extractable Al + 1/2 Fe of at least 2.0%, bulk density of 0.90 g/cm3 or less and phosphate retention of 85% or more.

s1213.label: In wet climates over millennia allophane crystallises to halloysite and Fe oxides and the carbon protection weakens

evidence.source: Torn et al. (1997) Nature 389:170-173; Shoji et al. (1993)
evidence.claim: Noncrystalline phases decline and crystalline clay and oxides rise on the oldest, wettest sites; carbon storage falls with them.

s1214.label: Microbial dormancy, the seed bank and resuscitation

evidence.source: Lennon & Jones 2011, Nature Reviews Microbiology 9:119-130 (Microbial seed banks: the ecological and evolutionary implications of dormancy)
evidence.claim: Dormancy lets a large fraction of a microbial community persist in a low-activity state and be reactivated, creating a seed bank that buffers environmental change.

s1215.label: Start: Active microbial cell faces starvation or drying

evidence.source: Lennon & Jones 2011, Nature Reviews Microbiology 9:119-130 (Microbial seed banks: the ecological and evolutionary implications of dormancy)
evidence.claim: Dormancy lets a large fraction of a microbial community persist in a low-activity state and be reactivated, creating a seed bank that buffers environmental change.

s1216.label: End: Cells revived and growing, or dead and recycled

evidence.source: Lennon & Jones 2011, Nature Reviews Microbiology 9:119-130 (Microbial seed banks: the ecological and evolutionary implications of dormancy)
evidence.claim: Dormancy lets a large fraction of a microbial community persist in a low-activity state and be reactivated, creating a seed bank that buffers environmental change.

s1217.label: Only about 0.1-2% of cells in bulk soil are active at a given time, with a much higher active share near roots and fresh substrate

evidence.source: Blagodatskaya & Kuzyakov 2013, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 67:192-211 (Active microorganisms in soil: critical review of estimation criteria and approaches)
evidence.claim: Estimated active microorganisms are a minor part (often 0.1-2%) of total soil microbial biomass in bulk soil, and larger in the rhizosphere.

s1218.label: Cell response to starvation or drying: sporulate, enter reversible non-spore dormancy, or die

evidence.source: Lennon & Jones 2011, Nature Reviews Microbiology 9:119-130
evidence.claim: Cells can form endospores or enter reversible low-activity states, or die when stress persists. Shares are an estimate with no direct soil census.

s1219.label: Sporulation (Bacillus, Clostridium, many Actinobacteria): endospores resist heat, UV and desiccation and survive for decades

evidence.source: Nicholson, Munakata, Horneck, Melosh & Setlow 2000, Microbiology and Molecular Biology Reviews 64:548-572 (Resistance of Bacillus endospores to extreme terrestrial and extraterrestrial environments)
evidence.claim: Endospores resist wet and dry heat, UV, desiccation and chemicals, and can remain viable for very long periods.

s1220.label: Non-spore dormancy: metabolic downshift, ribosome hibernation (100S dimers) and osmolyte accumulation

evidence.source: Yoshida & Wada 2014, WIREs RNA 5:723-732 (The 100S ribosome: ribosomal hibernation induced by stress)
evidence.claim: Hibernation factors dimerise 70S ribosomes into inactive 100S particles under stress, preserving them for rapid restart.

s1221.label: The dormant pool forms a seed bank that stores rare taxa and maintains diversity through bad periods

evidence.source: Jones & Lennon 2010, PNAS 107:5881-5886 (Dormancy contributes to the maintenance of microbial diversity)
evidence.claim: Dormancy retained a large part of lake bacterial diversity through unfavourable conditions, a storage effect.

s1222.label: Survival metabolism is orders of magnitude lower than growth metabolism (up to about 10^6-fold in the cited compilation)

evidence.source: Price & Sowers 2004, PNAS 101:4631-4636 (Temperature dependence of metabolic rates for microbial growth, maintenance, and survival)
evidence.claim: Metabolic rates of cells in growth, maintenance and survival modes span many orders of magnitude, with survival far below growth.

s1223.label: Rewetting of dry soil or a substrate pulse produces a CO2 flush (Birch effect) from released osmolytes and revived cells

evidence.source: Schimel 2018, Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics 49:409-432 (Life in dry soils: effects of drought on soil microbial communities and processes)
evidence.claim: Rewetting dry soil triggers a rapid respiration pulse that comes partly from cells rehydrating and partly from labile substrates.

s1224.label: Resuscitation-promoting factor (Rpf), a muralytic protein secreted by active cells, revives dormant neighbours at picomolar concentration

evidence.source: Mukamolova, Kaprelyants, Young, Young & Kell 1998, PNAS 95:8916-8921 (A bacterial cytokine)
evidence.claim: A secreted Rpf protein from Micrococcus luteus stimulated growth of dormant cells at picomolar concentrations.

s1225.label: Spores germinate when germinant receptors (for example GerA for L-alanine) sense nutrients

evidence.source: Setlow 2003, Current Opinion in Microbiology 6:550-556 (Spore germination)
evidence.claim: Nutrient germinants bind receptors in the spore inner membrane and trigger irreversible germination.

s1226.label: Reactivation proceeds in sequence: phylogenetically clustered groups resuscitate at different times over hours to days after rain

evidence.source: Placella, Brodie & Firestone 2012, PNAS 109:10931-10936 (Rainfall-induced carbon dioxide pulses result from sequential resuscitation of phylogenetically clustered microbial groups)
evidence.claim: Different clades resuscitated at different times after wetting a dry soil, with CO2 pulses tracking the waves.

s1227.label: Cell dies by starvation, lysis or predation and releases carbon and nitrogen

evidence.source: Blagodatskaya & Kuzyakov 2013, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 67:192-211
evidence.claim: Dead cells are a substantial part of total counted biomass in soil.

s1228.label: Relic DNA from dead cells makes up about 40% of soil DNA on average (up to 80%) and inflates diversity estimates

evidence.source: Carini et al. 2016, Nature Microbiology 2:16242 (Relic DNA is abundant in soil and obscures estimates of soil microbial diversity)
evidence.claim: Treating soils with propidium monoazide showed on average about 40% of prokaryotic DNA is extracellular relic DNA, with up to 80% in some samples.

s1229.label: Revived cells release Rpf and nutrients that wake neighbours, accelerating population recovery

evidence.source: Mukamolova et al. 1998, PNAS 95:8916-8921
evidence.claim: Rpf from active cells acts on other cells, a cross-feeding trigger.

s1230.label: Soil compaction and loss of macroporosity

evidence.source: Hamza & Anderson (2005), Soil compaction in cropping systems: a review of the nature, causes and possible solutions, Soil & Tillage Research 82:121-145
evidence.claim: Compaction reduces macroporosity, raises bulk density and penetration resistance, and reduces infiltration and aeration.

s1231.label: Start: Soil compaction and loss of macroporosity

evidence.source: Hamza & Anderson (2005), Soil compaction in cropping systems: a review of the nature, causes and possible solutions, Soil & Tillage Research 82:121-145
evidence.claim: Compaction reduces macroporosity, raises bulk density and penetration resistance, and reduces infiltration and aeration.

s1232.label: End: Soil compaction and loss of macroporosity

evidence.source: Hamza & Anderson (2005), Soil compaction in cropping systems: a review of the nature, causes and possible solutions, Soil & Tillage Research 82:121-145
evidence.claim: Compaction reduces macroporosity, raises bulk density and penetration resistance, and reduces infiltration and aeration.

s1233.label: Wheel or hoof load exceeds the soil precompression stress, and wet soil is much weaker so compacts at a lower load

evidence.source: Hamza & Anderson (2005), Soil & Tillage Research 82:121-145
evidence.claim: Soil water content strongly lowers soil strength, so the same axle load compacts wet soil far more.

s1234.label: Macropores collapse first: air-filled porosity falls and bulk density rises toward root-limiting values of roughly 1.4 to 1.8 g per cm3 depending on texture

evidence.source: Daddow & Warrington (1983), Growth-limiting soil bulk densities as influenced by soil texture, USDA Forest Service WSDG-TN-00005
evidence.claim: Root-limiting bulk density ranges from about 1.4 g per cm3 in clays to about 1.8 g per cm3 in sands.

s1235.label: Penetration resistance climbs above 1 to 2 MPa and root elongation drops sharply

evidence.source: Bengough, McKenzie, Hallett & Valentine (2011), Root elongation, water stress, and mechanical impedance, Journal of Experimental Botany 62:59-68
evidence.claim: Root elongation rate falls as penetrometer resistance rises through about 1 to 2 MPa.

s1236.label: Low air-filled porosity and conductivity slow infiltration and gas diffusion, raising runoff and anaerobic N2O production

evidence.source: Hansen, Maehlum & Bakken (1993), N2O and CH4 fluxes in soil influenced by fertilization and tractor traffic, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 25:621-630
evidence.claim: Compaction by tractor traffic increased N2O emissions through reduced aeration.

s1237.label: Subsoil compaction persists for decades because few roots, worms and frost cycles reach below plough depth

evidence.source: Hakansson & Reeder (1994), Subsoil compaction by vehicles with high axle load: extent, persistence and crop response, Soil & Tillage Research 29:277-304
evidence.claim: Compaction of the subsoil from heavy axle loads was found to persist for more than ten years.

s1238.label: Poor rooting means less root carbon and fewer biopores, leaving the soil more vulnerable to the next load

evidence.source: Hamza & Anderson (2005), Soil & Tillage Research 82:121-145
evidence.claim: Reduced root growth and organic matter in compacted soil lowers structural resilience; gain is an estimate.

s1239.label: Shrink-swell cracking and self-mulching in smectitic soils

evidence.source: Wilding & Tessier (1988), Genesis of Vertisols: shrink-swell phenomena, in Vertisols: Their Distribution, Properties, Classification and Management, Texas A&M University Printing Center
evidence.claim: Vertisols form through repeated shrink-swell cycling in smectitic parent material, producing cracks, slickensides and gilgai.

s1240.label: Start: Shrink-swell cracking and self-mulching in smectitic soils

evidence.source: Wilding & Tessier (1988), Genesis of Vertisols: shrink-swell phenomena, in Vertisols: Their Distribution, Properties, Classification and Management, Texas A&M University Printing Center
evidence.claim: Vertisols form through repeated shrink-swell cycling in smectitic parent material, producing cracks, slickensides and gilgai.

s1241.label: End: Shrink-swell cracking and self-mulching in smectitic soils

evidence.source: Wilding & Tessier (1988), Genesis of Vertisols: shrink-swell phenomena, in Vertisols: Their Distribution, Properties, Classification and Management, Texas A&M University Printing Center
evidence.claim: Vertisols form through repeated shrink-swell cycling in smectitic parent material, producing cracks, slickensides and gilgai.

s1242.label: Soil with 30 percent or more clay dominated by smectite holds water between the layers of expandable clay

evidence.source: IUSS Working Group WRB (2022), World Reference Base for Soil Resources, 4th ed., Vertisols
evidence.claim: Vertisols have a vertic horizon with at least 30 percent clay and shrink-swell features.

s1243.label: Drying shrinks the matrix: Vertisols have linear extensibility of 6 cm or more in the upper metre

evidence.source: Soil Survey Staff (2014), Keys to Soil Taxonomy, 12th ed., USDA-NRCS, Vertisols
evidence.claim: Vertisols are defined by a linear extensibility of 6.0 cm or more between the surface and 100 cm depth.

s1244.label: Cracks open to 0.5 m or more; first rain bypasses the matrix through them into the subsoil

evidence.source: Bouma & Dekker (1978), A case study on infiltration into dry clay soil. I. Morphological observations, Geoderma 20:27-40
evidence.claim: Initial infiltration into dry cracked clay is very fast through cracks and ends as cracks close.

s1245.label: Surface crumbs fall into cracks (self-mulching) and mix material downward while swelling pushes material up

evidence.source: Wilding & Tessier (1988), in Vertisols: Their Distribution, Properties, Classification and Management, Texas A&M
evidence.claim: Self-mulching crumbs falling into cracks drive pedoturbation in Vertisols.

s1246.label: Wetting swells the clay, closes cracks and cuts infiltration to the slow matrix rate

evidence.source: Bronswijk (1988), Modeling of water balance, cracking and subsidence of clay soils, Journal of Hydrology 97:199-212
evidence.claim: Crack volume changes with soil moisture, and closure on swelling restricts water entry to the matrix.

s1247.label: Shear between swelling blocks makes slickensides, and uneven mixing builds gilgai microrelief

evidence.source: Yaalon & Kalmar (1978), Dynamics of cracking and swelling clay soils: displacement of skeletal grains, optimum depth of slickensides, and rate of intra-pedonic turbation, Earth Surface Processes 3:31-42
evidence.claim: Slickensides develop at an optimum depth where swelling pressure causes shear, and cause continuous turbation.

s1248.label: Soil evaporation stages and capillary rise from shallow groundwater

evidence.source: Or, Lehmann, Shahraeeni & Shokri (2013), Advances in soil evaporation physics: a review, Vadose Zone Journal 12(4)
evidence.claim: Evaporation from soil proceeds in an energy-limited stage and a diffusion-limited stage separated by the formation of a dry surface layer.

s1249.label: Start: Soil evaporation stages and capillary rise from shallow groundwater

evidence.source: Or, Lehmann, Shahraeeni & Shokri (2013), Advances in soil evaporation physics: a review, Vadose Zone Journal 12(4)
evidence.claim: Evaporation from soil proceeds in an energy-limited stage and a diffusion-limited stage separated by the formation of a dry surface layer.

s1250.label: End: Soil evaporation stages and capillary rise from shallow groundwater

evidence.source: Or, Lehmann, Shahraeeni & Shokri (2013), Advances in soil evaporation physics: a review, Vadose Zone Journal 12(4)
evidence.claim: Evaporation from soil proceeds in an energy-limited stage and a diffusion-limited stage separated by the formation of a dry surface layer.

s1251.label: Stage I: evaporation runs near the potential rate while capillary flow keeps the surface wet; readily evaporable water is about 2-7 mm in sand, 8-10 mm in loam, 8-12 mm in clay

evidence.source: Allen, Pereira, Raes & Smith (1998), Crop evapotranspiration, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Table 19
evidence.claim: Readily evaporable water in stage I is 2-7 mm for sand, 8-10 mm for loam and 8-12 mm for clay.

s1252.label: A dry surface layer forms and stage II starts: loss is limited by vapour diffusion through the dry layer and falls to a small fraction of potential

evidence.source: Or, Lehmann, Shahraeeni & Shokri (2013), Vadose Zone Journal 12(4)
evidence.claim: Stage II rate is controlled by diffusion through the dry layer and is much lower than the atmospheric demand.

s1253.label: Organic mulch or litter cover cuts soil evaporation, by about 5 percent per 10 percent of surface covered

evidence.source: Allen et al. (1998), FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, ch. 7 and 11
evidence.claim: FAO-56 reduces the soil evaporation coefficient by 5 percent for each 10 percent of surface covered by mulch.

s1254.label: Capillary rise from a water table: fringe height is about 0.15 cm2 divided by the pore radius, from roughly 0.1-0.3 m in coarse sand to over 1.5 m in silt and clay

evidence.source: Hillel (1998), Environmental Soil Physics, Academic Press, ch. on capillarity
evidence.claim: Capillary rise height is inversely proportional to pore radius (h about 0.15 cm2 over r), so finer soils lift water higher.

s1255.label: Shallow saline groundwater delivers dissolved salts to the surface where evaporation leaves them behind

evidence.source: Rengasamy (2006), World salinization with emphasis on Australia, Journal of Experimental Botany 57:1017-1023
evidence.claim: Rising saline water tables and capillary rise are the main cause of dryland salinity in Australia.

s1256.label: Salt crust and accumulated salts lower the soil water potential and add a further barrier to loss

evidence.source: Nachshon, Weisbrod, Dragila & Shokri (2011), Coupling water and salt dynamics in evaporating porous media, Geophysical Research Letters
evidence.claim: Salt precipitation at the surface can slow evaporation by forming a crust.

s1257.label: Plant-available water from field capacity to wilting point

evidence.source: Saxton & Rawls (2006), Soil water characteristic estimates by texture and organic matter for hydrologic solutions, Soil Science Society of America Journal 70:1569-1578
evidence.claim: Water retention at -33 kPa and -1500 kPa can be estimated from texture and organic matter, giving available water of roughly 0.1 to 0.2 m3 per m3.

s1258.label: Start: Plant-available water from field capacity to wilting point

evidence.source: Saxton & Rawls (2006), Soil water characteristic estimates by texture and organic matter for hydrologic solutions, Soil Science Society of America Journal 70:1569-1578
evidence.claim: Water retention at -33 kPa and -1500 kPa can be estimated from texture and organic matter, giving available water of roughly 0.1 to 0.2 m3 per m3.

s1259.label: End: Plant-available water from field capacity to wilting point

evidence.source: Saxton & Rawls (2006), Soil water characteristic estimates by texture and organic matter for hydrologic solutions, Soil Science Society of America Journal 70:1569-1578
evidence.claim: Water retention at -33 kPa and -1500 kPa can be estimated from texture and organic matter, giving available water of roughly 0.1 to 0.2 m3 per m3.

s1260.label: Capillary and adsorptive forces hold water: by the Young-Laplace law pores wider than about 10 to 30 micrometres empty at field capacity (-10 to -33 kPa) and pores narrower than about 0.2 micrometres hold water beyond -1.5 MPa

evidence.source: Hillel (1998), Environmental Soil Physics, Academic Press, ch. on soil water potential
evidence.claim: Capillary radius is 0.15 cm2 divided by suction head, giving about 0.2 micrometre diameter at 1.5 MPa.

s1261.label: Field capacity is reached when downward drainage becomes negligible, about 2 to 3 days after wetting

evidence.source: Veihmeyer & Hendrickson (1931), The moisture equivalent as a measure of the field capacity of soils, Soil Science 32:181-193
evidence.claim: Field capacity was defined as water held after free drainage has become very slow, typically after 2 to 3 days.

s1262.label: Texture sets the available water: roughly 0.05-0.10 m3 per m3 in sand and about 0.15-0.20 in silt loam

evidence.source: Saxton & Rawls (2006), Soil Science Society of America Journal 70:1569-1578
evidence.claim: Plant-available water capacity is greatest in silt loams (about 0.2) and smallest in sands.

s1263.label: Organic matter adds only about 1.2 percent by volume of available water per 1 percent soil organic carbon

evidence.source: Minasny & McBratney (2018), Limited effect of organic matter on soil available water capacity, European Journal of Soil Science 69:39-47
evidence.claim: A 1 percent rise in organic carbon raised available water capacity by about 1.2 percent by volume on average, a smaller effect than often claimed.

s1264.label: Roots draw water down; many crops reduce transpiration once about 50 percent of available water is depleted

evidence.source: Allen et al. (1998), FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Table 22
evidence.claim: Depletion fraction p is about 0.5 for many field crops before stress sets in.

s1265.label: Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity falls by orders of magnitude as soil dries, so supply to roots limits uptake before the wilting point

evidence.source: Gardner (1960), Dynamic aspects of water availability to plants, Soil Science 89:63-73
evidence.claim: Flow to roots is limited by soil conductivity in drying soil, so uptake rate depends on moisture content.

s1266.label: Stomata close, transpiration and photosynthesis fall, and the plant enters drought stress

evidence.source: Sperry, Hacke, Oren & Comstock (2002), Water deficits and hydraulic limits to leaf water supply, Plant, Cell & Environment 25:251-263
evidence.claim: Declining soil-to-leaf conductance triggers stomatal closure to prevent hydraulic failure.

s1267.label: Soil respiration: temperature and moisture control and climate feedback

evidence.source: Bond-Lamberty & Thomson (2010), Temperature-associated increases in the global soil respiration record, Nature 464:579-582
evidence.claim: Global soil respiration was estimated at about 98 Pg C per year in 2008 and rising.

s1268.label: Start: Soil respiration: temperature and moisture control and climate feedback

evidence.source: Bond-Lamberty & Thomson (2010), Temperature-associated increases in the global soil respiration record, Nature 464:579-582
evidence.claim: Global soil respiration was estimated at about 98 Pg C per year in 2008 and rising.

s1269.label: End: Soil respiration: temperature and moisture control and climate feedback

evidence.source: Bond-Lamberty & Thomson (2010), Temperature-associated increases in the global soil respiration record, Nature 464:579-582
evidence.claim: Global soil respiration was estimated at about 98 Pg C per year in 2008 and rising.

s1270.label: Soil CO2 efflux reaches about 98 Pg C per year globally, far above fossil emissions of about 9 Pg C

evidence.source: Bond-Lamberty & Thomson (2010), Nature 464:579-582
evidence.claim: Global soil respiration was estimated at about 98 Pg C in 2008.

s1271.label: Warming speeds enzyme and respiration rates, with Q10 typically 1.5 to 3 and higher at low temperature

evidence.source: Lloyd & Taylor (1994), On the temperature dependence of soil respiration, Functional Ecology 8:315-323
evidence.claim: Soil respiration follows an Arrhenius-type curve in which apparent Q10 declines as temperature rises.

s1272.label: Moisture optimum near 60 percent water-filled pore space: drier soil limits substrate diffusion, wetter soil limits oxygen

evidence.source: Linn & Doran (1984), Effect of water-filled pore space on carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide production in tilled and nontilled soils, Soil Science Society of America Journal 48:1267-1272
evidence.claim: Aerobic microbial activity peaked at about 60 percent water-filled pore space.

s1273.label: Rewetting dry soil causes a CO2 and mineral N pulse within hours (Birch effect) from released osmolytes and exposed organic matter

evidence.source: Birch (1958), The effect of soil drying on humus decomposition and nitrogen availability, Plant and Soil 10:9-31
evidence.claim: Drying and rewetting stimulated a flush of mineralisation compared with continuously moist soil.

s1274.label: Warming-driven CO2 release adds to atmospheric CO2; models suggest tens of Pg C lost by 2050 (central estimate about 55 Pg C with similar uncertainty)

evidence.source: Crowther et al. (2016), Quantifying global soil carbon losses in response to warming, Nature 540:104-108
evidence.claim: A warming of about 1 degree was estimated to cause a loss of about 55 Pg C by 2050, with an uncertainty of similar magnitude.

s1275.label: Labile carbon is used up, so respiration per unit soil falls after several years of warming (Harvard Forest soil warming, 5 degrees)

evidence.source: Melillo et al. (2002), Soil warming and carbon-cycle feedbacks to the climate system, Science 298:2173-2176
evidence.claim: Extra soil CO2 release under warming lasted about 6 years and then declined as labile carbon was depleted.

s1276.label: Aerenchyma, radial oxygen loss and the oxidised rhizosphere of wetland plants

evidence.source: Colmer (2003), Long-distance transport of gases in plants: a perspective on internal aeration and radial oxygen loss from roots, Plant, Cell & Environment 26:17-36
evidence.claim: Aerenchyma carry O2 down roots of wetland species and part of it leaks radially into the rhizosphere.

s1277.label: Start: Aerenchyma, radial oxygen loss and the oxidised rhizosphere of wetland plants

evidence.source: Colmer (2003), Long-distance transport of gases in plants: a perspective on internal aeration and radial oxygen loss from roots, Plant, Cell & Environment 26:17-36
evidence.claim: Aerenchyma carry O2 down roots of wetland species and part of it leaks radially into the rhizosphere.

s1278.label: End: Aerenchyma, radial oxygen loss and the oxidised rhizosphere of wetland plants

evidence.source: Colmer (2003), Long-distance transport of gases in plants: a perspective on internal aeration and radial oxygen loss from roots, Plant, Cell & Environment 26:17-36
evidence.claim: Aerenchyma carry O2 down roots of wetland species and part of it leaks radially into the rhizosphere.

s1279.label: Waterlogging fills pores, and gas diffusion in water is roughly 10,000 times slower than in air, so soil goes anoxic within hours to days

evidence.source: Armstrong (1979), Aeration in higher plants, Advances in Botanical Research 7:225-332
evidence.claim: Gas diffusion through water-filled pores is about four orders of magnitude slower than through air-filled pores.

s1280.label: Wetland plants form aerenchyma (root gas space of tens of percent, up to about 40 to 50 percent in rice) that carries oxygen from shoot to root

evidence.source: Colmer (2003), Plant, Cell & Environment 26:17-36
evidence.claim: Rice and other wetland species develop root porosity of tens of percent by volume that enables long-distance O2 transport.

s1281.label: Radial oxygen loss leaks Oxygen into the soil, forming an oxidised zone a millimetre or so thick around roots

evidence.source: Colmer (2003), Plant, Cell & Environment 26:17-36
evidence.claim: Roots without a barrier to radial oxygen loss release O2 to the rhizosphere, which is oxidised at the millimetre scale.

s1282.label: Fe2+ is oxidised at the root surface and precipitates as an iron plaque that adsorbs phosphate and trace elements

evidence.source: Chen, Dixon & Turner (1980), Iron coatings on rice roots: morphology and models of development, Soil Science Society of America Journal 44:1113-1119
evidence.claim: Iron oxide coatings on rice roots form by oxidation of Fe2+ using radial oxygen loss.

s1283.label: In the oxic zone nitrifiers make nitrate that diffuses to anoxic soil and is denitrified, so a large share of applied nitrogen (an estimated 20 to 50 percent) is lost

evidence.source: Reddy & Patrick (1984), Nitrogen transformations and loss in flooded soils and sediments, CRC Critical Reviews in Environmental Control 13:273-309
evidence.claim: Coupled nitrification-denitrification at oxic-anoxic interfaces is a main N loss route in flooded soils; the percentage range is an estimate.

s1284.label: Oxidation removes toxic Fe2+, sulfide and organic acids that otherwise injure roots in flooded soil

evidence.source: Ponnamperuma (1972), The chemistry of submerged soils, Advances in Agronomy 24:29-96
evidence.claim: Reduced soils accumulate Fe2+, H2S and organic acids that are toxic to rice at high levels.

s1285.label: Nitrate leaching from the root zone to groundwater and coastal waters

evidence.source: Di & Cameron (2002), Nitrate leaching in temperate agroecosystems: sources, factors and mitigating strategies, Nutrient Cycling in Agroecosystems 64:237-256
evidence.claim: Nitrate leaching depends on soil nitrate at the start of drainage and on drainage volume, and cover crops and timing of N supply reduce it.

s1286.label: Start: Nitrate leaching from the root zone to groundwater and coastal waters

evidence.source: Di & Cameron (2002), Nitrate leaching in temperate agroecosystems: sources, factors and mitigating strategies, Nutrient Cycling in Agroecosystems 64:237-256
evidence.claim: Nitrate leaching depends on soil nitrate at the start of drainage and on drainage volume, and cover crops and timing of N supply reduce it.

s1287.label: End: Nitrate leaching from the root zone to groundwater and coastal waters

evidence.source: Di & Cameron (2002), Nitrate leaching in temperate agroecosystems: sources, factors and mitigating strategies, Nutrient Cycling in Agroecosystems 64:237-256
evidence.claim: Nitrate leaching depends on soil nitrate at the start of drainage and on drainage volume, and cover crops and timing of N supply reduce it.

s1288.label: Nitrate is not adsorbed by net-negative soil surfaces and moves with drainage water, taking base cations with it

evidence.source: Addiscott, Whitmore & Powlson (1991), Farming, Fertilizers and the Nitrate Problem, CAB International
evidence.claim: Nitrate behaves almost as a conservative solute in soil water, so drainage volume determines transport.

s1289.label: Most leaching occurs in autumn and winter, when the crop is gone, mineralisation continues and drainage is highest

evidence.source: Di & Cameron (2002), Nutrient Cycling in Agroecosystems 64:237-256
evidence.claim: Leaching losses concentrate in the drainage season after crop uptake ends.

s1290.label: Cover or catch crops take up residual nitrate; non-legume cover crops cut leaching by about 70 percent and legume covers by about 40 percent

evidence.source: Tonitto, David & Drinkwater (2006), Replacing bare fallows with cover crops in fertilizer-intensive cropping systems: a meta-analysis of crop yield and N dynamics, Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 112:58-72
evidence.claim: Non-legume cover crops reduced N leaching by about 70 percent and legume covers by about 40 percent relative to fallow.

s1291.label: Nitrate reaches drains and groundwater; the US drinking-water limit is 10 mg nitrate-N per litre

evidence.source: US EPA, National Primary Drinking Water Regulations, 40 CFR 141.62 (maximum contaminant level for nitrate 10 mg per L as N)
evidence.claim: The maximum contaminant level for nitrate is 10 mg per L as nitrogen.

s1292.label: Riparian buffers remove about two thirds of nitrate on average (large range) by denitrification and uptake

evidence.source: Mayer, Reynolds, McCutchen & Canfield (2007), Meta-analysis of nitrogen removal in riparian buffers, Journal of Environmental Quality 36:1172-1180
evidence.claim: Riparian buffers removed on average about 67 percent of nitrate in a large meta-analysis, with wide variation.

s1293.label: Nitrogen delivered by rivers fuels algal blooms and the seasonal hypoxic zone in the Gulf of Mexico

evidence.source: Rabalais, Turner & Wiseman (2002), Gulf of Mexico hypoxia, a.k.a. the dead zone, Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 33:235-263
evidence.claim: Nutrient loads from the Mississippi River drive stratified bottom-water hypoxia.

s1294.label: Micronutrient availability: pH, redox and plant mobilisation of Fe and Zn

evidence.source: Lindsay (1979), Chemical Equilibria in Soils, Wiley
evidence.claim: Fe3+ activity from oxide solubility falls 1000-fold per unit pH rise; Zn2+, Cu2+ and Mn2+ fall about 100-fold per pH unit.

s1295.label: Start: Micronutrient availability: pH, redox and plant mobilisation of Fe and Zn

evidence.source: Lindsay (1979), Chemical Equilibria in Soils, Wiley
evidence.claim: Fe3+ activity from oxide solubility falls 1000-fold per unit pH rise; Zn2+, Cu2+ and Mn2+ fall about 100-fold per pH unit.

s1296.label: End: Micronutrient availability: pH, redox and plant mobilisation of Fe and Zn

evidence.source: Lindsay (1979), Chemical Equilibria in Soils, Wiley
evidence.claim: Fe3+ activity from oxide solubility falls 1000-fold per unit pH rise; Zn2+, Cu2+ and Mn2+ fall about 100-fold per pH unit.

s1297.label: Fe3+ solubility from oxides falls about 1000-fold per pH unit, and Zn2+, Cu2+ and Mn2+ about 100-fold per unit

evidence.source: Lindsay (1979), Chemical Equilibria in Soils, Wiley
evidence.claim: Oxide and hydroxide solubility of Fe3+ varies with the third power of H+ and divalent metals with the second power.

s1298.label: In calcareous soil at pH 7.5 to 8.5 inorganic Fe3+ falls far below the roughly 10^-8 M plants need, so Fe chlorosis appears

evidence.source: Lindsay & Schwab (1982), The chemistry of iron in soils and its availability to plants, Journal of Plant Nutrition 5:821-840
evidence.claim: Inorganic Fe solubility at high pH is many orders of magnitude below plant needs, so chelation and reduction are required.

s1299.label: Dicots acidify the rhizosphere, reduce Fe3+ and take up Fe2+, while grasses release phytosiderophores that chelate Fe3+

evidence.source: Marschner & Romheld (1994), Strategies of plants for acquisition of iron, Plant and Soil 165:261-274
evidence.claim: Strategy I and Strategy II plants mobilise Fe by reduction and acidification or by phytosiderophore release.

s1300.label: Waterlogging reduces Fe3+ and Mn4+ so they dissolve, which can cause Fe or Mn toxicity in acid paddy soil

evidence.source: Ponnamperuma (1972), The chemistry of submerged soils, Advances in Agronomy 24:29-96
evidence.claim: Submergence raises soluble Fe2+ and Mn2+, sometimes to toxic concentrations in acid soils.

s1301.label: About half of cereal-growing soils worldwide have low plant-available Zn

evidence.source: Alloway (2009), Soil factors associated with zinc deficiency in crops and humans, Environmental Geochemistry and Health 31:537-548
evidence.claim: Zinc deficiency affects roughly half of cereal soils globally, linked to high pH, calcareous and low organic matter soils.

s1302.label: Organic matter binds Cu, Zn and Fe, holding them in forms that are slowly released; Cu is bound most strongly

evidence.source: McBride (1994), Environmental Chemistry of Soils, Oxford University Press
evidence.claim: Cu2+ forms the strongest complexes with soil organic matter among the divalent micronutrient cations (Irving-Williams order).

s1303.label: Over-liming pushes pH above 7 and induces Mn, Zn and Fe deficiency

evidence.source: Brady & Weil, The Nature and Properties of Soils, 15th ed. (2016), ch. 15 on micronutrients
evidence.claim: Excess lime lowers micronutrient solubility and can induce deficiency.

s1304.label: Nematode feeding groups, the c-p scale and nitrogen release

evidence.source: Yeates, Bongers, De Goede, Freckman & Georgieva 1993, Journal of Nematology 25:315-331 (Feeding habits in soil nematode families and genera: an outline for soil ecologists)
evidence.claim: Soil nematode families and genera can be assigned to bacterial feeders, fungal feeders, plant feeders, omnivores, predators and animal parasites by stoma structure.

s1305.label: Start: Nematodes in a water film encounter food

evidence.source: Yeates, Bongers, De Goede, Freckman & Georgieva 1993, Journal of Nematology 25:315-331 (Feeding habits in soil nematode families and genera: an outline for soil ecologists)
evidence.claim: Soil nematode families and genera can be assigned to bacterial feeders, fungal feeders, plant feeders, omnivores, predators and animal parasites by stoma structure.

s1306.label: End: Nitrogen released, prey regulated and community structure set

evidence.source: Yeates, Bongers, De Goede, Freckman & Georgieva 1993, Journal of Nematology 25:315-331 (Feeding habits in soil nematode families and genera: an outline for soil ecologists)
evidence.claim: Soil nematode families and genera can be assigned to bacterial feeders, fungal feeders, plant feeders, omnivores, predators and animal parasites by stoma structure.

s1307.label: Nematodes move only in water films and pores wider than their body (about 15-100 micrometres), so water-filled pores of that size set where they can feed

evidence.source: Elliott, Anderson, Coleman & Cole 1980, Oikos 35:327-335 (Habitable pore space and microbial trophic interactions)
evidence.claim: Bacteria in small pores are protected from protozoan and nematode grazers, so predator access is set by pore-size distribution (thresholds of order 3 and 30 micrometres are approximate).

s1308.label: Trophic type of the nematode that reaches the prey patch

evidence.source: Yeates et al. 1993, Journal of Nematology 25:315-331
evidence.claim: Trophic groups differ with soil, plant cover and management. Shares below are an illustrative estimate for a grassland topsoil, not a measured census.

s1309.label: Bacterial feeders (Rhabditidae, Cephalobidae) are fast-breeding opportunists (c-p 1-2) that boom after a bacterial flush

evidence.source: Bongers 1990, Oecologia 83:14-19 (The maturity index: an ecological measure of environmental disturbance based on nematode species composition)
evidence.claim: The colonizer-persister (c-p) scale ranks nematode families from 1 (short life cycle, high fecundity, tolerant) to 5 (long life cycle, sensitive).

s1310.label: Fungal feeders pierce hyphae with a stylet (Aphelenchoides, Tylenchidae) and increase under fungal-dominated decomposition

evidence.source: Yeates et al. 1993, Journal of Nematology 25:315-331
evidence.claim: Fungal-feeding nematodes pierce hyphae and sip contents.

s1311.label: Omnivore and predatory nematodes (Dorylaimida, Mononchida; c-p 4-5) breed slowly and are the first lost under disturbance

evidence.source: Bongers & Bongers 1998, Applied Soil Ecology 10:239-251 (Functional diversity of nematodes)
evidence.claim: K-strategist families have long generation times, low reproductive rates and high sensitivity to pollutants and disturbance.

s1312.label: Plant parasites (root-knot Meloidogyne, cyst Heterodera and Globodera, root-lesion Pratylenchus) feed on living roots

evidence.source: Jones et al. 2013, Molecular Plant Pathology 14:946-961 (Top 10 plant-parasitic nematodes in molecular plant pathology)
evidence.claim: Root-knot, cyst and root-lesion nematodes ranked as the most scientifically and economically important plant-parasitic genera.

s1313.label: Entomopathogenic nematodes (Steinernema, Heterorhabditis) carry symbiotic bacteria that kill insect larvae in 1-3 days

evidence.source: Kaya & Gaugler 1993, Annual Review of Entomology 38:181-206 (Entomopathogenic nematodes)
evidence.claim: Infective juveniles release symbiotic bacteria in the insect hemocoel, causing death within about 24-72 hours.

s1314.label: Grazers consume more nitrogen than they need and excrete the surplus as ammonium, speeding mineralization and raising plant N uptake

evidence.source: Ingham, Trofymow, Ingham & Coleman 1985, Ecological Monographs 55:119-140 (Interactions of bacteria, fungi, and their nematode grazers: effects on nutrient cycling and plant growth)
evidence.claim: Adding nematode grazers to microcosms with bacteria or fungi raised mineralization of nitrogen and plant growth.

s1315.label: Nematode-trapping fungi (Arthrobotrys oligospora) build adhesive traps when they sense nematode ascarosides

evidence.source: Hsueh et al. 2013, Current Biology 23:83-86 (Nematode-trapping fungi eavesdrop on nematode pheromones)
evidence.claim: Ascarosides from nematodes induced trap formation in Arthrobotrys oligospora and other nematode-trapping fungi.

s1316.label: Anhydrobiosis: nematodes dry slowly, accumulate trehalose and survive complete desiccation, reviving on rewetting

evidence.source: Crowe, Hoekstra & Crowe 1992, Annual Review of Physiology 54:579-599 (Anhydrobiosis)
evidence.claim: Trehalose and slow dehydration protect membranes and proteins so anhydrobiotic nematodes survive desiccation.

s1317.label: Enrichment and structure indices from nematode composition diagnose nutrient pulses and food-web complexity

evidence.source: Ferris, Bongers & de Goede 2001, Applied Soil Ecology 18:13-29 (A framework for soil food web diagnostics: extension of the nematode faunal analysis concept)
evidence.claim: Enrichment index (from c-p 1 bacterial feeders) and structure index (from c-p 3-5 groups) place a soil on a faunal profile.

s1318.label: Root exudates fuel bacteria, bacterial feeders return ammonium near roots, and plants release more exudate

evidence.source: Ingham et al. 1985, Ecological Monographs 55:119-140
evidence.claim: Grazed microcosms showed higher plant N uptake and plant growth.

s1319.label: Nematode feeding guilds and control of root feeders

evidence.source: Yeates, Bongers, De Goede, Freckman & Georgieva 1993, Journal of Nematology 25:315, Feeding habits in soil nematode families and genera: an outline for soil ecologists
evidence.claim: Soil nematode families are assigned to bacterial, fungal, plant-feeding, omnivore and predator guilds.

s1320.label: Start: Nematode feeding guilds and control of root feeders

evidence.source: Yeates, Bongers, De Goede, Freckman & Georgieva 1993, Journal of Nematology 25:315, Feeding habits in soil nematode families and genera: an outline for soil ecologists
evidence.claim: Soil nematode families are assigned to bacterial, fungal, plant-feeding, omnivore and predator guilds.

s1321.label: End: Nematode feeding guilds and control of root feeders

evidence.source: Yeates, Bongers, De Goede, Freckman & Georgieva 1993, Journal of Nematology 25:315, Feeding habits in soil nematode families and genera: an outline for soil ecologists
evidence.claim: Soil nematode families are assigned to bacterial, fungal, plant-feeding, omnivore and predator guilds.

s1322.label: Soil nematodes sort into feeding guilds: bacterivores, fungivores, plant parasites, omnivores and predators

evidence.source: Yeates et al. 1993, Journal of Nematology 25:315
evidence.claim: Mouthpart structure assigns each nematode family to a feeding guild.

s1323.label: Colonizer-persister scale: c-p 1 enrichment opportunists reproduce within days; c-p 5 predators and omnivores have long generations and are disturbance sensitive

evidence.source: Bongers 1990, Oecologia 83:14, The maturity index: an ecological measure of environmental disturbance based on nematode species composition
evidence.claim: The maturity index weights nematode taxa from c-p 1 (opportunists) to c-p 5 (persisters); it falls under disturbance.

s1324.label: Bacterivorous nematodes excrete ammonium because bacteria are N-rich prey; nematodes account for roughly 5-20% of net N mineralization (wide range)

evidence.source: Ingham, Trofymow, Ingham & Coleman 1985, Ecological Monographs 55:119, Interactions of bacteria, fungi, and their nematode grazers: effects on nutrient cycling and plant growth
evidence.claim: Microcosms with nematode grazers mineralized more N than microbes alone; the nematode share was modest, in the single-digit to roughly 20% range.

s1325.label: Plant-parasitic nematodes (root-knot Meloidogyne, cyst Heterodera and Globodera) feed on roots; root-knot nematodes induce giant cells that act as nutrient sinks

evidence.source: Jones et al. 2013, Molecular Plant Pathology 14:946, Top 10 plant-parasitic nematodes in molecular plant pathology
evidence.claim: Root-knot nematodes top the ranking; they reprogram root cells into giant cells that feed the parasite.

s1326.label: Antagonists hold root feeders in check: nematode-trapping fungi (Arthrobotrys) and Pasteuria bacterial spores that attach to the cuticle

evidence.source: Chen & Dickson 1998, Journal of Nematology 30:313, Review of Pasteuria penetrans: biology, ecology, and biological control potential
evidence.claim: Pasteuria endospores attach to root-knot nematode cuticle and sterilize or kill females; suppression grows with spore density.

s1327.label: Predatory and omnivorous nematodes (Mononchida, Dorylaimida) eat other nematodes, adding a trophic level that slows prey growth

evidence.source: Wardle 2002, Communities and Ecosystems: Linking the Aboveground and Belowground Components, Princeton University Press
evidence.claim: Higher nematode trophic levels regulate lower ones in soil food webs.

s1328.label: Disturbance reshapes the nematode community: tillage and fertilizer favour c-p 1 enrichment opportunists, while undisturbed soils keep c-p 4-5 taxa

evidence.source: Ferris, Bongers & de Goede 2001, Applied Soil Ecology 18:13, A framework for soil food web diagnostics: extension of the nematode faunal analysis concept
evidence.claim: Enrichment and structure indices separate nutrient-enriched and disturbed soils from structured, undisturbed food webs.

s1329.label: Springtail and mite grazing of fungi: stimulation, defence and dispersal

evidence.source: Hanlon & Anderson 1979, Oecologia 38:93, The effects of Collembola grazing on microbial activity in decomposing leaf litter
evidence.claim: Collembola grazing at moderate density stimulated litter respiration, at high density it reduced it.

s1330.label: Start: Springtail and mite grazing of fungi: stimulation, defence and dispersal

evidence.source: Hanlon & Anderson 1979, Oecologia 38:93, The effects of Collembola grazing on microbial activity in decomposing leaf litter
evidence.claim: Collembola grazing at moderate density stimulated litter respiration, at high density it reduced it.

s1331.label: End: Springtail and mite grazing of fungi: stimulation, defence and dispersal

evidence.source: Hanlon & Anderson 1979, Oecologia 38:93, The effects of Collembola grazing on microbial activity in decomposing leaf litter
evidence.claim: Collembola grazing at moderate density stimulated litter respiration, at high density it reduced it.

s1332.label: Collembola and mites graze hyphae and spores; moderate grazing stimulates hyphal regrowth and respiration, heavy grazing cuts hyphal biomass

evidence.source: Hanlon & Anderson 1979, Oecologia 38:93
evidence.claim: Litter respiration rose at moderate Collembola density and fell at high density.

s1333.label: Grazers fragment litter and produce faecal pellets with high surface area that bacteria colonize

evidence.source: Seastedt 1984, Annual Review of Entomology 29:25, The role of microarthropods in decomposition and mineralization processes
evidence.claim: Microarthropod faeces and fragmentation raise the surface available for microbial colonization.

s1334.label: Grazing mineralizes nitrogen held in fungal biomass; fauna as a whole contribute roughly a third of N mineralization in studied agroecosystems (estimate)

evidence.source: Verhoef & Brussaard 1990, Biogeochemistry 11:175, Decomposition and nitrogen mineralization in natural and agroecosystems: the contribution of soil animals
evidence.claim: Soil animals directly and indirectly contributed on the order of a third of N mineralization in the systems compared; range wide.

s1335.label: Grazers carry spores and bacteria on cuticles and in faeces, changing which fungi colonize next

evidence.source: Crowther, Boddy & Jones 2012, ISME Journal 6:1992, Functional and ecological consequences of saprotrophic fungus-grazer interactions
evidence.claim: Grazers disperse fungal propagules and alter fungal community structure through selective feeding.

s1336.label: Fungi defend with secondary metabolites: Aspergillus nidulans lacking them (laeA mutant) was eaten far more by the springtail Folsomia candida

evidence.source: Rohlfs, Albert, Keller & Kempken 2007, Biology Letters 3:523, Secondary chemicals protect mould from fungivory
evidence.claim: Secondary metabolite-deficient laeA mutants were preferred and consumed more by springtails than wild type.

s1337.label: Earthworm gut passage, casts and the drilosphere

evidence.source: Brown, Barois & Lavelle 2000, European Journal of Soil Biology 36:177, Regulation of soil organic matter dynamics and microbial activity in the drilosphere
evidence.claim: Earthworm mucus, casts and burrow linings form a drilosphere with distinct microbial activity and organic matter dynamics.

s1338.label: Start: Earthworm gut passage, casts and the drilosphere

evidence.source: Brown, Barois & Lavelle 2000, European Journal of Soil Biology 36:177, Regulation of soil organic matter dynamics and microbial activity in the drilosphere
evidence.claim: Earthworm mucus, casts and burrow linings form a drilosphere with distinct microbial activity and organic matter dynamics.

s1339.label: End: Earthworm gut passage, casts and the drilosphere

evidence.source: Brown, Barois & Lavelle 2000, European Journal of Soil Biology 36:177, Regulation of soil organic matter dynamics and microbial activity in the drilosphere
evidence.claim: Earthworm mucus, casts and burrow linings form a drilosphere with distinct microbial activity and organic matter dynamics.

s1340.label: Worms ingest soil, litter and microbes; gut mucus (water-soluble, energy-rich) stimulates microbial activity during transit

evidence.source: Brown, Barois & Lavelle 2000, European Journal of Soil Biology 36:177
evidence.claim: Intestinal mucus acts as a priming agent that activates dormant gut microbes.

s1341.label: The anoxic, nitrate-rich gut hosts denitrifiers and fermenters that emit Nitrous oxide

evidence.source: Drake & Horn 2007, Annual Review of Microbiology 61:169, As the worm turns: the earthworm gut as a transient habitat for soil microbial biomes
evidence.claim: The earthworm gut is anoxic and activates ingested denitrifiers, causing N2O emission.

s1342.label: Fresh casts hold more ammonium, nitrate, available phosphorus and microbial activity than bulk soil

evidence.source: Lee 1985, Earthworms: Their Ecology and Relationships with Soils and Land Use, Academic Press
evidence.claim: Casts are enriched in mineral N and extractable P relative to surrounding soil.

s1343.label: Meta-analysis: earthworm presence raises soil Nitrous oxide emission by about 42% and Carbon dioxide emission by about 33%

evidence.source: Lubbers et al. 2013, Nature Climate Change 3:187, Greenhouse-gas emissions from soils increased by earthworms
evidence.claim: Earthworms increased N2O by 42% and CO2 by 33% on average across studies.

s1344.label: Casts age, dry and harden; microaggregates inside casts protect organic carbon for months to years

evidence.source: Bossuyt, Six & Hendrix 2005, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 37:251, Protection of soil carbon by microaggregates within earthworm casts
evidence.claim: Microaggregates formed inside casts physically protected carbon from decomposition.

s1345.label: Mucus-lined burrow walls (drilosphere, a rim of a few millimetres) carry more microbial biomass, carbon and nitrogen than bulk soil

evidence.source: Brown, Barois & Lavelle 2000, European Journal of Soil Biology 36:177
evidence.claim: Burrow linings concentrate microbial activity and organic matter.

s1346.label: Worm-driven nutrient release raises plant production: about 23% more aboveground biomass and 25% more crop yield on average

evidence.source: van Groenigen, Lubbers, Vos, Brown, De Deyn & van Groenigen 2014, Scientific Reports 4:6365, Earthworms increase plant production: a meta-analysis
evidence.claim: Earthworm presence increased aboveground biomass by 23% and crop yield by 25% in meta-analysis.

s1347.label: Disease-suppressive soils and the rhizosphere cry for help

evidence.source: Weller, Raaijmakers, Gardener & Thomashow 2002, Annual Review of Phytopathology 40:309, Microbial populations responsible for specific soil suppressiveness to plant pathogens
evidence.claim: Specific suppressiveness is caused by identifiable antagonist populations, transferable between soils.

s1348.label: Start: Disease-suppressive soils and the rhizosphere cry for help

evidence.source: Weller, Raaijmakers, Gardener & Thomashow 2002, Annual Review of Phytopathology 40:309, Microbial populations responsible for specific soil suppressiveness to plant pathogens
evidence.claim: Specific suppressiveness is caused by identifiable antagonist populations, transferable between soils.

s1349.label: End: Disease-suppressive soils and the rhizosphere cry for help

evidence.source: Weller, Raaijmakers, Gardener & Thomashow 2002, Annual Review of Phytopathology 40:309, Microbial populations responsible for specific soil suppressiveness to plant pathogens
evidence.claim: Specific suppressiveness is caused by identifiable antagonist populations, transferable between soils.

s1350.label: Soil-borne pathogens (Fusarium oxysporum, Gaeumannomyces tritici, Rhizoctonia solani) infect roots

evidence.source: Mendes et al. 2011, Science 332:1097, Deciphering the rhizosphere microbiome for disease-suppressive bacteria
evidence.claim: A Rhizoctonia-suppressive soil was dissected to identify the bacterial taxa that protect sugar beet.

s1351.label: Infected plants change exudates (for example malic acid) that recruit antagonists such as Bacillus subtilis: the cry for help

evidence.source: Rudrappa, Czymmek, Pare & Bais 2008, Plant Physiology 148:1547, Root-secreted malic acid recruits beneficial soil bacteria
