evidence.claim: Arabidopsis infected by Pseudomonas syringae secreted malic acid that recruited Bacillus subtilis FB17 and protected leaves.

s1352.label: Disease-induced assembly: a consortium of Stenotrophomonas, Xanthomonas and Microbacterium is enriched in the rhizosphere after downy-mildew infection

evidence.source: Berendsen et al. 2018, ISME Journal 12:1496, Disease-induced assemblage of a plant-beneficial bacterial consortium
evidence.claim: Infection enriched a three-member consortium that induced resistance and protected the next plant generation.

s1353.label: Pseudomonas fluorescens make 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol (DAPG) that inhibits Gaeumannomyces; suppression needs about 10^5 DAPG-producing cfu per g root

evidence.source: Raaijmakers & Weller 1998, Molecular Plant-Microbe Interactions 11:144, Natural plant protection by 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol-producing Pseudomonas spp. in take-all decline
evidence.claim: Take-all decline soils carried at least about 10^5 cfu DAPG producers per g wheat root.

s1354.label: Take-all decline: disease falls after a few seasons of wheat monoculture as DAPG producers build up

evidence.source: Weller et al. 2002, Annual Review of Phytopathology 40:309
evidence.claim: Take-all decline arises with continued wheat monoculture and is transferable to conducive soil.

s1355.label: General suppression: high microbial biomass and activity compete for carbon and Iron; pasteurized soil loses suppression

evidence.source: Weller et al. 2002, Annual Review of Phytopathology 40:309
evidence.claim: General suppression is lost on sterilization and scales with total microbial activity.

s1356.label: Pyoverdine siderophores sequester Iron, starving pathogens, especially in neutral to alkaline soil where Fe is scarce

evidence.source: Kloepper, Leong, Teintze & Schroth 1980, Current Microbiology 4:317, Pseudomonas siderophores: a mechanism explaining disease-suppressive soils
evidence.claim: Siderophore-producing pseudomonads reduced Fusarium wilt in soils; effect reversed with added iron.

s1357.label: Induced systemic resistance: rhizobacteria prime plant defences through jasmonate and ethylene signalling without direct antagonism

evidence.source: Pieterse, Zamioudis, Berendsen, Weller, Van Wees & Bakker 2014, Annual Review of Phytopathology 52:347, Induced systemic resistance by beneficial microbes
evidence.claim: Beneficial rhizobacteria prime the whole plant for faster defence activation.

s1358.label: Rhizosphere phosphorus mobilization: phosphatases, organic acids and fast re-sorption

evidence.source: Richardson & Simpson 2011, Plant Physiology 156:989, Soil microorganisms mediating phosphorus availability
evidence.claim: Microbial and plant enzymes and organic acids mobilize organic and sorbed soil P for plant uptake.

s1359.label: Start: Rhizosphere phosphorus mobilization: phosphatases, organic acids and fast re-sorption

evidence.source: Richardson & Simpson 2011, Plant Physiology 156:989, Soil microorganisms mediating phosphorus availability
evidence.claim: Microbial and plant enzymes and organic acids mobilize organic and sorbed soil P for plant uptake.

s1360.label: End: Rhizosphere phosphorus mobilization: phosphatases, organic acids and fast re-sorption

evidence.source: Richardson & Simpson 2011, Plant Physiology 156:989, Soil microorganisms mediating phosphorus availability
evidence.claim: Microbial and plant enzymes and organic acids mobilize organic and sorbed soil P for plant uptake.

s1361.label: Soil solution Phosphate seldom exceeds about 10 uM (often 1-2 uM), so roots deplete a zone around themselves

evidence.source: Raghothama 1999, Annual Review of Plant Physiology and Plant Molecular Biology 50:665, Phosphate acquisition
evidence.claim: Free inorganic phosphate in soil solution is typically below 10 uM and diffuses slowly.

s1362.label: Low Phosphate induces plant and microbial phosphatases and phytases that hydrolyse organic P (about 30-65% of total soil P in many soils)

evidence.source: Richardson & Simpson 2011, Plant Physiology 156:989
evidence.claim: Organic P is often 30-65% of total soil P and requires phosphatase or phytase to become available.

s1363.label: Phytate (inositol hexakisphosphate) is the main identified organic P but sorbs strongly to Fe and Al oxides and clay, limiting access

evidence.source: Turner, Papházy, Haygarth & McKelvie 2002, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 357:449, Inositol phosphates in the environment
evidence.claim: Inositol phosphates are the dominant identified soil organic P and are stabilized by mineral sorption.

s1364.label: Roots and microbes exude citrate, malate and oxalate and extrude H+ to desorb phosphate from Fe and Al oxides and dissolve Ca phosphates

evidence.source: Jones 1998, Plant and Soil 205:25, Organic acids in the rhizosphere: a critical review
evidence.claim: Citrate and other carboxylates mobilize P by ligand exchange and chelation of Fe and Al.

s1365.label: Phosphate-solubilizing bacteria (Pseudomonas, Bacillus) form gluconic acid via PQQ-glucose dehydrogenase; field inoculation responses are inconsistent

evidence.source: Rodriguez & Fraga 1999, Biotechnology Advances 17:319, Phosphate solubilizing bacteria and their role in plant growth promotion
evidence.claim: Gluconic acid production by PQQ-dependent glucose dehydrogenase is the best-documented solubilization mechanism.

s1366.label: Released phosphate is re-adsorbed to Fe and Al oxides within minutes to hours, so uptake must compete with fast sorption

evidence.source: Hinsinger 2001, Plant and Soil 237:173, Bioavailability of soil inorganic P in the rhizosphere as affected by root-induced chemical changes: a review
evidence.claim: Phosphate sorption is rapid, then slows, so root-released P is short-lived.

s1367.label: Microbial biomass holds a few percent of total soil P but turns over fast, so microbes immobilize and release a large P flux

evidence.source: Brookes, Powlson & Jenkinson 1984, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 16:169, Phosphorus in the soil microbial biomass
evidence.claim: Microbial biomass P is a small fraction (about 1-5%) of total soil P but exchanges rapidly with the available pool.

s1368.label: Roots take up Phosphate by high-affinity PHT1 transporters, directly or through mycorrhizal hyphae

evidence.source: Raghothama 1999, Annual Review of Plant Physiology and Plant Molecular Biology 50:665
evidence.claim: High-affinity PHT1 phosphate transporters are induced under P deficiency.

s1369.label: Rising phosphate supply represses starvation responses, lowering phosphatase and organic acid release

evidence.source: Richardson & Simpson 2011, Plant Physiology 156:989
evidence.claim: Phosphatase and carboxylate release are induced by P deficiency and repressed when P is sufficient.

s1370.label: Microarthropods: springtails and oribatid mites as fungal grazers and litter processors

evidence.source: Petersen & Luxton 1982, Oikos 39:287-388 (A comparative analysis of soil fauna populations and their role in decomposition processes)
evidence.claim: Collembola and mites are typically among the most abundant soil arthropods, with litter-layer densities around 10^4-10^5 per square metre and substantial contribution to decomposition.

s1371.label: Start: Microarthropods enter litter and fungal patches

evidence.source: Petersen & Luxton 1982, Oikos 39:287-388 (A comparative analysis of soil fauna populations and their role in decomposition processes)
evidence.claim: Collembola and mites are typically among the most abundant soil arthropods, with litter-layer densities around 10^4-10^5 per square metre and substantial contribution to decomposition.

s1372.label: End: Litter fragmented, fungi regulated and nutrients released

evidence.source: Petersen & Luxton 1982, Oikos 39:287-388 (A comparative analysis of soil fauna populations and their role in decomposition processes)
evidence.claim: Collembola and mites are typically among the most abundant soil arthropods, with litter-layer densities around 10^4-10^5 per square metre and substantial contribution to decomposition.

s1373.label: Microarthropods number about 10^4-10^5 per square metre in forest floors and live in air-filled pores and litter spaces

evidence.source: Petersen & Luxton 1982, Oikos 39:287-388
evidence.claim: Densities and biomass of Collembola and mites across ecosystems, concentrated in the litter and upper organic layers.

s1374.label: Feeding guild of the microarthropod: fungivore, litter feeder, predator or omnivore

evidence.source: Schneider et al. 2004, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 36:1769-1774 (Trophic niche differentiation in soil microarthropods (Oribatida, Acari): evidence from stable isotope ratios 15N/14N)
evidence.claim: 15N signatures divide oribatid mites into primary decomposers, secondary decomposers (fungal feeders), and predators or scavengers, so guilds are real but overlap. Shares are an estimate for a forest floor.

s1375.label: Fungivorous springtails (Folsomia, Onychiurus) graze hyphae selectively and shift fungal community composition

evidence.source: Chahartaghi et al. 2005, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 37:1718-1725 (Feeding guilds in Collembola based on nitrogen stable isotope ratios and fatty acids)
evidence.claim: Collembola species differ in 15N values and fatty acid markers, grouping into fungal feeders, litter feeders and more specialised feeders.

s1376.label: Light grazing stimulates fungal respiration and growth; heavy grazing suppresses fungal biomass and litter decomposition

evidence.source: Hanlon & Anderson 1979, Oecologia 38:93-99 (The effects of Collembola grazing on microbial activity in decomposing leaf litter)
evidence.claim: Collembola grazing at moderate density increased CO2 output from litter, while high density reduced microbial activity.

s1377.label: Grazing on mycorrhizal and saprotrophic hyphae changes how carbon moves through fungal networks

evidence.source: Johnson et al. 2005, Science 309:1047-1049 (Soil invertebrates disrupt carbon flow through fungal networks)
evidence.claim: Collembola grazing altered the movement of plant-derived carbon through ectomycorrhizal and saprotrophic networks.

s1378.label: Oribatid mites have slow life histories, low fecundity, and many parthenogenetic species, so populations recover slowly after disturbance

evidence.source: Maraun & Scheu 2000, Ecography 23:374-382 (The structure of oribatid mite communities (Acari, Oribatida): patterns, mechanisms and implications for future research)
evidence.claim: Oribatid communities are structured by slow reproduction and a high share of parthenogenetic species, with long generation times of months to a year.

s1379.label: Springtails reproduce fast (Folsomia candida completes a generation in roughly a month at 20 C) and can rebound within weeks

evidence.source: Fountain & Hopkin 2005, Annual Review of Entomology 50:201-222 (Folsomia candida (Collembola): a standard soil arthropod)
evidence.claim: F. candida is parthenogenetic, lays eggs repeatedly and completes its life cycle in a few weeks at 20 C.

s1380.label: Predatory mites (Mesostigmata) feed on springtails, nematodes and mite larvae and regulate prey numbers

evidence.source: Koehler 1999, Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment 74:395-410 (Predatory mites (Gamasina, Mesostigmata))
evidence.claim: Gamasine mites are major predators in soil, feeding on Collembola, nematodes and other small animals.

s1381.label: Faecal pellets increase surface area and microbial colonisation and form organic microaggregates

evidence.source: Rusek 1985, Quaestiones Entomologicae 21:497-514 (Soil microstructures: contributions on specific soil organisms)
evidence.claim: Microarthropod faecal pellets are a main component of organic horizon microstructure in forest soils.

s1382.label: Fragmentation and grazing speed litter decomposition: presence of fauna raises mass loss by roughly a third on average

evidence.source: Garcia-Palacios, Maestre, Kattge & Wall 2013, Ecology Letters 16:1045-1053 (Climate and litter quality differently modulate the effects of soil fauna on litter decomposition across biomes)
evidence.claim: Fauna-exclusion experiments across biomes show fauna accelerate litter decomposition, strongest in humid climates and with high-quality litter. The size (about one quarter to over one third) varies by dataset.

s1383.label: Grazers release ammonium and phosphate; soil animals together are estimated to supply on the order of 10-40% of N mineralisation

evidence.source: Verhoef & Brussaard 1990, Biogeochemistry 11:175-211 (Decomposition and nitrogen mineralization in natural and agro-ecosystems: the contribution of soil animals)
evidence.claim: Estimates across systems attribute roughly 10-40% of N mineralisation to soil fauna, mostly via their effect on microbes.

s1384.label: Fungal food falls when grazing is heavy, which lowers springtail numbers again

evidence.source: Hanlon & Anderson 1979, Oecologia 38:93-99
evidence.claim: High grazing reduced fungal activity, limiting the food of the grazers.

s1385.label: Matric potential and the soil water retention curve

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, Academic Press, chapters on soil water potential and retention
evidence.claim: Retention curve gives water content as a function of matric potential and is the basis for field capacity, wilting point and available water.

s1386.label: Start: Matric potential and the soil water retention curve

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, Academic Press, chapters on soil water potential and retention
evidence.claim: Retention curve gives water content as a function of matric potential and is the basis for field capacity, wilting point and available water.

s1387.label: End: Matric potential and the soil water retention curve

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, Academic Press, chapters on soil water potential and retention
evidence.claim: Retention curve gives water content as a function of matric potential and is the basis for field capacity, wilting point and available water.

s1388.label: Capillary and adsorptive forces bind water to particles, giving soil water a negative matric potential

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, soil water potential chapter
evidence.claim: Total soil water potential is the sum of matric, gravitational, osmotic and pressure components; matric potential is negative in unsaturated soil and falls as soil dries.

s1389.label: Pore radius sets suction by capillarity, h(cm) = 0.15/r(cm): pores of 15 micrometre radius empty near -10 kPa while 0.1 micrometre pores hold water to about -1.5 MPa

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics (Jurin law); Brady & Weil, The Nature and Properties of Soils, 15th ed., ch. 5
evidence.claim: h = 2 sigma cos(theta) / (rho g r) gives h of about 0.15 cm2 divided by r in cm; pores under about 0.2 micrometre diameter hold water at the wilting point (-1.5 MPa).

s1390.label: Texture shapes the curve: sands release most water by -10 kPa while clays hold much water below -1.5 MPa

evidence.source: Saxton & Rawls 2006, Soil Science Society of America Journal 70:1569-1578
evidence.claim: Pedotransfer functions from texture and organic matter: water content at -1500 kPa is roughly 0.03-0.05 m3/m3 for sand and 0.25-0.30 for clay, with field capacity rising with clay.

s1391.label: Organic matter adds only a modest amount of available water, about 0.012 m3 per m3 per 1% organic carbon

evidence.source: Minasny & McBratney 2018, European Journal of Soil Science 69:39-47, Limited effect of organic matter on soil available water capacity
evidence.claim: A 1% (10 g/kg) increase in organic carbon raised available water capacity by only about 1.2% by volume, far less than older rules of thumb.

s1392.label: Soil water potential relative to plant thresholds

evidence.source: Allen, Pereira, Raes & Smith 1998, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56; Brady & Weil 15th ed.
evidence.claim: Field capacity is near -10 to -33 kPa and permanent wilting near -1500 kPa; the shares here are an estimate (plus or minus 10 points) of time in each state for a temperate rainfed crop soil.

s1393.label: Above field capacity macropores drain within one to three days and then internal drainage nearly stops

evidence.source: Brady & Weil, The Nature and Properties of Soils, 15th ed., ch. 5
evidence.claim: Field capacity is the water content when rapid drainage has ceased, usually 2-3 days after wetting a well-drained soil.

s1394.label: Between field capacity and wilting point plants take up water freely until about half of the available water is used, after which stomata begin to close

evidence.source: Allen et al. 1998, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, ch. 8 and Table 22
evidence.claim: Depletion fraction p at which transpiration starts to fall is about 0.5 for many crops, ranging 0.3-0.7 with crop and evaporative demand.

s1395.label: Below the permanent wilting point (-1.5 MPa) water sits in films a few nanometres thick, so mesophyte uptake stops though some desert plants extract water to -3 to -6 MPa

evidence.source: Kramer & Boyer 1995, Water Relations of Plants and Soils, Academic Press; Briggs & Shantz 1912, Botanical Gazette 53:20-37
evidence.claim: Wilting coefficient of mesophytes corresponds to about -1.5 MPa; xerophytes withstand much lower water potentials.

s1396.label: Hysteresis: on wetting the soil holds less water at a given suction than on drying, because of ink-bottle pore necks and the advancing contact angle

evidence.source: Haines 1930, Journal of Agricultural Science 20:97-116; Hillel 1998
evidence.claim: Wetting and drying branches of the retention curve differ at the same suction; trapped air and pore-neck geometry cause the difference.

s1397.label: Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity and Richards flow

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, chapters on water flow in unsaturated soil
evidence.claim: Flux equals conductivity times potential gradient, and conductivity is a strong function of water content.

s1398.label: Start: Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity and Richards flow

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, chapters on water flow in unsaturated soil
evidence.claim: Flux equals conductivity times potential gradient, and conductivity is a strong function of water content.

s1399.label: End: Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity and Richards flow

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, chapters on water flow in unsaturated soil
evidence.claim: Flux equals conductivity times potential gradient, and conductivity is a strong function of water content.

s1400.label: Flux follows Buckingham-Darcy, q = -K(h) times the gradient of total potential, and combined with mass balance gives the Richards equation

evidence.source: Richards 1931, Physics 1:318-333, Capillary conduction of liquids through porous mediums
evidence.claim: Extended Darcy law to unsaturated media with water-content dependent conductivity; basis of the Richards equation.

s1401.label: Flow through a pore scales with radius to the fourth power, so doubling radius gives 16 times the flow and large pores dominate conductivity

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics (Poiseuille law)
evidence.claim: Poiseuille flow in a capillary is proportional to r^4, so conductivity is governed by the widest water-filled pores.

s1402.label: Saturated conductivity spans about three orders of magnitude by texture: sand about 20 cm/h, silt loam about 0.7 cm/h, clay about 0.03-0.1 cm/h

evidence.source: Rawls, Brakensiek & Saxton 1982, Transactions of the ASAE 25:1316-1320
evidence.claim: Mean saturated hydraulic conductivity by USDA texture class, from about 21 cm/h in sand to below 0.1 cm/h in clays.

s1403.label: Surface seals, compaction or water repellency throttle the top boundary, so rain exceeding the seal conductivity runs off

evidence.source: Assouline 2004, Vadose Zone Journal 3:570-591, Rainfall-induced soil surface sealing
evidence.claim: Seal saturated conductivity is one to three orders of magnitude below that of the underlying soil, controlling infiltration and runoff.

s1404.label: Hydraulic conductivity drops steeply as suction rises because the largest pores drain first

evidence.source: van Genuchten 1980, Soil Science Society of America Journal 44:892-898; Mualem 1976, Water Resources Research 12:513-522
evidence.claim: Closed-form K(h) from the retention curve predicts K falling by many orders of magnitude between saturation and dry soil.

s1405.label: With Carsel & Parrish parameters in the van Genuchten-Mualem model, K at -10 kPa is about 1e-8 of Ks for sand but about 4e-3 of Ks for clay, so at that suction clay conducts more than sand

evidence.source: Carsel & Parrish 1988, Water Resources Research 24:755-769
evidence.claim: Sand: alpha 0.145 per cm, n 2.68, Ks 713 cm/d; clay: alpha 0.008 per cm, n 1.09, Ks 4.8 cm/d; substituting at h = 100 cm gives the quoted ratios (derived estimate).

s1406.label: Infiltration rate starts high and declines toward the saturated conductivity as the wetted zone deepens

evidence.source: Green & Ampt 1911, Journal of Agricultural Science 4:1-24
evidence.claim: Infiltration rate falls as 1/depth of the wetting front, approaching Ks at long times.

s1407.label: In dry soil conductivity is so low that supply to roots, not root uptake capacity, limits transpiration, so plants wilt with some water still in the soil

evidence.source: Gardner 1960, Soil Science 89:63-73, Dynamic aspects of water availability to plants
evidence.claim: At low soil water content the soil conductivity becomes limiting for root water uptake.

s1408.label: Roots move water at night by hydraulic lift from moist deep layers to dry shallow layers

evidence.source: Richards & Caldwell 1987, Oecologia 73:486-489; Neumann & Cardon 2012, New Phytologist 194:337-352
evidence.claim: Sagebrush roots lifted water from deep moist soil into dry upper soil overnight, raising its water potential.

s1409.label: Soil evaporation stages and vapour transport

evidence.source: Or, Lehmann, Shahraeeni & Shokri 2013, Vadose Zone Journal 12(4), Advances in soil evaporation physics
evidence.claim: Evaporation proceeds through stage 1 (atmosphere limited), stage 2 (hydraulic-supply limited) and stage 3 (vapour diffusion).

s1410.label: Start: Soil evaporation stages and vapour transport

evidence.source: Or, Lehmann, Shahraeeni & Shokri 2013, Vadose Zone Journal 12(4), Advances in soil evaporation physics
evidence.claim: Evaporation proceeds through stage 1 (atmosphere limited), stage 2 (hydraulic-supply limited) and stage 3 (vapour diffusion).

s1411.label: End: Soil evaporation stages and vapour transport

evidence.source: Or, Lehmann, Shahraeeni & Shokri 2013, Vadose Zone Journal 12(4), Advances in soil evaporation physics
evidence.claim: Evaporation proceeds through stage 1 (atmosphere limited), stage 2 (hydraulic-supply limited) and stage 3 (vapour diffusion).

s1412.label: Stage 1: a wet surface evaporates at the atmospheric demand rate, typically 3-8 mm per day in sunny weather

evidence.source: Allen, Pereira, Raes & Smith 1998, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, ch. 7
evidence.claim: Evaporation from wet bare soil approaches the reference evapotranspiration, a few to about 8 mm/day depending on climate.

s1413.label: Evaporating 1 mm of water absorbs about 2.45 MJ per square metre, cooling the surface

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, evaporation chapter
evidence.claim: Latent heat of vaporisation is 2.45 MJ per kg of water at 20 C, so 1 mm over 1 m2 absorbs 2.45 MJ.

s1414.label: A cooler surface has lower saturation vapour pressure, about 6-7% lower per degree Celsius, which slows evaporation

evidence.source: Monteith & Unsworth 2013, Principles of Environmental Physics, 4th ed., Clausius-Clapeyron relation
evidence.claim: Saturation vapour pressure rises about 6-7% per kelvin near 20 C.

s1415.label: Stage 1 ends when the readily evaporable water is used: about 2-7 mm for sand and 8-12 mm for loam and clay

evidence.source: Allen et al. 1998, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Table 19
evidence.claim: Readily evaporable water REW is 2-7 mm for sands, 8-10 mm for loams and 8-12 mm for clays.

s1416.label: Stage 2: liquid flow to the drying front limits loss, so cumulative evaporation grows with the square root of time

evidence.source: Black, Gardner & Thurtell 1969, Soil Science Society of America Journal 33:655-660; Ritchie 1972, Water Resources Research 8:1204-1213
evidence.claim: After stage 1 cumulative evaporation is proportional to the square root of time since the end of stage 1.

s1417.label: Stage 3: the drying front retreats below the surface and vapour diffusion through the dry layer limits loss, often below about 0.5 mm per day

evidence.source: Or et al. 2013, Vadose Zone Journal 12(4)
evidence.claim: Once the hydraulic connection to the surface breaks, evaporation is limited by diffusion across the dry layer at rates a small fraction of stage 1.

s1418.label: Temperature gradients drive vapour from warm to cold soil, and at night vapour condenses near the cold surface; the vapour flux can exceed pure Fick diffusion by several-fold

evidence.source: Philip & de Vries 1957, Transactions of the American Geophysical Union 38:222-232
evidence.claim: Vapour transport in soils under temperature gradients is enhanced relative to Fick diffusion by an enhancement factor of several (estimate about 2-10).

s1419.label: Straw mulch or surface residue lowers soil evaporation by about 10-50% depending on cover and climate

evidence.source: Jalota & Prihar 1998, Reducing Soil Water Evaporation with Tillage and Straw Mulching, Iowa State University Press
evidence.claim: Mulches reduce evaporation by shading and by insulating the surface; reported reductions vary from about 10 to 50%.

s1420.label: Globally transpiration is about 61% of land evapotranspiration, so soil and canopy evaporation supply the other 39%

evidence.source: Schlesinger & Jasechko 2014, Agricultural and Forest Meteorology 189-190:115-117
evidence.claim: Transpiration averages 61 plus or minus 15% of terrestrial evapotranspiration from isotope and flux data.

s1421.label: Capillary rise from shallow groundwater and salt accumulation

evidence.source: Hillel 2000, Salinity Management for Sustainable Irrigation, World Bank
evidence.claim: Shallow water tables feed evaporation and salt accumulation in irrigated and cleared lands.

s1422.label: Start: Capillary rise from shallow groundwater and salt accumulation

evidence.source: Hillel 2000, Salinity Management for Sustainable Irrigation, World Bank
evidence.claim: Shallow water tables feed evaporation and salt accumulation in irrigated and cleared lands.

s1423.label: End: Capillary rise from shallow groundwater and salt accumulation

evidence.source: Hillel 2000, Salinity Management for Sustainable Irrigation, World Bank
evidence.claim: Shallow water tables feed evaporation and salt accumulation in irrigated and cleared lands.

s1424.label: Capillary fringe above the water table: rise follows Jurin h = 0.15/r cm, about 0.3-0.5 m in fine sand and 1-2 m in silt

evidence.source: Lohman 1972, USGS Professional Paper 708, Ground-water hydraulics
evidence.claim: Table of capillary rise by grain size: tens of centimetres in sand to metres in silt.

s1425.label: Evaporation and root uptake pull water up when K at the table depth permits: the maximum steady upward flux falls roughly as depth to the table raised to a power of 2-4

evidence.source: Gardner 1958, Soil Science 85:228-232
evidence.claim: Steady-state solutions for evaporation from a water table give a maximum flux decreasing as a power of the table depth set by the K(h) exponent.

s1426.label: Shallow groundwater can supply tens of percent of crop water use where the table is within about 1-2 m

evidence.source: Ayars, Christen, Soppe & Meyer 2006, Irrigation Science 24:147-160, The resource potential of in-situ shallow ground water use in irrigated agriculture
evidence.claim: Reported contributions of shallow groundwater to crop evapotranspiration range from a few percent to well above half, depending on depth, soil and salinity (estimate 10-70%).

s1427.label: Evaporation leaves salts behind so they accumulate at the surface when upward flux exceeds leaching; soil with ECe above 4 dS/m is called saline

evidence.source: US Salinity Laboratory Staff 1954, Diagnosis and Improvement of Saline and Alkali Soils, Agriculture Handbook 60
evidence.claim: Saline soils have saturation-extract electrical conductivity above 4 dS/m at 25 C.

s1428.label: Leaching requirement LR = ECiw / (5 ECe - ECiw): irrigating with 1 dS/m water on a crop tolerating ECe 4 dS/m needs about 5% extra water

evidence.source: Ayers & Westcot 1985, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29 Rev. 1, Water quality for agriculture
evidence.claim: LR = ECw/(5 ECe - ECw); with ECw 1 and ECe 4 this equals 1/19, about 5%.

s1429.label: Salts lower osmotic potential by about 0.036 MPa per dS/m and cut yield by roughly 7-12% per dS/m above threshold for wheat and maize

evidence.source: Maas & Hoffman 1977, Journal of the Irrigation and Drainage Division ASCE 103:115-134
evidence.claim: Maize threshold ECe 1.7 dS/m with 12% yield loss per dS/m; wheat threshold 6.0 with 7.1% per dS/m.

s1430.label: Lower transpiration and a surface salt crust cut upward flux, partly self-limiting the salinisation

evidence.source: Hillel 2000, Salinity Management for Sustainable Irrigation, World Bank
evidence.claim: Salinity reduces transpiration and surface crusts suppress evaporation, which damp further upward salt movement.

s1431.label: Secondary salinisation: rising water tables after clearing or irrigation bring salts into the root zone; drainage and lowering the table restore the soil

evidence.source: Rengasamy 2006, Journal of Experimental Botany 57:1017-1023, World salinization with emphasis on Australia
evidence.claim: Clearing deep-rooted vegetation raises water tables and mobilises stored salt, causing dryland salinity.

s1432.label: Earthworm drilosphere: gut passage, casts, middens and greenhouse gas effects

evidence.source: Brown, Barois & Lavelle 2000, European Journal of Soil Biology 36:177-198 (Regulation of soil organic matter dynamics and microbial activity in the drilosphere and the role of interactions with other edaphic functional domains)
evidence.claim: The drilosphere (casts, burrows, middens, gut) is a functional domain of enhanced microbial activity regulated by earthworms.

s1433.label: Start: Earthworm encounters litter and soil in moist conditions

evidence.source: Brown, Barois & Lavelle 2000, European Journal of Soil Biology 36:177-198 (Regulation of soil organic matter dynamics and microbial activity in the drilosphere and the role of interactions with other edaphic functional domains)
evidence.claim: The drilosphere (casts, burrows, middens, gut) is a functional domain of enhanced microbial activity regulated by earthworms.

s1434.label: End: Casts, burrows and nutrients change soil function

evidence.source: Brown, Barois & Lavelle 2000, European Journal of Soil Biology 36:177-198 (Regulation of soil organic matter dynamics and microbial activity in the drilosphere and the role of interactions with other edaphic functional domains)
evidence.claim: The drilosphere (casts, burrows, middens, gut) is a functional domain of enhanced microbial activity regulated by earthworms.

s1435.label: Worm ingests soil and litter, casting of the order of 10-40 tonnes per hectare per year in temperate pasture

evidence.source: Lavelle 1988, Biology and Fertility of Soils 6:237-251 (Earthworm activities and the soil system)
evidence.claim: Annual cast production ranges from a few to over 100 t per ha depending on species and climate; Darwin 1881 estimated roughly 10-20 t per ha in English pasture.

s1436.label: Gut mucus supplies easily used carbon that activates dormant soil microbes (the Sleeping Beauty effect) while digestion is partly mutualistic

evidence.source: Lavelle, Lattaud, Trigo & Barois 1995, Plant and Soil 170:23-33 (Mutualism and biodiversity in soils)
evidence.claim: Gut mucus provides a labile carbon source that wakes microbes, setting up an external rumen-like mutualism between worms and gut microbes.

s1437.label: Fresh casts are enriched in ammonium, nitrate, extractable phosphorus and microbial biomass compared with surrounding soil

evidence.source: Lee 1985, Earthworms: Their Ecology and Relationships with Soils and Land Use (Academic Press), ch. on effects on soil chemistry
evidence.claim: Casts typically have higher mineral N, available P, exchangeable cations and organic carbon than the soil they came from.

evidence.source: Martin 1991, Biology and Fertility of Soils 11:234-238 (Short-term and long-term effects of the endogeic earthworm Millsonia anomala on organic matter of a tropical soil)
evidence.claim: Fresh casts mineralise faster than soil, but aged compact casts protect organic carbon. Shares below are an estimate, not a measured partition.

s1439.label: Casts dry or age into compact, water-stable aggregates that physically protect organic carbon

evidence.source: Martin 1991, Biology and Fertility of Soils 11:234-238
evidence.claim: Compact casts of Millsonia anomala slowed the mineralisation of included organic matter over the long term.

s1440.label: Moist, nutrient-rich casts act as hotspots where nitrate reduction raises nitrous oxide and CO2 emission

evidence.source: Lubbers et al. 2013, Nature Climate Change 3:187-194 (Greenhouse-gas emissions from soils increased by earthworms)
evidence.claim: Meta-analysis found earthworm presence raised soil N2O emission by about 42% and CO2 emission by about 33% on average.

s1441.label: Burrow walls and linings hold more carbon, mucus and microbial activity than bulk soil (drilosphere)

evidence.source: Don et al. 2008, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 40:1803-1812 (Organic carbon sequestration in earthworm burrows)
evidence.claim: Burrow walls were enriched in organic carbon and nitrogen and had higher microbial activity than adjacent bulk soil.

s1442.label: Anecic worms (Lumbricus terrestris) build litter-and-cast middens at burrow entrances with higher microbial activity and N

evidence.source: Subler & Kirsch 1998, Biology and Fertility of Soils 26:243-249 (Spring dynamics of soil carbon, nitrogen, and microbial activity in earthworm middens in a no-till cornfield)
evidence.claim: Middens held more carbon, nitrogen and microbial biomass and activity than surrounding soil.

s1443.label: Higher mineral N and improved structure raise aboveground plant production by about 25% on average

evidence.source: van Groenigen et al. 2014, Scientific Reports 4:6365 (Earthworms increase plant production: a meta-analysis)
evidence.claim: Meta-analysis found earthworm presence raised crop yield by about 25% and aboveground biomass by about 23%, mainly via nitrogen and plant growth effects.

s1444.label: Non-native Lumbricus and Amynthas worms invading northern hardwood forests consume the forest floor and reduce its mass and thickness

evidence.source: Hale, Frelich, Reich & Pastor 2005, Ecosystems 8:911-927 (Effects of European earthworm invasion on soil characteristics in northern hardwood forests of Minnesota, USA)
evidence.claim: Where earthworms had invaded, forest floor mass fell sharply compared with uninvaded areas.

s1445.label: Tillage and some agrochemicals reduce earthworm abundance and species richness, especially anecic species

evidence.source: Chan 2001, Soil and Tillage Research 57:179-191 (An overview of some tillage impacts on earthworm population abundance and diversity)
evidence.claim: Conventional tillage lowers earthworm numbers relative to no-till, with large-bodied burrowing species most affected.

s1446.label: In dry or hot soil worms coil in mucus-lined chambers (aestivation) and cocoons carry the population

evidence.source: Edwards & Bohlen 1996, Biology and Ecology of Earthworms, 3rd ed. (Chapman & Hall), ch. on population dynamics and environmental factors
evidence.claim: Earthworms enter diapause or aestivation in dry or warm conditions and survive as cocoons.

s1447.label: Earthworm richness and abundance are higher at mid-latitudes with moist temperate climate than in many tropical sites

evidence.source: Phillips et al. 2019, Science 366:480-485 (Global distribution of earthworm diversity)
evidence.claim: Global mapping across 6,928 sites showed richness and abundance driven mainly by climate, with higher values in temperate regions.

s1448.label: Gas diffusion and air-filled porosity control of soil aeration

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, soil aeration chapter
evidence.claim: Gas exchange between soil and atmosphere is dominated by diffusion through air-filled pores.

s1449.label: Start: Gas diffusion and air-filled porosity control of soil aeration

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, soil aeration chapter
evidence.claim: Gas exchange between soil and atmosphere is dominated by diffusion through air-filled pores.

s1450.label: End: Gas diffusion and air-filled porosity control of soil aeration

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, soil aeration chapter
evidence.claim: Gas exchange between soil and atmosphere is dominated by diffusion through air-filled pores.

s1451.label: Fick's law: gas flux = -Ds dC/dz, where Ds is the soil gas diffusion coefficient

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics
evidence.claim: Diffusive flux is proportional to the concentration gradient with a soil-specific coefficient Ds below the free-air value D0.

s1452.label: Gases diffuse about 10,000 times faster in air than in water (O2 about 2e-5 versus 2e-9 m2/s), so water-filled pores block aeration

evidence.source: Glinski & Stepniewski 1985, Soil Aeration and Its Role for Plants, CRC Press
evidence.claim: Diffusion coefficients of O2 are about four orders of magnitude lower in water than in air.

s1453.label: Millington-Quirk model Ds/D0 = e^(10/3)/phi^2: at porosity 0.5, cutting air-filled porosity from 0.30 to 0.10 reduces Ds/D0 from about 0.07 to 0.002

evidence.source: Millington & Quirk 1961, Transactions of the Faraday Society 57:1200-1207
evidence.claim: Relative diffusivity Ds/D0 = epsilon^(10/3) / phi^2 (epsilon air-filled and phi total porosity); the quoted values follow by substitution.

s1454.label: Aeration is adequate above about 10% air-filled porosity, equivalent to an oxygen diffusion rate above about 0.2 microgram per cm2 per minute

evidence.source: Grable & Siemer 1968, Soil Science Society of America Journal 32:180-186
evidence.claim: Root elongation of corn declined when oxygen diffusion rate fell below about 0.2 microgram cm-2 min-1, which occurs near 10% air-filled porosity.

s1455.label: Respiration consumes O2 and produces CO2, so the steady-state CO2 excess scales with respiration divided by Ds: halving Ds doubles the excess

evidence.source: De Jong & Schappert 1972, Soil Science 113:328-333, Calculation of soil respiration and activity from CO2 profiles in the soil
evidence.claim: A diffusion-production model gives CO2 concentration at depth proportional to production rate divided by Ds.

s1456.label: Soil air at depth commonly holds 0.3-3% CO2, about 10 to 100 times atmospheric (0.04%)

evidence.source: Brady & Weil, The Nature and Properties of Soils, 15th ed., soil aeration section
evidence.claim: Soil air CO2 is often several tenths to a few percent, much higher than the atmosphere, with O2 correspondingly lower.

s1457.label: Wetting cuts Ds: aerobic activity peaks near 60% water-filled pore space and N2O production rises above it as denitrification takes over

evidence.source: Linn & Doran 1984, Soil Science Society of America Journal 48:1267-1272
evidence.claim: CO2 production was greatest near 60% water-filled pore space, whereas N2O production increased at higher values.

s1458.label: Aggregates wider than roughly 5-10 mm can hold anoxic cores in wet soil because O2 diffusing through water cannot meet microbial demand

evidence.source: Sexstone, Revsbech, Parkin & Tiedje 1985, Soil Science Society of America Journal 49:645-651
evidence.claim: Microelectrode profiles showed O2 depletion within a few millimetres of aggregate surfaces in wet soil and denitrification in the anoxic interiors.

s1459.label: Compaction and surface seals cut air-filled porosity and connectivity, lowering Ds and raising N2O emissions and lowering methane uptake

evidence.source: Ball, Scott & Parker 1999, Soil & Tillage Research 53:29-39
evidence.claim: Compacted wet soils had higher N2O fluxes and lower CH4 oxidation than uncompacted soil.

s1460.label: Soil thermal regime and heat flow

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, soil thermal regime chapters; Campbell & Norman 1998, An Introduction to Environmental Biophysics
evidence.claim: Soil temperature results from the surface energy balance and conduction of heat with water-dependent thermal properties.

s1461.label: Start: Soil thermal regime and heat flow

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, soil thermal regime chapters; Campbell & Norman 1998, An Introduction to Environmental Biophysics
evidence.claim: Soil temperature results from the surface energy balance and conduction of heat with water-dependent thermal properties.

s1462.label: End: Soil thermal regime and heat flow

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, soil thermal regime chapters; Campbell & Norman 1998, An Introduction to Environmental Biophysics
evidence.claim: Soil temperature results from the surface energy balance and conduction of heat with water-dependent thermal properties.

s1463.label: Net radiation splits into latent, sensible and ground heat flux; for grass reference surfaces ground heat flux is about 10% of net radiation by day and 50% at night

evidence.source: Allen, Pereira, Raes & Smith 1998, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, equations 45-46
evidence.claim: Hourly ground heat flux G = 0.1 Rn in daylight and 0.5 Rn at night for a grass reference surface.

s1464.label: Heat conducts by Fourier's law with thermal diffusivity D = lambda/C, typically 0.2-0.8e-6 m2/s in mineral soils

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics; Jury & Horton 2004, Soil Physics, 6th ed.
evidence.claim: Thermal diffusivity of soils is of order 1e-7 to 1e-6 m2/s and peaks at intermediate water content.

s1465.label: The daily temperature wave damps with depth: the amplitude falls by a factor e at d = sqrt(2D/omega), about 0.12 m (daily) and 2.2 m (annual) for D = 0.5e-6 m2/s, leaving under 5% of the surface daily swing below about 0.35 m

evidence.source: Campbell & Norman 1998, An Introduction to Environmental Biophysics, 2nd ed., soil temperature chapter
evidence.claim: Damping depth d = sqrt(2D/omega); with D = 0.5e-6 and omega = 7.27e-5 per s this gives 0.117 m, and 2.2 m for the annual wave (derived).

s1466.label: Water raises volumetric heat capacity (water 4.18, mineral about 2.0, air about 0.001 MJ per m3 per K), so wet soil warms more slowly than dry soil

evidence.source: De Vries 1963, in Van Wijk (ed.), Physics of Plant Environment, North-Holland; Hillel 1998
evidence.claim: Volumetric heat capacity of soil is the volume-weighted sum of solid, water and air components, dominated by water in wet soil.

s1467.label: Thermal conductivity rises steeply with water: dry sand about 0.3 W/m/K versus about 2-2.5 when saturated (quartz 7.7)

evidence.source: Farouki 1981, Thermal Properties of Soils, CRREL Monograph 81-1
evidence.claim: Dry sand conductivity is about 0.25-0.35 W/m/K; saturated sand reaches about 2-2.5 W/m/K as water bridges particle contacts.

s1468.label: Evaporation removes 2.45 MJ per mm, so wet bare soil stays cooler than dry soil, whose surface can exceed 50 C in summer sun

evidence.source: Hillel 1998, Environmental Soil Physics, soil temperature chapter
evidence.claim: Evaporative cooling and low heat capacity of dry surface layers make dry bare soils much hotter than moist ones at midday.

s1469.label: Snow insulates: with conductivity 0.1-0.5 W/m/K, about 30 cm of snow can hold soil near 0 C when air is -20 C

evidence.source: Zhang 2005, Reviews of Geophysics 43:RG4002, Influence of snow cover on the ground thermal regime
evidence.claim: Snow thermal conductivity is far below that of soil; deep snow cover decouples soil from winter air temperature and raises mean ground temperature by several degrees.

s1470.label: Lloyd-Taylor function: respiration proportional to exp[309/(T-227)] gives Q10 about 3.3 near 0-10 C, 2.3 near 10-20 C and 1.9 near 20-30 C

evidence.source: Lloyd & Taylor 1994, Functional Ecology 8:315-323
evidence.claim: Soil respiration fits R = Rref exp(E0 (1/(Tref-T0) - 1/(T-T0))) with E0 about 309 K and T0 about 227 K; Q10 values follow by substitution.

s1471.label: Warm soil speeds decomposition and nitrogen mineralisation and extends root and microbial activity

evidence.source: Davidson & Janssens 2006, Nature 440:165-173
evidence.claim: Decomposition of soil organic matter is temperature sensitive, with kinetic Q10 of about 2 modulated by substrate availability.

s1472.label: Warming-driven soil carbon loss is estimated at about 55 Pg C by 2050 in the top metre

evidence.source: Crowther et al. 2016, Nature 540:104-108, Quantifying global soil carbon losses in response to warming
evidence.claim: Meta-analysis scaled to global soil carbon stocks gave about 55 Pg C loss by 2050 under a 1 C rise, with largest losses in cold regions.

s1473.label: Northern permafrost soils hold about 1,300 Pg C (range 1,100-1,500), more than the atmosphere

evidence.source: Hugelius et al. 2014, Biogeosciences 11:6573-6593
evidence.claim: Northern circumpolar permafrost region stores about 1,300 Pg C with quantified uncertainty 1,100-1,500.

s1474.label: Deeper summer thaw exposes frozen organic matter to decomposition, releasing CO2 and methane; 5-15% of permafrost carbon may be released by 2100 under high emissions

evidence.source: Schuur et al. 2015, Nature 520:171-179, Climate change and the permafrost carbon feedback
evidence.claim: Expert assessment projects release of about 5-15% of permafrost carbon by 2100 under high-emission scenarios.

s1475.label: Shrink-swell cycles and crack dynamics in clay soils

evidence.source: Coulombe, Wilding & Dixon 1996, Advances in Agronomy 57:289-375, Overview of Vertisols: characteristics and impacts on society
evidence.claim: Vertisols swell and crack seasonally, producing slickensides, gilgai and distinctive hydrology.

s1476.label: Start: Shrink-swell cycles and crack dynamics in clay soils

evidence.source: Coulombe, Wilding & Dixon 1996, Advances in Agronomy 57:289-375, Overview of Vertisols: characteristics and impacts on society
evidence.claim: Vertisols swell and crack seasonally, producing slickensides, gilgai and distinctive hydrology.

s1477.label: End: Shrink-swell cycles and crack dynamics in clay soils

evidence.source: Coulombe, Wilding & Dixon 1996, Advances in Agronomy 57:289-375, Overview of Vertisols: characteristics and impacts on society
evidence.claim: Vertisols swell and crack seasonally, producing slickensides, gilgai and distinctive hydrology.

s1478.label: Wetting hydrates the cations between smectite layers: Ca-smectite swells to about 1.9 nm basal spacing, whereas Na-smectite at low salt swells osmotically beyond 4 nm

evidence.source: Norrish 1954, Discussions of the Faraday Society 18:120-134, The swelling of montmorillonite
evidence.claim: Ca-montmorillonite expands in discrete steps to about 1.9 nm, whereas Na-montmorillonite swells osmotically to much larger spacings at low electrolyte concentration.

s1479.label: Shrinkage curve: after a structural phase, volume loss in the proportional phase equals water loss (slope near 1), then residual and zero shrinkage

evidence.source: Haines 1923, Journal of Agricultural Science 13:296-310; Peng & Horn 2005, Soil Science Society of America Journal 69:584-592
evidence.claim: Soil shrinkage curves have structural, proportional, residual and zero shrinkage phases; in the proportional phase volume change equals water volume change.

s1480.label: COLE = (moist length / dry length) - 1; classes: under 0.03 low, 0.03-0.06 moderate, 0.06-0.09 high, 0.09 or more very high

evidence.source: Soil Survey Staff 2014, Keys to Soil Taxonomy, 12th ed.; Grossman et al. 1968, Soil Science Society of America Proceedings 32:570-573
evidence.claim: Linear extensibility of 3, 6 and 9 cm per 100 cm marks the moderate, high and very high classes, from clod bulk density at 33 kPa and dry.

s1481.label: Vertisols need at least 30% clay, cracks at least 1 cm wide at 50 cm depth when dry, and slickensides or wedge-shaped peds

evidence.source: Soil Survey Staff 2014, Keys to Soil Taxonomy, 12th ed., Vertisols
evidence.claim: Vertisols have 30% or more clay in all horizons to 50 cm, deep wide cracks when dry, and slickensides or wedge-shaped aggregates.

s1482.label: Drying shrinks the soil, first as vertical subsidence then as cracks; total shrinkage is split between subsidence and crack volume by a geometry factor between 1 (vertical only) and 3 (isotropic)

evidence.source: Bronswijk 1988, Journal of Hydrology 97:199-212; Bronswijk 1991, Soil Science Society of America Journal 55:1220-1226
evidence.claim: Crack volume derives from the volume change not expressed as subsidence, set by a geometry factor of 1-3.

s1483.label: Cracks act as evaporation channels, so drying reaches deeper layers and cracks extend deeper

evidence.source: Adams & Hanks 1964, Soil Science Society of America Proceedings 28:281-284, Evaporation from soil shrinkage cracks
evidence.claim: Shrinkage cracks substantially increase evaporation from clay soil by exposing deeper wet surfaces.

s1484.label: First rain after drought runs down cracks as bypass flow and wets the subsoil from below before the matrix swells

evidence.source: Bouma & Dekker 1978, Geoderma 20:27-40; Beven & Germann 1982, Water Resources Research 18:1311-1325
evidence.claim: Infiltration into dry cracked clay is initially rapid through cracks, followed by sharp decline as swelling closes them.

s1485.label: Swelling closes the cracks within hours to days, collapsing infiltration capacity so ponding and runoff rise

evidence.source: Bouma & Dekker 1978, Geoderma 20:27-40
evidence.claim: Infiltration rate of a dry clay fell by orders of magnitude within hours as cracks swelled shut.

s1486.label: Repeated shrink-swell shears the soil along oblique planes, forming slickensides, wedge-shaped peds and gilgai microrelief

evidence.source: Coulombe, Wilding & Dixon 1996, Advances in Agronomy 57:289-375
evidence.claim: Slickensides and gilgai are diagnostic products of seasonal swelling pressure in smectitic soils.

s1487.label: Surface granulation (self-mulching) and material falling into cracks churn the profile, slowing horizon differentiation

evidence.source: Wilding & Tessier 1988, in Wilding & Puentes (eds), Vertisols: their distribution, properties, classification and management, Texas A&M
evidence.claim: Pedoturbation by shrink-swell mixes surface and subsoil, limiting profile development in Vertisols.

s1488.label: Swelling pressure lifts and cracks foundations, roads and pipes; expansive soils cost the USA about 2.3 billion dollars per year (1973 estimate)

evidence.source: Jones & Holtz 1973, Civil Engineering 43(8):49-51, Expansive soils - the hidden disaster
evidence.claim: Estimated annual damage in the United States of about 2.3 billion dollars from expansive soils.

s1489.label: Soil compaction: stress, density, root limitation and recovery

evidence.source: Batey 2009, Soil Use and Management 25:335-345, Soil compaction and soil management - a review
evidence.claim: Compaction lowers porosity, aeration and infiltration, restricts root growth and can last for many years.

s1490.label: Start: Soil compaction: stress, density, root limitation and recovery

evidence.source: Batey 2009, Soil Use and Management 25:335-345, Soil compaction and soil management - a review
evidence.claim: Compaction lowers porosity, aeration and infiltration, restricts root growth and can last for many years.

s1491.label: End: Soil compaction: stress, density, root limitation and recovery

evidence.source: Batey 2009, Soil Use and Management 25:335-345, Soil compaction and soil management - a review
evidence.claim: Compaction lowers porosity, aeration and infiltration, restricts root growth and can last for many years.

s1492.label: Axle and tyre loads or hooves apply stress; contact stress near the surface is about the tyre inflation pressure (roughly 50-250 kPa) and heavy axles above about 6 Mg compact subsoil below 0.4 m

evidence.source: Soane & van Ouwerkerk 1994, Soil Compaction in Crop Production, Elsevier; Hakansson & Reeder 1994, Soil & Tillage Research 29:277-304
evidence.claim: Surface stress approximates tyre inflation pressure; stress penetrates deeper with axle load, so high axle loads compact the subsoil.

s1493.label: Compaction is greatest at an intermediate water content (Proctor optimum), where water lubricates grains but does not yet carry the load

evidence.source: Proctor 1933, Engineering News-Record 111:245-248; Soane et al. 1981, Soil & Tillage Research 1:207-237
evidence.claim: Dry density after a given compactive effort peaks at the optimum water content and declines on either side.

s1494.label: Bulk density rises and porosity phi = 1 - rho_b/2.65 falls (1.3 to 1.6 g/cm3 takes porosity from 51% to 40%), mostly at the expense of macropores

evidence.source: Brady & Weil, The Nature and Properties of Soils, 15th ed., ch. 4; Alaoui, Lipiec & Gerke 2011, Soil & Tillage Research 115-116:1-15
evidence.claim: Porosity follows from bulk density and a particle density of 2.65 g/cm3; compaction collapses the largest pores first.

s1495.label: Penetration resistance rises; root elongation is strongly limited above about 2 MPa and a penetrometer reads 2-8 times the pressure that roots experience

evidence.source: Bengough & Mullins 1990, Journal of Soil Science 41:341-358
evidence.claim: Penetrometer resistance exceeds root growth pressure by a factor of 2-8; 2 MPa commonly marks severe restriction.

s1496.label: Saturated conductivity and air-filled porosity fall, often by one to two orders of magnitude, as continuous macropores are lost

evidence.source: Alaoui, Lipiec & Gerke 2011, Soil & Tillage Research 115-116:1-15
evidence.claim: Compaction reduces macroporosity, pore continuity and saturated hydraulic conductivity, sometimes by orders of magnitude.

s1497.label: Roots stay shallow and take up less water and nutrients; reported yield losses range 2.5-50% across crops

evidence.source: Hamza & Anderson 2005, Soil & Tillage Research 82:121-145
evidence.claim: Review of compaction effects on crop growth reports yield reductions between about 2.5% and 50%.

s1498.label: Wet compacted soil turns anaerobic and emits more N2O by denitrification

evidence.source: Ball, Scott & Parker 1999, Soil & Tillage Research 53:29-39
evidence.claim: Field N2O fluxes were higher in compacted soil because of reduced aeration.

s1499.label: Reduced infiltration raises runoff, ponding and erosion

evidence.source: Batey 2009, Soil Use and Management 25:335-345
evidence.claim: Compaction lowers infiltration and increases surface runoff and erosion risk.

s1500.label: Subsoil compaction below the tilled layer persists for more than a decade because it escapes tillage and has little frost or biological action

evidence.source: Hakansson & Reeder 1994, Soil & Tillage Research 29:277-304
evidence.claim: Effects of heavy-axle compaction below the plough layer remained after many years.

s1501.label: Natural recovery by freeze-thaw, wet-dry cycles, deep perennial roots and earthworm burrowing slowly rebuilds pores

evidence.source: Dexter 1991, Soil & Tillage Research 20:87-100, Amelioration of soil by natural processes
evidence.claim: Wetting-drying, freezing-thawing and biological activity are the natural agents loosening compacted soil.

s1502.label: Controlled traffic farming confines wheels to permanent lanes covering roughly 15-20% of the field instead of most of it

evidence.source: Tullberg, Yule & McGarry 2007, Soil & Tillage Research 97:272-281
evidence.claim: Controlled traffic confines wheel compaction to permanent lanes and reduces trafficked area to a small fraction of the field.

s1503.label: Soil protists: flagellates, amoebae and ciliates as selective bacterial grazers

evidence.source: Geisen et al. 2018, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 42:293-323 (Soil protists: a fertile frontier in soil biology research)
evidence.claim: Soil protists include phagotrophs, phototrophs and parasites across several supergroups, and bacterivorous protists shape bacterial communities and nutrient cycling.

s1504.label: Start: Bacteria in a water film meet protist grazers

evidence.source: Geisen et al. 2018, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 42:293-323 (Soil protists: a fertile frontier in soil biology research)
evidence.claim: Soil protists include phagotrophs, phototrophs and parasites across several supergroups, and bacterivorous protists shape bacterial communities and nutrient cycling.

s1505.label: End: Prey community reshaped and nitrogen released

evidence.source: Geisen et al. 2018, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 42:293-323 (Soil protists: a fertile frontier in soil biology research)
evidence.claim: Soil protists include phagotrophs, phototrophs and parasites across several supergroups, and bacterivorous protists shape bacterial communities and nutrient cycling.

s1506.label: Active protists reach about 10^4-10^6 per gram of soil, mostly flagellates and naked amoebae, with fewer ciliates and testate amoebae

evidence.source: Foissner 1999, Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment 74:95-112 (Soil protozoa as bioindicators: pros and cons, methods, diversity, representative examples)
evidence.claim: Typical soils hold thousands to hundreds of thousands of flagellates and amoebae per gram, with ciliates and testate amoebae less numerous.

s1507.label: Which protist group dominates the grazing in the pore

evidence.source: Foissner 1999, Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment 74:95-112
evidence.claim: Groups differ in numbers by soil type and moisture. Shares below are an estimate, not a measured census.

s1508.label: Flagellates (Cercomonas, Spumella) graze suspended bacteria in water films and move through narrow pores

evidence.source: Geisen et al. 2018, FEMS Microbiology Reviews 42:293-323
evidence.claim: Heterotrophic flagellates are small, fast-growing grazers of free bacteria.

s1509.label: Naked amoebae (Acanthamoeba, Naegleria) crawl over surfaces and graze attached bacteria and biofilm

evidence.source: Foissner 1999, Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment 74:95-112
evidence.claim: Naked amoebae are the most common protist group in many soils and feed on surface-attached bacteria.

s1510.label: Ciliates and testate amoebae need larger water-filled pores or litter and graze larger prey including other protists

evidence.source: Foissner 1999, Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment 74:95-112
evidence.claim: Ciliates need wetter, larger habitat and are less frequent in dry mineral soil.

s1511.label: Grazing is selective: protists reject large, filamentous, pigmented or toxic cells, so grazing shifts bacterial community structure

evidence.source: Ronn, McCaig, Griffiths & Prosser 2002, Applied and Environmental Microbiology 68:6094-6105 (Impact of protozoan grazing on bacterial community structure in soil microcosms)
evidence.claim: Protozoan grazing in soil microcosms changed bacterial community composition rather than only reducing numbers.

s1512.label: Pseudomonas produce toxins (2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol, hydrogen cyanide) and other metabolites that help them escape protist grazing

evidence.source: Jousset, Lara, Wall & Valverde 2006, Applied and Environmental Microbiology 72:7083-7090 (Secondary metabolites help biocontrol strain Pseudomonas fluorescens CHA0 to escape protozoan grazing)
evidence.claim: Antibiotic metabolites of strain CHA0 reduced grazing losses and survival of protozoa.

s1513.label: Surplus nitrogen from bacterial prey is excreted as ammonium, and grazed rhizosphere communities favour auxin-producing bacteria that branch roots

evidence.source: Bonkowski 2004, New Phytologist 162:617-631 (Protozoa and plant growth: the microbial loop in soil revisited)
evidence.claim: Protozoa increase nitrogen availability and shift bacteria toward auxin-producing types, raising root branching and plant growth beyond nitrogen release alone.

s1514.label: When water or food runs out, protists encyst, and cysts survive drying and years of dormancy

evidence.source: Foissner 1987, Progress in Protistology 2:69-212 (Soil protozoa: fundamental problems, ecological significance, adaptations in ciliates and testaceans, bioindicators, and guide to the literature)
evidence.claim: Soil protozoa form resistant cysts that survive desiccation and long periods without food.

s1515.label: Resistant prey (toxic, large or biofilm-embedded) dominate after heavy grazing, which lowers food for the grazers

evidence.source: Jousset et al. 2006, Applied and Environmental Microbiology 72:7083-7090
evidence.claim: Defended strains persisted under grazing, while palatable strains declined.

s1516.label: White-rot and brown-rot fungi: two routes to lignin and cellulose decay

evidence.source: Floudas et al. 2012, Science 336:1715, The Paleozoic origin of enzymatic lignin decomposition reconstructed from 31 fungal genomes
evidence.claim: White-rot fungi carry class II peroxidases; brown-rot lineages lost them.

s1517.label: Start: White-rot and brown-rot fungi: two routes to lignin and cellulose decay

evidence.source: Floudas et al. 2012, Science 336:1715, The Paleozoic origin of enzymatic lignin decomposition reconstructed from 31 fungal genomes
evidence.claim: White-rot fungi carry class II peroxidases; brown-rot lineages lost them.

s1518.label: End: White-rot and brown-rot fungi: two routes to lignin and cellulose decay

evidence.source: Floudas et al. 2012, Science 336:1715, The Paleozoic origin of enzymatic lignin decomposition reconstructed from 31 fungal genomes
evidence.claim: White-rot fungi carry class II peroxidases; brown-rot lineages lost them.

s1519.label: White-rot basidiomycetes secrete class II peroxidases (lignin, manganese, versatile) and laccases that oxidize lignin and leave a pale, cellulose-rich residue

evidence.source: Floudas et al. 2012, Science 336:1715
evidence.claim: Class II peroxidases are the signature enzymes of white-rot Agaricomycetes.

s1520.label: Manganese peroxidase oxidizes Mn(II) to Mn(III) chelated by oxalate, a diffusible oxidant that attacks lignin beyond the enzyme's reach

evidence.source: Hofrichter 2002, Enzyme and Microbial Technology 30:454, Review: lignin conversion by manganese peroxidase
evidence.claim: Chelated Mn(III) acts as a diffusible mediator oxidizing phenolic lignin units.

s1521.label: Brown-rot fungi lack class II peroxidases and use Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2 gives hydroxyl radicals) to depolymerize cellulose, leaving modified lignin

evidence.source: Eastwood et al. 2011, Science 333:762, The plant cell wall-decomposing machinery underlies the functional diversity of forest fungi
evidence.claim: Brown-rot genomes have reduced oxidative and cellulolytic enzyme sets and rely on oxidative radical chemistry.

s1522.label: Hypothesis: class II peroxidases arose about 295 million years ago, coinciding with the end of major coal formation (competing explanations exist)

evidence.source: Floudas et al. 2012, Science 336:1715
evidence.claim: Molecular clock places the origin of lignin-degrading peroxidases near the Carboniferous-Permian boundary.

s1523.label: Lignin is co-metabolized: fungi need cellulose or another carbon source and H2O2 from oxidases; lignin alone does not support growth

evidence.source: Kirk & Farrell 1987, Annual Review of Microbiology 41:465, Enzymatic combustion: the microbial degradation of lignin
evidence.claim: Ligninolysis is a secondary-metabolic, co-metabolic process that exposes cellulose rather than feeding on lignin.

s1524.label: Partly oxidized lignin fragments and fungal melanin enter the dissolved pool and can become humic precursors

evidence.source: Kogel-Knabner 2002, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 34:139, The macromolecular organic composition of plant and microbial residues as inputs to soil organic matter
evidence.claim: Lignin-derived and microbial residues contribute aromatic and phenolic structures to soil organic matter.

s1525.label: Mineral nitrogen released as litter decays represses ligninolytic enzymes and phenol oxidase in lignin-rich litter, slowing late-stage decay while speeding early cellulose decay

evidence.source: Carreiro, Sinsabaugh, Repert & Parkhurst 2000, Ecology 81:2359, Microbial enzyme shifts explain litter decay responses to simulated nitrogen deposition
evidence.claim: N additions raised cellulase but lowered phenol oxidase activity in high-lignin litter, slowing late-stage decay.

s1526.label: Cord-forming mycelial networks: foraging, translocation and rerouting

evidence.source: Boddy 1999, Mycologia 91:13, Saprotrophic cord-forming fungi: meeting the challenge of heterogeneous environments
evidence.claim: Cord-forming fungi forage with fans of hyphae and translocate nutrients between resource patches.

s1527.label: Start: Cord-forming mycelial networks: foraging, translocation and rerouting

evidence.source: Boddy 1999, Mycologia 91:13, Saprotrophic cord-forming fungi: meeting the challenge of heterogeneous environments
evidence.claim: Cord-forming fungi forage with fans of hyphae and translocate nutrients between resource patches.

s1528.label: End: Cord-forming mycelial networks: foraging, translocation and rerouting

evidence.source: Boddy 1999, Mycologia 91:13, Saprotrophic cord-forming fungi: meeting the challenge of heterogeneous environments
evidence.claim: Cord-forming fungi forage with fans of hyphae and translocate nutrients between resource patches.

s1529.label: Cord-forming basidiomycetes (Phanerochaete velutina, Hypholoma fasciculare) explore soil as fans of fine hyphae from a resource base

evidence.source: Boddy 1999, Mycologia 91:13
evidence.claim: Foraging mycelia form search fans that explore soil beyond the colonized resource.

s1530.label: Reaching a nutrient-rich patch triggers hyphal proliferation there and thickening of cords back to the base

evidence.source: Fricker, Boddy & Bebber 2007, in Howard & Gow (eds), Biology of the Fungal Cell, Springer, Network organisation of mycelial fungi
evidence.claim: Links to successful patches are reinforced while the search front elsewhere remains sparse.

s1531.label: Cords and rhizomorphs translocate carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus over decimetres to metres, driven by source-sink gradients

evidence.source: Wells & Boddy 1990, New Phytologist 116:285, Wood decay, and phosphorus and fungal biomass allocation, in mycelial cord systems
evidence.claim: Radiolabelled phosphorus was moved through cords between wood blocks and soil over tens of centimetres.

s1532.label: Fungi import soil nitrogen into N-poor surface litter and speed its decomposition (fungal translocation in no-till residue)

evidence.source: Frey, Elliott, Paustian & Bethlenfalvay 2000, Soil Biology and Biochemistry 32:689, Fungal translocation as a mechanism for soil nitrogen inputs to surface residue decomposition in a no-tillage agroecosystem
evidence.claim: Labelled 15N moved from soil into surface residue through fungal hyphae.

s1533.label: Unused links are pruned and their contents recycled, concentrating flux on productive paths

evidence.source: Bebber, Hynes, Darrah, Boddy & Fricker 2007, Proceedings of the Royal Society B 274:2307, Biological solutions to transport network design
evidence.claim: Mycelial networks reinforce used links and prune others, giving efficient, resilient topology.

s1534.label: After grazing or cutting, redundant loops reroute transport and the network stays connected

evidence.source: Fricker, Bebber & Boddy 2008, in Boddy, Frankland & van West (eds), Ecology of Saprotrophic Basidiomycetes, Elsevier, Mycelial networks: structure and dynamics
evidence.claim: Looped network structure gives fault tolerance to damage.

s1535.label: Ectomycorrhizal organic nitrogen mining and the Gadgil effect

evidence.source: Lindahl & Tunlid 2015, New Phytologist 205:1443, Ectomycorrhizal fungi: potential organic matter decomposers, yet not saprotrophs
evidence.claim: Ectomycorrhizal fungi retain oxidative enzymes to mobilize organic N but get carbon from their host.

s1536.label: Start: Ectomycorrhizal organic nitrogen mining and the Gadgil effect

evidence.source: Lindahl & Tunlid 2015, New Phytologist 205:1443, Ectomycorrhizal fungi: potential organic matter decomposers, yet not saprotrophs
evidence.claim: Ectomycorrhizal fungi retain oxidative enzymes to mobilize organic N but get carbon from their host.

s1537.label: End: Ectomycorrhizal organic nitrogen mining and the Gadgil effect

evidence.source: Lindahl & Tunlid 2015, New Phytologist 205:1443, Ectomycorrhizal fungi: potential organic matter decomposers, yet not saprotrophs
evidence.claim: Ectomycorrhizal fungi retain oxidative enzymes to mobilize organic N but get carbon from their host.

s1538.label: Ectomycorrhizal fungi (Cortinarius, Russula, Suillus) secrete peroxidases and proteases that mine organic nitrogen from soil organic matter

evidence.source: Bodeker et al. 2014, New Phytologist 203:245, Ectomycorrhizal Cortinarius species participate in enzymatic oxidation of humus in northern forest ecosystems
evidence.claim: Cortinarius species expressed Mn peroxidase genes and oxidized humus in boreal forest soil.

s1539.label: Fungi retain much of the mined nitrogen and pass only part to the tree when fungal N demand is high, aggravating tree N limitation

evidence.source: Nasholm, Hogberg, Franklin, Metcalfe, Gruffman, Ishida, Hogberg, Wallander 2013, New Phytologist 198:214, Are ectomycorrhizal fungi alleviating or aggravating nitrogen limitation of tree growth in boreal forests?
evidence.claim: Fungal N retention can lower N delivered to the host at low soil N.

s1540.label: Ectomycorrhizal fungi compete with free-living decomposers for N and may slow decomposition (the Gadgil effect): trenching to remove ectomycorrhizal roots raised litter mass loss in a pine plantation

evidence.source: Gadgil & Gadgil 1971, Nature 233:133, Mycorrhiza and litter decomposition
evidence.claim: Litter decomposed faster in trenched plots without mycorrhizal roots than in untrenched plots.

s1541.label: Evidence for the Gadgil effect is mixed: trenching also changes soil moisture and root input, confounding the result

evidence.source: Fernandez & Kennedy 2016, New Phytologist 209:1382, Revisiting the Gadgil effect: do interguild fungal interactions control carbon cycling in forest soils?
evidence.claim: Reviewed trenching studies; results varied and moisture and other confounders were common.

s1542.label: Ecosystems dominated by ectomycorrhizal and ericoid plants store about 70% more soil carbon per unit nitrogen than arbuscular-dominated ones

evidence.source: Averill, Turner & Finzi 2014, Nature 505:543, Mycorrhiza-mediated competition between plants and decomposers drives soil carbon storage
evidence.claim: Soil C per unit N was about 70% higher in ectomycorrhizal and ericoid than in arbuscular mycorrhizal systems in a global dataset.

s1543.label: Carbon cost to the host: roughly 10-20% of net primary production goes to ectomycorrhizal fungi (estimate)

evidence.source: Hobbie 2006, Ecology 87:563, Carbon allocation to ectomycorrhizal fungi correlates with belowground allocation in culture studies
evidence.claim: Isotope and allocation estimates place ectomycorrhizal carbon use at roughly 10-20% of NPP, with wide uncertainty.

s1544.label: Common mycorrhizal networks: what the evidence supports and what it does not

evidence.source: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema 2023, Nature Ecology and Evolution 7:501, Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests
evidence.claim: Review of the evidence for common mycorrhizal networks and their interpretation.

s1545.label: Start: Common mycorrhizal networks: what the evidence supports and what it does not

evidence.source: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema 2023, Nature Ecology and Evolution 7:501, Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests
evidence.claim: Review of the evidence for common mycorrhizal networks and their interpretation.

s1546.label: End: Common mycorrhizal networks: what the evidence supports and what it does not

evidence.source: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema 2023, Nature Ecology and Evolution 7:501, Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests
evidence.claim: Review of the evidence for common mycorrhizal networks and their interpretation.

s1547.label: Hyphae of one fungal genet can connect the roots of different plants, forming a common mycorrhizal network

evidence.source: Selosse, Richard, He & Simard 2006, Trends in Ecology and Evolution 21:621, Mycorrhizal networks: des liaisons dangereuses?
evidence.claim: Shared fungal genets link plants in the field, but network function is not established by presence alone.

s1548.label: Isotope labelling showed net carbon transfer from paper birch to Douglas-fir through ectomycorrhizal hyphae, but soil and other routes are hard to exclude

evidence.source: Simard et al. 1997, Nature 388:579, Net transfer of carbon between ectomycorrhizal tree species in the field
evidence.claim: 13C and 14C labelling detected carbon movement between species in both directions with a net transfer in one direction.

s1549.label: Seedlings connected to mature trees survived or grew better in some field experiments

evidence.source: Booth & Hoeksema 2010, Ecology 91:2294, Mycorrhizal networks counteract competitive effects of canopy trees on seedling survival
evidence.claim: Seedlings with access to the canopy tree network had higher survival than those isolated by mesh barriers.

s1550.label: Re-examinations find the mother-tree claim of large, adaptive carbon sharing weakly supported and overstated in citations

evidence.source: Henriksson et al. 2023, New Phytologist 239:19, Re-examining the evidence for the mother tree hypothesis: resource sharing among trees via ectomycorrhizal networks
evidence.claim: Concluded that evidence for resource sharing that benefits receiving trees is limited, and field proof of fitness gains is lacking.

s1551.label: Arbuscular fungal networks move phosphorus from resource-rich to resource-poor patches in controlled experiments

evidence.source: Whiteside et al. 2019, Current Biology 29:2043, Mycorrhizal fungi respond to resource inequality by moving phosphorus from rich to poor patches across networks
evidence.claim: Fungal networks in root organ culture shifted P toward nutrient-poor patches.

s1552.label: Biological soil crusts: cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses on dryland surfaces

evidence.source: Elbert et al. 2012, Nature Geoscience 5:459, Contribution of cryptogamic covers to the global cycles of carbon and nitrogen
evidence.claim: Cryptogamic covers fix about 49 Tg N per year and take up about 3.9 Pg C per year.

s1553.label: Start: Biological soil crusts: cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses on dryland surfaces

evidence.source: Elbert et al. 2012, Nature Geoscience 5:459, Contribution of cryptogamic covers to the global cycles of carbon and nitrogen
evidence.claim: Cryptogamic covers fix about 49 Tg N per year and take up about 3.9 Pg C per year.

s1554.label: End: Biological soil crusts: cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses on dryland surfaces

evidence.source: Elbert et al. 2012, Nature Geoscience 5:459, Contribution of cryptogamic covers to the global cycles of carbon and nitrogen
evidence.claim: Cryptogamic covers fix about 49 Tg N per year and take up about 3.9 Pg C per year.

s1555.label: Filamentous cyanobacteria (Microcoleus vaginatus) pioneer bare dryland soil and bind particles with polysaccharide sheaths after wetting

evidence.source: Belnap & Gardner 1993, Great Basin Naturalist 53:40, Soil microstructure in soils of the Colorado Plateau: the role of the cyanobacterium Microcoleus vaginatus
evidence.claim: Sheath-forming filaments bind sand and silt into a coherent surface layer.

s1556.label: Cryptogamic covers (crusts, lichens, mosses) fix about 49 Tg N per year and take up about 3.9 Pg C per year globally

evidence.source: Elbert et al. 2012, Nature Geoscience 5:459
evidence.claim: Global estimate of cryptogamic N fixation near 49 Tg per year and C uptake near 3.9 Pg per year.

s1557.label: Crusts raise the threshold wind speed for erosion and trap dust that carries nutrients

evidence.source: Belnap & Gillette 1998, Journal of Arid Environments 39:133, Vulnerability of desert biological soil crusts to wind erosion: the influences of crust development, soil texture, and disturbance
evidence.claim: Well-developed crusts raised the threshold friction velocity for sand movement; disturbance lowered it sharply.

s1558.label: Crust effects on infiltration vary: rough lichen and moss crusts raise infiltration, smooth cyanobacterial crusts on fine soils can reduce it

evidence.source: Belnap 2006, Hydrological Processes 20:3159, The potential roles of biological soil crusts in dryland hydrologic cycles
evidence.claim: Crust morphology and soil texture decide whether infiltration is raised or lowered.

s1559.label: Fixed nitrogen leaks as ammonium and amino acids to the soil beneath and neighbouring plants and microbes

evidence.source: Belnap 2003, in Belnap & Lange (eds), Biological Soil Crusts: Structure, Function, and Management, Springer, The world at your feet: desert biological soil crusts
evidence.claim: Crusts are major nitrogen and carbon sources in nutrient-poor dryland soils.

s1560.label: Trampling, vehicles and fire crush crusts; cyanobacterial crust recovers in years to decades, mosses and lichens in decades to centuries (wide ranges)

evidence.source: Belnap & Eldridge 2003, in Belnap & Lange (eds), Biological Soil Crusts: Structure, Function, and Management, Springer, Disturbance and recovery of biological soil crusts
evidence.claim: Recovery times range from a few years for cyanobacterial cover to many decades for lichens and mosses.

s1561.label: Crust loss lets wind erosion bury and abrade remaining crust, increasing dust and lowering soil fertility

evidence.source: Belnap & Gillette 1997, Land Degradation and Development 8:355, Disturbance of biological soil crusts: impacts on potential wind erodibility of sandy desert soils in southeastern Utah
evidence.claim: Crushed crusts raised potential wind erodibility by an order of magnitude or more.

s1562.label: Predatory bacteria: Bdellovibrio and Myxococcus hunting soil prey

evidence.source: Hungate et al. 2021, mBio 12:e00466-21 (The functional significance of bacterial predators)
